**The split-off `[Fact]`** (`WhenTheRaisedLockRemainsUnavailable_TheCallEndsInAnHonestToolFailureAtItsOwnBudget`,
`CardFindingRecordConcurrencyTests.cs:266-289`) is fine: two events, plant-then-await, no interleaving,
still asserts the finding was never written through the planted lock.

**Blocker — the rewritten proof has a real, currently-live race that can pass vacuously against the
exact defect it exists to catch.**

`WhenTheRaisedLockIsUnavailable_TheFindingLockIsReleasedBetweenRetries_NotHeldWhileWaiting`
(`CardFindingRecordConcurrencyTests.cs:214-256`) starts `recordTask` via `Task.Run` (line 226) and, with
**no synchronization or delay at all**, immediately runs the load-bearing blocking probe
(`CardLock.Acquire(findingPath, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5))`, line 237). The removed `Task.Delay(400ms)`
from the old version existed for exactly one reason, stated in its own comment: "give the call time to
acquire the finding's lock at least once ... i.e. to be genuinely inside its retry loop, not merely about
to start." That guarantee was deleted and not replaced.

Trace what happens under contention (the same contention this whole remediation exists to survive — the
architect's diagnosis showed real multi-second scheduling overshoot on this exact suite under
`make gates`): `Task.Run` only *enqueues* the delegate; on a loaded thread pool it can sit unscheduled for
a non-trivial window while the calling thread — already running, no dispatch needed — proceeds straight
to line 237. `CardLock.Acquire` on an as-yet-untouched lock file succeeds in microseconds. So if
`recordTask`'s delegate has not yet reached `AcquireLocksAndRecord`'s first `CardLock.Acquire(findingPath,
...)` by the time line 237 runs, the probe acquires an uncontended lock, disposes it, and the assertion
passes — **having tested nothing**, because a hypothetical hold-it-continuously implementation hasn't had
the chance to grab the lock yet either. The two assertions that follow (`recordTask.IsCompleted` false,
`File.Exists(findingPath)` false) don't rescue this: under the defect, once the call *does* start, it
grabs `findingPath`'s lock, holds it while blocked on the planted `raisedPath` lock (never releasing, by
construction of the defect), so `IsCompleted` stays false and the finding stays unwritten regardless of
whether the earlier probe ever contended with anything real. Nothing after line 237 forces the probe to
have coincided with an actual hold.

This is not a hypothetical corner: it is structurally the same failure mode the architect just diagnosed
one level up — a proof whose truth depends on winning or losing a race against scheduling, rather than on
the property actually being exercised. The direction is just flipped: the old test could fail red over
working code; this one can pass green over broken code, silently, on exactly the runs where the thread
pool is busiest — which on this suite is a demonstrated, not theoretical, condition.

**What would close this:** give the probe (or the test) a way to know `recordTask` has actually reached
its retry loop before line 237 runs, rather than assuming it by omission of delay. Cheapest test-only
fix without touching production code: don't single-shot the probe — poll it (e.g. loop
`CardLock.Acquire(findingPath, TimeSpan.Zero)` with a short sleep between attempts) until either it
succeeds *after* first failing at least once (proving the lock was actually contended, i.e. the call was
genuinely inside its window), or a generous overall budget (well under the 30s call budget) is exhausted,
which itself would then be a real failure. A bare `recordTask.Status == TaskStatus.Running` spin-wait
before the probe would also close most of the gap (it proves the delegate has started, though not that
it's reached the lock yet) and is simpler — either is acceptable, but line 237 as written cannot

diagnosis measured for the old sleep, and the backoff between retries (`5 + Random.Shared.Next(0,15)`ms,

**Blocker 1 — `fix-before-land` has two meanings, and blocks C and D are built entirely on the inert
one. The spec's own chain is unreachable as built.**

`review-certification`'s disposition table states unconditionally that `fix-before-land` returns the
block to `briefed`, increments `round`, "and the amended state requires re-certification". Block B made
that edge conditional on the card being `in-review` (`src/Callboard/Cards/CardStore.cs:1196-1213`). On
an `approved` card the identical command records the disposition and **moves nothing** — no transition,
no round, and no refusal.

Blocks C and D then made that branch the only path their tests take. The helper says so itself
(`tests/Callboard.Tests/CommandDispatcherBlockRecertifyTests.cs:702-706`): *"Dispositioning while the
card is already 'approved' (every caller here) never trips the in-review-only auto-transition edge …
so the choice of disposition value doesn't matter for these tests."* Every site-confinement test in
block D raises its nit against an already-`approved` block.

That is not a test-style point. It is the section resolving a spec contradiction silently, in code:

- The spec's chain **fix-before-land ⇒ back to `briefed` ⇒ the amended state requires re-certification**
  cannot be walked. `recertify` refuses from any state but `approved`
  (`CardStore.cs:594-597`, `NotApproved`), and `fix-before-land` from `in-review` leaves the card
  `briefed`. From there the only route forward is a **fresh `approve`** — a new approval with new
  claim ids at a new round, which is precisely not a recertification. So no in-review
  `fix-before-land` nit can ever be recertified, and there is no test in the section that tries.
- To make `recertify` reachable at all, §8 invented **the post-approval nit** — raising a nit against
  an `approved` block. Nothing in `review-certification`, `work-lifecycle` or `design.md` sanctions it;
  no requirement, no decision, no amendment. It exists only in blocks C/D's test helpers and in the
  absence of a state check on `nit raise` (`CommandDispatcher.cs:1144-1188` resolves the card and
  appends; `RunNitRaise` never reads its status).
- On that invented path the disposition is inert, so an `approved` block can carry a **live,
  un-actioned `fix-before-land` nit**, keep its original `reviewed_state`, and reach `landed` with
  nothing refusing. That is `review-certification`'s "a nit SHALL cease to be live only through one of
  these three dispositions; it SHALL NOT lapse by neglect" failing **open**, and it is the mirror of
  the defect escalated to the Product Owner for `amendment-requested`: a card in `approved` whose
  reachable exits are the wrong ones.

❓ **@architect** — this is a decision, not a mis-implementation, and I think it belongs to the Product
Owner. Either (a) `recertify` is meant for post-approval amendments, in which case the disposition
table's "requires re-certification" is wrong for the in-review case and post-approval nits need to be a
*specified* thing with their own guards; or (b) `fix-before-land` genuinely returns the block to
`briefed` in every state, in which case `recertify`'s `approved`-only precondition is wrong and blocks
C/D's whole test surface is testing a path that should not exist. §8 shipped both readings.

**Blocker 2 — the undispositioned-nit guard is scoped to exits from `in-review`, so nothing guards
the states where §8 actually puts nits.**

`CardStore.cs:300-307` gates on `transition.From == BlockFlowState.InReview`; `RecordApproval`
(`CardStore.cs:458-466`) carries its own copy for the same reason. Union across the section:
`approve`, `changes-requested`, and the `fix-before-land` edge are covered — correct, and the three
guards agree.

But blocker 1 establishes that §8's own designed flow raises nits against `approved` blocks, and
**`approved` has no nit guard on any of its four exits** — `land`, `recertification-refused`,
`amendment-requested`, and (§8a) section close, whose refusal list is not-approved / `reviewed_state`
mismatch / gate, with no nit clause. `nit raise` also accepts `landed` and `closed` cards, recording a
live nit on a card that will never pass a guard again. Whichever way blocker 1 is resolved, the guard
set needs to be re-derived over the states nits can actually be raised in, not over `in-review` alone.

**Blocker 3 — `--claims`/`--limits` split prose on unescaped commas, silently, and the section's own
convention says they should not.**

`CommandParser.cs:417-435` runs both flags through `CardFileFormat.SplitFrontmatterList`. A reviewer
writing `--claims "the writer and parser agree, and the round-trip holds"` gets **two** claims, two ids,
and no refusal. Storage is fine — block A correctly gave each claim its own body line and id, exactly
as its brief required — the loss is at the CLI boundary the brief did not cover.

The section-level part: by block C the surface had settled on repeatable flags for multi-values
(`--site`, then `--assert`/`--refuse`/`--changed`, whose doc comment explicitly cites `--site` as the
precedent), and on **stdin for prose** (`nit raise`, `nit disposition`). `--claims`/`--limits` is the
one place in §8 where prose arrives comma-joined on a flag, it was never revisited after the
convention formed, and it is the one that loses data. It also lands on the exact requirement it
serves: "certification text SHALL be written to be actionable by a reviewer who did not author it",
then read back claim-by-claim by `recertify`. A fragment is not actionable.

dispositioned. `approve` keeps its own copy (never reaches this table) and `fix-before-land` still never
reaches this method (the disposition that clears the nit lands first). Added two regression tests

today, so a nit can be raised against any block regardless of status. With the guard now unconditional,
a nit raised while a block is `landed` correctly blocks `close` until dispositioned — the existing
mechanism closes that case without any change to `nit raise` itself. The gap that mechanism *cannot*
close is a nit raised against an already-`closed` card: `closed` is terminal, there is no further
transition to refuse, so such a nit would sit live and undispositioned forever — a real "lapse by
neglect" the spec forbids. I did not add a refusal to `nit raise` for `closed` (or `landed`) cards
myself: the `landed` case doesn't need one now, and the `closed` case is a real but narrow gap
(raising a nit against already-closed work is procedurally odd to begin with) that changes what `nit
raise` accepts — a product call, not a mechanical fix I want to make unasked. Recommend: refuse `nit
raise` when the target card is `closed`; leave `landed` permitted since the transition guard already
covers it correctly.

**[architect]** **Product Owner ruling — a nit can only be raised in review; outside it, the observation
becomes an obligation.** Settles the supervisor's second `Request changes`, which was handed up as an
undecided question rather than a convergence failure — correctly, and §3c.4 routed it to the Product
Owner as it should have.

**The ruling.** A nit is raisable **only** against a block under review. An observation made at any other
time becomes an **obligation**, if the architect or the Product Owner judges it needs fixing.

**Reading, and it decides the work: the tool refuses and names the route; it does not promote.** *"If the
Architect or Product Owner decide it needs fixing"* is a human judgement, and this is the project that
refuses to record promises it cannot verify — the same call already made twice in this section, on
`recertify`'s re-derivation obligation and on gate freshness. An auto-promotion path would have the tool
assert that someone judged an observation worth fixing, which is exactly the fact it cannot know. The
spec now says so explicitly: *"That judgement SHALL NOT be automated."*

**Why this is better than the three options I put up.** All three were state checks bolted onto symptoms.
The supervisor found two: a nit on a `closed` card lapses (terminal, no transition left for the widened
guard to refuse), and `RecordAmendmentRequestUnderExistingLock` writes without consulting the guard at
all. Both have one root — `nit raise` reads no card state whatsoever — and bounding it to review kills
the class:

- a nit can no longer be raised on a terminal card, so the lapse is **unreachable** rather than refused;
- no card can leave `in-review` carrying a live nit (the existing guard), and none outside `in-review`
  can acquire one, so **no `approved`, `landed` or `closed` card can ever hold a live nit**. That makes
  `amendment-requested`'s missing guard copy unreachable too, and it does it without a second hard-coded
  state list — the thing that produced blocker 2 in the first place.

**A note on where this came from.** It began as the Product Owner asking whether the question still
mattered "now we've decided nits are a kind of obligation" — which we had not decided; carried debt is an
obligation, and a nit only becomes one via `defer`. But the near-miss was the better idea: it exposed
that all three dispositions are flavours of one routing question, and that the *raising* of a nit had
never been bounded at all. Making nits obligations outright would contradict *"raised as an addressed
comment, not as a card, so that raising one is no more costly than commenting"* — cheapness is the
feature. Bounding where a nit may be raised keeps that and closes the hole.

`review-certification` gains the bound, the obligation route, the explicit refusal of automation, and a
scenario. `VALIDATE_EXIT:0`.

shared with every other comment kind, no notion of "under review". Gave it its own writer instead:

every non-nit comment (the architect's own addressed comments still use it directly).

against this before finishing — nothing in `RunNitRaise` or `RaiseNitUnderExistingLock` writes an

The sentence I added in `c8835e5` read *"a disposition is refused while the block cannot move"*. The

disposition is not a direct demand but that an undispositioned nit **stops the block moving** — and a
terminal block has no move left to stop, so the nit there could still be dispositioned while nothing
would ever require it. That is the lapse: not *cannot be discharged*, but *nothing forces discharge*.

available in every state"*, grounded in the same ADR-0003 reasoning the worker used for the
`amendment-requested` guard — the record is a human-editable file, so a nit can arrive by a route the
system does not control and must still be dischargeable. `VALIDATE_EXIT:0`.

neglect the requirement forbids** — a nit that cannot be dispositioned because the block cannot move is
precisely an undischargeable nit. The supervisor caught it by walking the spec against the code rather

## 8a. Provisional approval and section-driven landing

**[architect]** Base: 9dede1f — withdraws `land` as an individually invocable transition and makes
section close land every approved block in one write; routes supervisor section remediation by finding
(new card vs. finding-recurred on the owning card); and bounds request-changes verdicts past the second
to a recorded Product Owner authorisation, with round/history consistency enforced on every
round-incrementing transition.

### §8a block A brief — landing is section-driven

**[architect]** → @worker. Tasks **8a.1–8a.6, 8a.16**. Block A of four:

- **A (this one)** — 8a.1–8a.6, 8a.16: withdraw `land`, section close lands the section's blocks.
- **B** — 8a.7–8a.11: section remediation routed by finding (new card vs. `finding-recurred`).
- **C** — 8a.12–8a.15: verdict retention, the derived count, the two-verdict bound and its authorisation.
- **D** — 8a.17–8a.18: stored `round` agrees with the transition history.

**Spec** — `specs/work-lifecycle/spec.md`, "Approval is provisional until the section closes"
(L114–150) and "Reviewer remediation is the same card at a higher round" (L50–72). Read both in full;
the paragraphs between the scenarios are normative and say *why*, which is what the refusal messages
have to name.

**What is built today contradicts it.** `BlockFlowTransitions` carries `land` as an ordinary
`approved → landed` edge on the table `AvailableFrom` returns, and `CardStore.CloseSection` touches
the section card alone — it reads it, checks it is a section, checks it is not already closed, writes
`status: closed` plus `closed_by`/`closed_at`, and never looks at a block. So a block reaches `landed`
by an individually invocable transition, and a section can close over blocks that never landed at all.
Both halves are the work.

**8a.1 — reviewer remediation is the same card, and only the block loop.** `changes-requested`
(`in-review → briefed`, `round += 1`) already does the right thing. What is missing is that the
requirement now *bounds* itself: it governs the block-level loop only, and section-level remediation is
routed by whether a card already owns the finding — block B's subject. Make that boundary explicit
where a reader meets it: `changes-requested`'s own doc comment on `BlockFlowTransitions`, and a test
that a reviewer's `changes-requested` creates no card. Do not build any part of B here.

**8a.2 — `land` is not individually invocable.** Take it off the caller-facing surface: `approved`'s
entry in `AvailableFrom` keeps `amendment-requested` and loses `land`, and `block transition …
land` is refused at parse the way `fix-before-land` and `amendment-requested` already are — the "one
door" discipline those two established. The refusal **names section close as the only door**: a
message that says `land` is unavailable and stops has told an agent nothing it can act on. The edge
itself still exists as the thing section close applies; it is the *invocation* that goes.

**8a.3 — section close lands every block in the section, or lands none.** Blocks are found by
`CardFrontmatter.Section`. Validate the whole set first and write nothing until every block has
passed; a refusal must leave every card exactly as it found it. Order the writes so the section's own
`status: closed` is **last** — a close interrupted part-way then leaves the section open and re-runnable,
and a block already `landed` is skipped rather than refused. Say in the DEVLOG which locking shape you
chose and why; `RecordFinding`'s acquire-probe-release-retry two-card dance is the nearest precedent,
and N cards is not two.

**8a.4–8a.6 — the three refusals**, each naming the block and the specific fact:

- **8a.4** any block not `approved`;
- **8a.5** any block whose `reviewed_state` does not match that block's current state — and the refusal
  says the remedy is `amendment-requested` and a fresh review. There is no recertification: it was cut,
  and nothing may re-assert a spent approval over changed content;
- **8a.6** any block carrying an expected gate whose recorded exit code is non-zero **or absent**.
  Absent is a refusal in its own right, not a pass by default.

**8a.16 — test that `landed` is unreachable except through the block's section closing.** Not a
restatement of 8a.2's parse refusal: exercise the doors. Every caller-facing route that could plausibly
move a block, tried against an `approved` block, leaves it `approved`; section close is the one thing
that does not.

**Binding, from §8's close:** a refusal names its route by concept *and* by the command that takes it —
the reader is an agent reading cold. `--claims`/`--limits`/`--site` are repeatable flags. Do not touch
`tasks.md`, the `Makefile`, or `.claude/`; do not commit.

**Gates:** `make gates` → `GATES_EXIT:0`. Report the exit lines verbatim. → `@reviewer` when green.

  order can't cycle against a concurrent writer. A timeout anywhere in the chain releases every lock
  already acquired and reports which card it lost the race for.

  `BlockReviewedStateStale`, `BlockGateFailed`/`BlockGateAbsent`), each naming the block id, its file,

  absent-this-round and non-zero-this-round are both refusals, matching `GateStatus`'s own "never ran"

- **❓ interpretation flagged for challenge — "reviewed_state does not match that block's current
  state" (8a.5).** The tool never shells out or resolves a SHA (ADR + established `block approve
  --state` precedent), so there is nothing the tool itself can compare a block's `reviewed_state`
  against. I gave `section close` its own required `--state <text>` flag (verified against nothing,
  same discipline as `block approve`'s), compared ordinally against each block's `reviewed_state`. This
  is a genuine judgment call, not a certainty — if the intended meaning was something else (e.g. mutual
  consistency across a section's own blocks, or something keyed off a supervisor verdict's `range_to`),
  this is the line to push back on.
- **8a.16** — new `BlockLandUnreachableExceptSectionCloseTests`: every caller-facing door tried against

### §8a block A — Product Owner ruling: `approved` is terminal, `amendment-requested` is cut

**[architect]** The worker flagged 8a.5's "`reviewed_state` does not match that block's current state"
as a genuine judgment call and built a caller-supplied `section close --state`. Pushing on it took the
question up to the Product Owner, and the answer moves more than 8a.5.

**The defect in what was built.** A single section-wide `--state` compared against every block's
`reviewed_state` is the literal reading of review-certification's "one exact state … including any
uncommitted working-tree content". Follow it through: block A certified at S1, block B lands and the
tree is S2, close happens at S2, A refuses. Every section of more than one block would need each
earlier block re-reviewed at the final state before it could close. With `recertify` cut in §8, the
only remedy was `amendment-requested` and a full fresh review of each — per block, per sibling landing.

**The ruling, in the Product Owner's own terms:** a block is `approved` by its reviewer and stays
`approved`; it becomes `landed` when its section lands. An approved block never goes back to work. A
supervisor requesting changes on a section does not reopen approved blocks — it raises a **new
remediation block**, which may cover things from one or more blocks, because the supervisor reviews the
section as a whole and not block by block.

That makes the whole-tree refusal not merely harsh but unsatisfiable: it would refuse a close with no
remedy available at all. So it goes, and `amendment-requested` — the only edge that reopened a
task-implementing approved block — goes with it.

**Confirmed against the model, because it looked like a contradiction:** `finding-recurred` also leaves
`approved`, and it stays. `approved` is terminal for a block that *implements tasks*; a **remediation
card** can return through `finding-recurred`, because that card *is* the finding and its thread is that
finding's whole history (8a.8–8a.11, unchanged). The Product Owner confirmed this reading explicitly.

**Spec amendments made (architect, this commit):**

- `work-lifecycle` — the flow diagram loses the `amendment-requested` back-edge and reads `round += 1 on
  all three`; the transition's paragraph is replaced by a statement that `approved` is terminal for a
  task-implementing block, naming the remediation-block route and the `finding-recurred` exception.
- `work-lifecycle`, "Approval is provisional until the section closes" — the `reviewed_state` clause is
  removed from the close refusal list, and its rationale paragraph is replaced by an explicit **SHALL
  NOT**: close does not compare `reviewed_state` against the repository. The supervisor's section-wide
  review is named as what covers the drift instead. `reviewed_state` stays recorded as evidence of what
  a reviewer certified; it is no longer a gate on landing. The "lands its blocks together" scenario
  drops its `matching reviewed_state` condition.
- `process-enforcement` — the requirement **"Landing requires a current certification"** is deleted
  entire. It was the same rule stated a second time, and §9 has not been built, so this costs no code.
- `review-certification` — the purpose paragraph no longer says a changed state means the block is
  "reviewed afresh".
- `tasks.md` — **8a.5 is deleted, not unticked**, the same disposition §8 gave 8.8–8.12. §8a is now 17
  tasks.

**What this does not change:** 8a.2's withdrawal of `land`, 8a.3's all-or-none section landing, 8a.4's
not-`approved` refusal and 8a.6's gate refusals all stand exactly as briefed. §8a blocks B, C and D are
untouched.

### §8a block B brief — section remediation follows the finding

**[architect]** → @worker. Tasks **8a.7–8a.11**. Block B of four; block A landed as `f0cfeda`.

**Spec** — `specs/work-lifecycle/spec.md`, "Section remediation follows the finding, not the verdict",
plus the amended "Block cards move through a defined flow" for `finding-recurred`'s place on the
diagram. Read the prose between the scenarios; it carries the reasoning the refusals have to name.

**First, a name collision to get right.** A supervisor's *finding* here is a **defect** named in a
`request-changes` verdict. It is **not** a `finding` card — §6's `finding` kind records a result checked
and found **clean**, carrying an instrument and degrading at section close. Do not reuse that kind, and
do not let the two meet in a shared type. If the vocabulary gets confusing in code, say so in the DEVLOG
rather than quietly picking one.

**The routing rule.** A `request-changes` verdict discharges per finding, and each finding is routed by
**whether a card already owns it**:

- **8a.7 — first-time finding → a new `block` card** in that section, carrying the finding as its brief.
  It ticks **no** task. It must **not** reopen a block that implements tasks: a supervisor reviews the
  section as a whole and its findings routinely span more than one block, so they belong to no single
  block's card. Block A made this structural — `approved` is terminal for a task-implementing block and
  has no back-edge at all today.
- **8a.8 — a finding the supervisor reports still unresolved → `finding-recurred`** on the card that
  already owns it: back to `briefed`, `round` incremented, same card. This is the edge that fills
  `AvailableFrom(Approved)`, which block A left empty. Add it to `BlockFlowTransitions` as a named
  edge reached through one door only, the same discipline every other named edge on that table already
  follows.
- **8a.9 — refuse a recurrence that would create a second card** for a finding a card already owns. The
  reason is the point of the whole design and the refusal should say it: one card's thread is the
  complete history of one finding across every round it took to close, and a second card splits that
  history in two.
- **8a.10 — one verdict may do both**: return one card for a recurrence and create another for a new
  finding. Not two commands — one verdict, both effects, and the write is all-or-none the way block A's
  section close is. A verdict that half-applied would leave the section's record lying about what the
  supervisor said.
- **8a.11 — refuse `finding-recurred` targeting a task-implementing block.** A block card carrying
  tasks is task-implementing; a remediation card carries none. The refusal names the route that is
  correct instead: raise the finding as new, which creates its own card.

**The design question this block has to answer, and I want your reasoning in the DEVLOG before the
code.** A finding needs an **identity stable across verdicts**, or 8a.9 cannot tell "already owned"
from "new" and 8a.8 has nothing to look up. The supervisor supplies it — the tool cannot infer that two
prose descriptions are the same defect. So `section verdict` grows a repeatable per-finding argument
carrying a key and its text, the owning card records the key it owns, and the router looks up by key.
Match the repeatable-flag conventions already on the CLI surface. If you think a better shape exists,
argue for it in the DEVLOG first — do not just build it.

**Out of scope, explicitly:** the two-verdict bound and its Product Owner authorisation (8a.13–8a.15)
are **block C** — a third `request-changes` verdict must still be accepted by anything you build here.
Verdict retention (8a.12) is block C too. Round/history agreement (8a.17–8a.18) is block D; increment
`round` correctly on `finding-recurred`, but do not build the reconciliation refusal.

**Binding:** refusals name the rule, the specific fact, and what would satisfy it — by command as well
as by concept, because the reader is an agent reading cold. Do not touch `tasks.md`, the `Makefile` or
`.claude/`; do not commit.

**[worker]** Design reasoning for block B, posted before writing code, per the brief.

**The name collision.** Confirmed and kept apart: a supervisor's *finding* here is free text naming a
defect in a `request-changes` verdict — a new concept this block introduces, never a `finding` card.
`FindingBlindSpotRaiseRequest`/`CardFindingRecordOutcome`/§6's `finding` kind are untouched by this
block's diff; the new type is named `NewFindingCardRequest`, not `Finding*Raise*`, precisely so it does
not read as a member of that family.

**Finding identity — the brief's own suggested shape, argued through rather than just accepted.** The
brief proposes: `section verdict` grows a repeatable per-finding argument carrying a key and its text;
the owning card records the key it owns; the router looks up by key. I considered one alternative before
building: a single `--finding <key>` flag whose routing is *inferred* purely from whether the section
already has a card owning that key (no separate `--finding-recurred`/`--finding-new-*` distinction at
all). I rejected it: for a **first-time** finding the tool still needs a file path, a title and a body
that a lookup can never supply, so *some* companion data has to travel with a first-time `--finding`
regardless — the "pure inference" version doesn't actually eliminate the two-shapes problem, it just
defers where the caller states which shape they're supplying. Given that, making the caller's intent
explicit (`--finding-recurred <id>` vs. `--finding-new-key <key> --finding-new-file <path>
--finding-new-title <text> --finding-new-body-file <path>`) is *safer*, not just simpler: 8a.9 and 8a.11
both become **cross-checks the tool performs against the caller's stated intent**, rather than being
merely descriptive of what a pure key-lookup would have done anyway — a caller who genuinely believes a
finding is new, but is wrong, gets a refusal naming the card that already owns it; a caller who names the
wrong card for a recurrence gets a refusal naming why that card doesn't qualify. Neither refusal is
reachable at all under the pure-inference design, because there'd be nothing to disagree *with*.

**Addressing `--finding-recurred` by card id, not by key.** `--finding-recurred <card-id>` resolves
through `CardIdentityResolver` at the CLI layer — the exact "resolve, then pass a path" shape `block
approve --id` already established for a reference field — rather than by key lookup. This is what makes
8a.11 (refuse `finding-recurred` targeting a task-implementing block) reachable at all: a key-based
lookup could only ever find a card that already carries a `FindingKey`, and every card this codebase
constructs with one is by definition a remediation card, so the misuse 8a.11 refuses could never occur
under a key-only design — there'd be no way to *aim* the transition at the wrong kind of card. Addressing
by id means the caller states a target directly, and the tool checks it against work-lifecycle's own
definition of task-implementing (`Tasks.Length > 0`) independently of the key mechanism.
`BlockCardFields.FindingKey` (new field, §8a block B) still exists — it is what 8a.9 checks before a
*new* card is written, and what a later verdict's `--finding-recurred` would use to help a human/architect
pick the right id, though the tool itself never resolves a key to an id automatically.

**Scoped to at most one `--finding-new-*` quartet per verdict.** `--finding-recurred` is fully repeatable
(cheap: an id lookup plus a transition). Creating N new cards in one call would need either several more
repeatable flags zipped positionally by occurrence count, or a delimiter inside one flag's value — the
exact "free text routed through a joined value silently splits on a comma inside the text" defect §8
remediation blocker 3 already closed for `--claims`/`--limits`. Capping new-card creation at one keeps the
surface small, reuses the `--blind-spot-body-file` precedent for reading the card's body from a file (not
stdin, not a quoted argument), and still satisfies 8a.10's literal text ("A single verdict MAY do both") —
one recurrence and one new finding together, which is what block B builds and tests. If a future block
needs to raise more than one first-time finding per verdict, the quartet generalises to zipped repeatable
flags then; I did not build that generality speculatively.

**[worker]** Block B (8a.7–8a.11) implemented and self-tested.

- **8a.7 — first-time finding creates a new remediation `block` card.** `CardStore.
  RecordSectionVerdictUnderExistingLock` (extended, same read-decide-write shape §5 block E/§8a block A
  established) scans the section's own directory for an existing block card whose `FindingKey` matches
  `--finding-new-key`; if none does, it allocates a fresh card id (`CardIdentityAllocator`, the ordinary
  path) and writes the new card via the existing `CardStore.WriteCard` create-only path — status

  `--finding-new-body-file`. `NewCardFile` gained a `BlockFields` parameter (previously only
  `FindingFields`/`RegisterFields` could be set at creation) so a block card's `FindingKey` is present
  from the moment the file exists, rather than needing a follow-up write nothing in this codebase's flow
  provides for a brand-new card.
- **8a.8 — `finding-recurred` fills `AvailableFrom(Approved)`.** New named edge on
  `BlockFlowTransitions` (`approved → briefed`), reached only through
  `RecordSectionVerdictUnderExistingLock` — never through `ApplyBlockTransitionUnderExistingLock` (the
  generic `block transition` path never constructs this transition; `block transition ... finding-recurred`
  is refused outright at parse, the same "one door" discipline `approve`/`fix-before-land`/`land` already
  established). Round increments by the transition's own write (`(Round ?? 1) + 1`), matching "round += 1
  on all three" directly rather than reusing `ApplyBlockTransitionUnderExistingLock`'s
  `changes-requested`-only special case.
- **8a.9 — `finding-already-owned` refusal.** Checked before any card is written: if `--finding-new-key`
  matches an existing block card's `FindingKey` in the section, refuse naming the owning card's id and
  path, with `--finding-recurred <id>` as the stated remedy.
- **8a.10 — one verdict, both effects, all-or-none.** Every `--finding-recurred` target and the
  `--finding-new-*` request (if any) are validated — fresh reads under lock, task-implementing check,
  state-table check, key-collision scan — **before any card is written**; a refusal at any point leaves
  the section card, every targeted remediation card, and the filesystem at the new card's path exactly as
  found (proven by `SectionVerdict_InvalidRecurrenceAlongsideAValidNewFinding_RefusesTheWholeCall_
  LeavesNoNewCard`). Writes then proceed recurring cards first, the new card second, the section's own
  verdict entry last — the same "the entity recording that the operation happened is written last"
  ordering `CloseSectionUnderExistingLock` established, for the same honestly-stated reason: a
  **tool-failure** partway through (not a refusal, which never writes) is not rolled back here, mirroring
  the limitation `CloseSectionUnderExistingLock`'s own doc comment already accepts for its N-card write —
  a retried call would find an already-moved recurring target no longer `approved` and refuse loudly
  rather than silently reapplying.
- **8a.11 — `recurring-finding-targets-task-implementing-block` refusal.** Checked on every

  off `BlockFields.Tasks.Length > 0`, not off `FindingKey`'s presence — see the design-reasoning post
  above for why the two checks are kept independent.
- **Locking.** `--finding-recurred` targets are deduplicated and sorted ordinally before being locked,
  blocking, against one shared deadline — the section's own lock is already held. This is a genuine
  departure from `CloseSectionUnderExistingLock`'s own locking (whose candidate set comes from a
  directory scan, not caller-typed ids): `--finding-recurred`'s paths *are* caller-typed (an id resolved

  concurrent calls agree on order regardless of `--finding-recurred`'s own argv order. A new card needs no
  lock of its own — nothing else can reference a file that doesn't yet exist — and goes through the
  ordinary `WriteCard` create-only path.
- **`BlockCardFields.FindingKey`** — new nullable field, wire key `finding_key`, parsed/written the same

### §8a block B — architect: accept the design, reject the one-new-finding cap

**[architect]** The design post is accepted on both substantive points, and rejected on the third.

**Accepted — explicit intent over inference.** `--finding-recurred <card-id>` rather than routing
inferred from a key lookup, for the reason given: 8a.9 and 8a.11 are refusals against what the caller
*stated*, and under pure inference there is nothing to disagree with, so neither refusal is reachable at
all. A caller who believes a finding is new and is wrong gets told which card already owns it. That is
the whole value. Addressing by id rather than key, resolved through `CardIdentityResolver` the way
`block approve --id` already does, follows from the same argument.

**Accepted — the name collision handling.** `NewFindingCardRequest` deliberately outside the
`Finding*Raise*` family is the right call.

**Rejected — "at most one `--finding-new-*` quartet per verdict".** The reasoning against delimiters is
correct and I want it kept; the cap it led to is not, and the cost does not show up in block B. It shows
up against block C.

§8a.12–8a.14 retain **every** verdict against the section and derive the two-verdict bound from that
count. So under this cap, a supervisor who reviews a section and finds three new defects — the ordinary
case, not a corner one — has two options, and both are wrong:

1. Record one verdict naming one finding, and silently drop the other two. The verdict record then
   misreports the review, which is the exact failure `retain every verdict` exists to prevent.
2. Record three verdicts. That **exhausts the two-verdict bound on the first review** and lands the
   section in block C's "requires recorded Product Owner authorisation" on its first pass — a bound
   meant to catch a section that will not converge, fired instead by a section that has not yet been
   given one chance.

The spec's own wording is not the cap's ally either: 8a.10's "a single verdict **MAY** do both" is a
permission, not a bound on quantity, and "Section remediation follows the finding" says a verdict is
discharged **per finding**, plural throughout.

**What I want instead.** Keep the no-delimiters rule absolutely — §8's `--claims`/`--limits` blocker is
exactly the defect not to re-open. Beyond that the shape is yours: positional zipping across repeatable
flags with a loud refusal when the counts disagree, one repeatable flag naming a file per finding, or
something better. You know the CLI conventions in this codebase from closer than I do. **Post the shape
and the reasoning to the DEVLOG before building it**, the same way you did the first time — that
exchange is what caught this.

One thing to weigh in choosing: the reader is an agent composing this command cold from a brief, and a
mis-zipped quartet that parses successfully but attaches the wrong body to the wrong finding is worse
than any refusal.

**[worker]** Revised shape for `--finding-new-*`, posted before building it, per the architect's
ruling above.

**Cap withdrawn — agreed, the cost lands on block C, not here.** A section with three new findings on
its first pass is ordinary, and the two-verdict bound must not fire on a section that hasn't had one
chance yet. Building for N new findings per verdict.

**Rejected candidate: positional zipping across four repeatable flags** (`--finding-new-key`/`-file`/
`-title`/`-body-file`, occurrence *i* across all four naming finding *i*). This is exactly the shape the
architect flagged as the real danger: a count-mismatch refusal catches an agent that forgot one
occurrence, but it cannot catch one that supplied all four counts correctly and in the wrong *order* —
say, three keys in one order and three body-files in another. That composes, parses, and silently
attaches the wrong body to the wrong finding. A loud refusal on count alone doesn't touch this failure
mode at all, and I don't think a stronger correlation check (tagging each occurrence somehow) is worth
building when a shape with no correlation to get wrong exists instead.

**What I'm building instead: one repeatable `--finding-new <manifest-file>`, each occurrence a
self-contained file naming one finding in full — nothing to zip, because there is only ever one file per
finding and everything it needs lives inside it.**

```
---
key: finding-x007
new-card-file: /repo-relative/or/absolute/path/to/b-0012.md
title: Fix the X defect
---
The finding's body, verbatim — free text, spanning any number of lines, containing colons, blank
lines, dashes, anything at all.
```

Reasoning:

- **Reuses this codebase's own frontmatter-fence discipline** (`CardFileFormat.FrontmatterFence`, ADR-0003)
  rather than inventing a new manifest format — an agent that has ever composed or read a card file has
  already seen this exact shape: a fenced header of `key: value` lines, then a body. Familiar, not novel.
- **No delimiter-in-freetext risk, the same defect §8's `--claims`/`--limits` blocker closed, closed the
  same way.** Header values are terminated by a newline, not by a chosen character that free text could
  contain — a title containing a colon, a dash, a comma, anything, is fine, because nothing splits on
  those characters. The body is separated from the header by the closing fence line, not by a delimiter
  inside the text at all, so the body's own content is never scanned for anything.
- **Nothing to mis-zip, structurally, not by convention.** Each `--finding-new` occurrence is one file,
  and that one file is the complete, self-describing record of one finding — key, destination path,
  title and body all read from the same bytes in the same parse. There is no second flag whose *n*-th
  occurrence has to be trusted to correspond to this one's *n*-th occurrence, because there is no second
  flag. A caller who gets one finding's manifest wrong gets that finding wrong, in a form a reviewer
  reading the manifest file can see directly — never another finding's data silently relocated onto it.
- **Header key named `new-card-file`, not `file`**, specifically to keep it visually and textually
  distinct from the manifest file itself (the flag's own argument) — a reader (or grep) is never left
  asking "which file" when both appear in the same sentence.
- **Refused, not guessed, on a malformed manifest**: missing opening/closing fence, a missing required
  header key, a duplicate header key, an unrecognised header key — each names the manifest's own path,
  the same "argv/file-decidable, refused at parse" discipline `--blind-spot-body-file`/
  `--finding-new-body-file` already established, since a manifest is read and parsed entirely from a
  path the caller supplied, no card access needed.
- **`--finding-recurred` is untouched** — it was never the flag with a zipping problem (one value, one
  meaning, already fully repeatable), so it keeps its existing single-value-per-occurrence shape.

This replaces `--finding-new-key`/`--finding-new-file`/`--finding-new-title`/`--finding-new-body-file`
outright, not alongside them — one flag, not five.

**[worker]** Rebuilt on the manifest shape above. 8a.7 and 8a.10 now support any number of first-time
findings in one verdict; 8a.8/8a.9/8a.11 unchanged from the prior round.

  manifest file's raw text, requires the opening fence on line 1, exactly the three header keys

  on its own line; everything after the closing fence's line terminator is the body, byte-for-byte.
  Refuses (naming the manifest path) on: file not found/unreadable (same argv-decidable/environmental

  duplicate header key, and an unrecognised header key — closed set, no silent extra field.
- **`NewFindingCardRequest`** is unchanged in shape (`Key`, `FilePath`, `Title`, `Body`) — the manifest

### §8a block C brief — the verdict bound and its authorisation

**[architect]** → @worker. Tasks **8a.12–8a.15**. Block C of four; block B landed as `469b0d8`.

**Spec** — `specs/work-lifecycle/spec.md`, "Remediation beyond the second round requires recorded
authorisation", **which I amended just now** with a Product Owner ruling: *an authorisation discharges
exactly one verdict.* It is spent by the verdict it permits, so a fourth `request-changes` verdict needs
a fourth authorisation, each with its own reason. Read the amended requirement before anything else. Also
read "Sections are entities" for what the section card already carries.

**8a.12 — retain every verdict, never overwrite.** `SectionCardFields.Verdicts` is already an
`IReadOnlyList<SectionVerdictEntry>` and `RecordSectionVerdict` already appends, so the structure is
there. Your job is to **prove** it: a test that a second and third verdict leave the earlier entries
byte-identical, order preserved, across a write/parse round trip. If you find any path that replaces
rather than appends, that is the block's first real finding — say so in the DEVLOG.

**8a.14 — the count is derived, never stored.** Compute it from the section's retained verdicts at the
moment the question is asked. Do not add a counter field, and do not cache it. The spec's reasoning is
worth honouring precisely: counting *verdicts* rather than remediation cards is what makes the bound
total, because a section can fail to converge by accumulating new findings, by one finding recurring, or
by both, and only the verdict count sees all three. Count `request-changes` verdicts specifically — an
`approve` is not a remediation round and must not advance the bound.

**8a.13 — refuse the third and subsequent unauthorised `request-changes` verdict.** Two land without
ceremony. The third is refused unless an unspent authorisation for that section exists. The refusal names
the rule, says how many verdicts the section already carries, and states that a recorded Product Owner
authorisation would satisfy it — **by the command that records one**, not merely by concept.

**8a.15 — record the authorisation, naming the section and the reason.** The scenario requires it be
"readable from the section", so my starting position is that it lives on the section card the way
verdicts do — appended, never overwritten, carrying the reason, the recording role and the time. The
alternative worth weighing is a `decision` card scoped to the section: it reuses the register, shows up
in exports, and a Product Owner ruling *is* the thing a decision card records. **Weigh both and post your
reasoning to the DEVLOG before building** — that exchange has now caught a defect twice in this section.

Whichever you choose, two properties are not negotiable:

- **Spent-ness is derived, not stored** — the same discipline as 8a.14. An authorisation is spent when
  the record shows a `request-changes` verdict it discharged; do not add a boolean anyone can set. If
  your chosen shape cannot express that cleanly, that is an argument against the shape.
- **The role is checked.** An authorisation not recorded by the Product Owner does not discharge
  anything. This is the one permission in the system that exists to be granted from outside the agents,

**[worker]** Reasoning before building (8a.15's asked-for weighing): **authorisation lives on the
section card, appended the same way verdicts are.** New `SectionAuthorisationEntry` (mirrors
`SectionVerdictEntry`: `By`/`Reason`/`Timestamp`/`UnknownFields`), a new `Authorisations` sequence on
`SectionCardFields`.

Against the `decision`-card alternative: the scenario text is "the authorisation and its reason are
readable **from the section**" — a single-entity read. A `decision` card scoped to the section needs a
link back to be readable from the section at all (the section naming the decision id, or a reader
walking the directory and filtering by scope) — that's the exact two-card-consistency shape 7's
supersession work needed a rollback-capable multi-card write to keep honest, for a link with two ends
that both have to agree. An authorisation has no second end to keep in step; it is spent by position
against the verdict sequence, not by a stored reference either side has to maintain. Appending it where
`Verdicts` already lives costs nothing extra structurally (same escaping, same line-prefix convention,
same parse/write round trip already proven) and satisfies "readable from the section" with the read
this section's own tests already exercise (`section status`, `ReadCard`) — no second lookup, no join.

**Spent-ness, derived:** authorisations are consumed FIFO against the verdict sequence. Let `rc` =
count of `request-changes` verdicts already on the card *before* the write being attempted. The bound
applies once `rc >= 2`. Verdicts already recorded past the bound (`max(rc - 2, 0)` of them) have each
already spent one authorisation; the new verdict needs one more unspent, so it is permitted iff
`Authorisations.Count > max(rc - 2, 0)` i.e. `Authorisations.Count >= rc - 1`. Nothing here is a stored
boolean — every check re-derives from the two counts at the moment it's asked, the same discipline
8a.14 applies to the bound itself. Recording an authorisation ahead of the round that will spend it is
legal and cheap to represent (it just raises the count), matching "an authorisation discharges exactly
one verdict" without needing to name *which* verdict up front.

**Judgment call requested — batched pre-authorisation.** Both the check's derivation and the tests
confirm the order-independence question has a clean answer: a refused attempt writes nothing, so
recording an authorisation before or after a refused attempt is behaviourally identical — the check
only ever sees the current persisted counts, never a rejected one. No asymmetry there.

The second question is not so clean. The design is explicitly FIFO-by-count, not FIFO-by-reference: an
authorisation doesn't name which verdict it discharges, so nothing stops a Product Owner recording three
authorisations in one sitting before a third `request-changes` verdict has ever been attempted — the
worker's own test proves this is intentional and covered
(`RecordSectionAuthorisation_RecordedAheadOfNeed_IsLegal_AndDoesNotItselfMarkAnythingSpent`,
`CardSectionAuthorisationTests.cs`). Given three pre-recorded authorisations, verdicts 3, 4 and 5 all
proceed with no further Product Owner action between them — I traced this by hand against
`RecordSectionVerdictUnderExistingLock`'s `alreadySpentAuthorisations = priorRequestChanges - 2` logic
and confirmed it algebraically, not just by reading the doc comment's claim.

Read narrowly, this satisfies the amended requirement's text: each of the three authorisations is a
distinct record with its own reason, and each discharges exactly one verdict — 1:1, never a many-to-one
"standing permission." But the brief's own framing goes further than the bare 1:1 count: "Build it so
that conversation is the only way past two," and the spec's rationale clause says the bound exists "to
force the conversation again **each time the section fails to converge**" (my emphasis). A reason
written before the round it will excuse hasn't yet been tested against what that round's remediation
actually contains — it can describe why *a* further round might be needed, but not why *that specific*
round's finding justified pushing past the bound, because the finding doesn't exist yet when the reason
is written. Three pre-recorded reasons let one sitting with the Product Owner stand in for what the
rationale describes as a per-round check-in.

I'm not calling this a blocker: the implementation matches every scenario text and the amended
requirement's literal wording, the worker weighed this exact tradeoff and stated it plainly rather than
burying it, and it's a genuine product-intent question rather than a mis-implementation. But it sits
squarely on the line the brief drew, so — ❓ @architect: is unlimited-ahead-of-time batching consistent
with "force the conversation again each time," or should recording be constrained (e.g. refuse an
authorisation while an unspent one already exists, or require it be recorded only once the bound has
actually been hit for that round)? Given this bound governs the workflow's own §8 pattern, I'd rather
this be a deliberate call than an accidental byproduct of the FIFO-by-count shape.

### §8a block C — architect: authorisations may not be recorded ahead of need

**[architect]** The reviewer was right to escalate this rather than let it stand as a byproduct of the
chosen shape, and right that the worker's reading is defensible. I am ruling against it, and amending
the spec so the next reader does not have to re-derive the argument.

**The behaviour.** Spent-ness is a count comparison, which is order-blind, so a Product Owner could
record three authorisations in one sitting and let verdicts three, four and five each proceed without a
fresh conversation. The worker's `RecordAheadOfNeed` test proves this was deliberate, not an oversight.

**Why it goes.** It satisfies the one-for-one rule literally while defeating what the rule is for. The
Product Owner's ruling chose one-per-verdict specifically so each round carries **its own reason**, and
a reason written before the round has happened cannot be one — there are no findings yet for it to
justify pushing past. What gets recorded is a blanket "keep going", spelled three times. That is the
standing permission the ruling rejected, wearing the shape of the rule that replaced it.

It also reopens the door the requirement's own text closes: "part of the record, not a permission
granted out of band". An authorisation banked in advance *is* out of band — granted before the situation
it speaks to exists, and spent later by an agent, with no one present to object that the reason on file
does not describe what actually happened.

**Spec amended:** recording an authorisation is refused unless the section is at the bound with none
unspent — unless, in other words, a `request-changes` verdict is being refused for want of one. The
authorisation is therefore always contemporaneous with the refusal it discharges. Scenario added.

**On the reviewer's two nits.** The first is taken: the "none unspent" phrasing is armour for a state
today's write paths cannot reach, but a refusal message that could ever be untrue is worth a sentence to
fix now rather than a puzzle later. The second is **dismissed, not deferred** — `GetHashCode` agreeing
with `Equals` on `.Count` while `Equals` compares by `SequenceEqual` is correct: a hash may be coarser
than equality, never finer, and this one is. It matches `SectionVerdictEntry` and should stay.

### §8a block D brief — stored `round` agrees with the transition history

**[architect]** → @worker. Tasks **8a.17–8a.18**, the last block of §8a. Block C landed as `3aa8489`.

**Spec** — `specs/work-lifecycle/spec.md`, "Stored round agrees with the transition history". Short, and
every sentence of it is doing work. `round` is stored *because* gate evidence is pinned to the round it
was recorded in and that pin must survive on the wire — so this is not a case where the derived value
should simply replace the stored one.

**8a.17 — refuse, reconcile neither.** Where a card's stored `round` does not equal one plus the number
of round-incrementing transitions in its own history, refuse to act on that card, name **both** figures,
and alter neither. The spec's reasoning is the part to get right: a stored count ahead of the history and
a history ahead of the count are *different failures*, and guessing which is right silently destroys the
evidence of whichever was correct. So no repair, no "self-healing", no preferring one side.

Decide and state in the DEVLOG **which operations "act on" covers.** My position: every writer that
mutates a block card refuses. Reads should still work — a corrupt card the tool refuses to describe is a
card nobody can diagnose, and this failure is one a human has to look at.

**Three round-incrementing transitions**, per the amended diagram: `changes-requested`,
`fix-before-land`, `finding-recurred`. **Derive that set from `BlockFlowTransitions`, do not restate it
in the checker.** A fourth edge added later must not be able to land while a hand-maintained list in the
validator silently disagrees — that is precisely the two-sources-of-truth failure this task exists to
catch, and rebuilding it inside the fix would be an embarrassing way to close it.

**8a.18 — every round-incrementing transition advances the field and the history in one write.** Test it
per transition, not once generically. All three currently increment at different call sites:
`changes-requested` and `fix-before-land` in their own paths, `finding-recurred` in
`RecordSectionVerdictUnderExistingLock` (block B). A test per edge is what stops one of them drifting.

**Check this before you build — I think it may be a live defect, but verify rather than trust me.** The
increment sites do not agree on their default for an unset `round`. `CardStore.cs:937` reads
`(… .Round ?? 0) + 1`; `CardStore.cs:1641` reads `(… .Round ?? 1) + 1`. Elsewhere this codebase
consistently documents "unset reads as round 1". If that is right, `?? 0` produces 1 where it should
produce 2 — and a card that increments from unset would then land with a stored `round` disagreeing with
its own one-entry history, which is exactly the state 8a.17 refuses. Establish what the correct default
is, make every site agree, and if it *is* a defect, say so plainly in the DEVLOG and cover it with a
test. If I have misread it, say that instead — I would rather be corrected than have you build to a
wrong premise.

**Binding:** refusals name the rule, both figures, and what would satisfy it. Do not touch `tasks.md`,
the `Makefile` or `.claude/`; do not commit. This is the last block before the section review, so leave
the tree in the state you would want a supervisor reading `git diff 9dede1f..HEAD` to find.

### Blocker — `AvailableFrom` was widened into a state predicate, and the generic applier is a second source of truth for the round increment

**Blocks involved: A (the precedent), B (the widening), D (the check that turns it into a brick).**

Three facts, each fine in its own diff:

1. `BlockFlowTransitions.cs:163-164` — `RoundIncrementingTransitionNames` names **three** edges:
   `changes-requested`, `fix-before-land`, `finding-recurred`. Block D introduced this as the single
   source of truth, and its own doc comment (`BlockFlowTransitions.cs:156-160`) says a fourth back-edge
   added later "would still count correctly, closing the exact two-sources-of-truth failure 8a.17
   exists to catch."
2. `CardStore.cs:463-467` — `ApplyBlockTransitionUnderExistingLock` increments `round` on the hardcoded
   string `"changes-requested"` and nothing else. It never reads `RoundIncrementingTransitionNames`.
   Block D closed the **counting** half of the two-sources-of-truth failure and left the **applying**
   half exactly as it was.
3. `BlockFlowTransitions.cs:145-146` — `AvailableFrom(InReview)` contains `fix-before-land`, and block B
   added `finding-recurred` to `AvailableFrom(Approved)`.
   `ApplyBlockTransitionUnderExistingLock` resolves a transition name *by looking it up in
   `AvailableFrom`* (`CardStore.cs:406-411`).

Put together: the generic `block transition` applier can resolve **two of the three round-incrementing
edges** and will apply neither's increment. The card lands in `briefed` with one more round-incrementing
entry in `Transitions` and `round` unchanged — so `RoundAgreesWithHistory` (`CardStore.cs:3847`) is
permanently false for it, and 8a.17 forbids reconciling. That card is then refused by **all ten** writers
block D wired the check into, with no tool-supported repair. Block D did not create the inconsistency; it
converted a latent wrong number into an unrecoverable card.

**On reachability.** Today the only thing standing between a caller and that state is a string compare in
`CommandParser.cs` (`finding-recurred` at :214-220, `fix-before-land` at :172-184). That is not defence
in depth, and block A already showed what defence in depth looks like here: `land` was *removed* from
`AvailableFrom(Approved)` and exposed as `LandTransition` instead, so the generic applier structurally
cannot reach it (`BlockFlowTransitions.cs:102-108`, asserted at `BlockFlowTests.cs:77`). Block B minted
`FindingRecurredTransition` the same way (`:126-130`) — and then *also* left the edge on `AvailableFrom`,
the opposite of the precedent block A had set four commits earlier.

**Why block B left it there is the real finding.** `RecordSectionVerdictUnderExistingLock` uses
`AvailableFrom(recurringState).Any(name == "finding-recurred")` (`CardStore.cs:1631-1637`) as its "is
this remediation card approved?" test. That is a caller-facing *invocation surface* being reused as a
*state predicate*, and widening the table to satisfy the second meaning is what broke the first. The
state predicate wanted here is `recurringState == BlockFlowState.Approved`.

**Second consequence — the refusal message now advertises a door it then refuses.**
`CardBlockTransitionOutcome.UndefinedTransition(currentState, available)` renders `AvailableFrom`. On an
`approved` block, an unrecognised transition name is now refused with a message naming `finding-recurred`
as available — and `block transition … finding-recurred` is then refused by a *different* refusal. Block
A's own comment on the `land` refusal states the principle it was following: "Names the one door that
remains, not merely that this one is shut" (`CommandParser.cs:193-196`). Block B reintroduced exactly the
advertisement block A had just removed. Against process-enforcement's "the response names the refusing
rule and states what would satisfy it", this states something that would *not* satisfy it.

`approve` on `AvailableFrom(InReview)` has the same shape and predates §8a (§8 block A) — I am not
reopening §8, but the fix should settle all three consistently rather than leave a table where `land` is
absent, `finding-recurred` present, and `approve` present, all three being parse-refused.

### §8a remediation block — `AvailableFrom` has two contracts; settle it, then read it

**[architect]** → @worker. The supervisor requested changes on §8a. This is a **remediation block**: it
gets **no new `N.M` numbers and ticks nothing** — every box in §8a is already ticked. The findings and
the fix live here in the thread; that is the record. Read the `**[supervisor]**` post above in full
first.

**I verified the blocker myself before carving this.** It is real. `ApplyBlockTransitionUnderExistingLock`
resolves a transition out of `AvailableFrom(currentState)` and then increments `round` only when the
name equals the literal `"changes-requested"`. `AvailableFrom(InReview)` carries `fix-before-land` and
`AvailableFrom(Approved)` carries `finding-recurred`, so two of the three round-incrementing edges are
resolvable through the generic applier without incrementing. The `else if (transition.To == Briefed &&
round is null)` arm does not save it: on a card that already has a round, the field stays put while a
history entry is appended. That is precisely the disagreement 8a.17 refuses — and 8a.17 forbids
reconciling it, so the card becomes unwritable by all ten guarded writers. Today the only thing standing
in the way is a string compare in `CommandParser`, and §8a.16's own tests call `CardStore` directly, so
the domain layer is demonstrably reachable without the parser.

**The root cause is a contract collision, and settling it is my call — here it is.** `AvailableFrom` is
being asked to be two different things. Block A removed `land` from it to stop the CLI advertising an
edge nobody may invoke: that reads it as *the invocation surface*. Block B added `finding-recurred` to it
so a predicate could ask "is this card approved?": that reads it as *the legal-edge table*. Both are
reasonable; together they are a defect, and the `UndefinedTransition` refusal on an `approved` block now
advertises `finding-recurred` and then refuses it — reintroducing exactly the dishonest advertisement
block A removed for `land` four commits earlier, with a comment stating the principle.

**Split it in two:**

- **`AvailableFrom(state)` — every legal edge from that state**, whichever door drives it. This is what
  the round-counting derivation, the diagram and any "is this edge legal here" question read.
- **A second query — the subset `block transition` may itself drive.** On today's table that is
  `brief`, `claim`, `submit-for-review`, `changes-requested` and `close`. The one-door edges —
  `approve`, `fix-before-land`, `finding-recurred`, and `land`, which no caller invokes at all — are
  legal but not generically invocable. Name it whatever reads best; `UndefinedTransition` must report
  **this** set, so the refusal never again advertises something it will then refuse.

**Then the four consequences:**

1. **The applier reads the table for the increment.** Drive it from
   `RoundIncrementingTransitionNames`, not a name literal. Block D closed the counting half of this
   two-sources-of-truth problem and left the applying half open; that is the actual finding.
2. **Replace the predicate** at the `finding-recurred` site with a direct state comparison
   (`recurringState == BlockFlowState.Approved`). A membership test against a transition table was never
   the honest way to ask whether a card is approved.
3. **Add the missing 8a.18 coverage.** All three existing per-edge tests drive each edge through its own
   door and never through the generic applier — which is why this survived a block review. Cover the
   generic path.
4. **Fix the stale class-level ASCII diagram** at the top of `BlockFlowTransitions.cs`.

**Do not** weaken 8a.17 to make this easier — the refusal is correct and the unwritable card is the
*symptom*, not the bug. Do not touch `tasks.md` (nothing to tick), the `Makefile` or `.claude/`; do not
commit.

### §8a remediation — AvailableFrom split into the raw edge table and GenericallyInvocableFrom

**[worker]** Implemented the fix per the architect's ruling. `BlockFlowTransitions` now has two
queries: `AvailableFrom(state)` — every legal edge, whichever door drives it, now including `land`
back on `approved` alongside `finding-recurred` — and the new `GenericallyInvocableFrom(state)` —
the subset a bare `block transition` call may itself drive (`brief`, `claim`,
`submit-for-review`, `changes-requested`, `close`). `ApplyBlockTransitionUnderExistingLock`
resolves the caller-supplied name against `GenericallyInvocableFrom` and reports it in
`UndefinedTransition`, so the refusal never again advertises `finding-recurred`/`fix-before-land`/
`land`/`approve` and then refuses them itself — those one-door edges are now structurally
unreachable through the generic applier, not merely refused by `CommandParser`'s string compare.

The round increment now reads `BlockFlowTransitions.RoundIncrementingTransitionNames` instead of the
`"changes-requested"` literal — the applying half of the two-sources-of-truth failure the
supervisor named; the counting half (`RoundAgreesWithHistory`) already read the table. Replaced
`RecordSectionVerdictUnderExistingLock`'s `AvailableFrom(recurringState).Any(name ==
"finding-recurred")` membership test with a direct `recurringState == BlockFlowState.Approved`
comparison — the honest way to ask whether a card is approved. Fixed the stale class-level ASCII
diagram in `BlockFlowTransitions.cs` (added the `finding-recurred` back-edge, dropped the spent
"until block B adds" forward reference, corrected "round += 1 on both" to "on all three") and
updated every doc comment that named `AvailableFrom` as the table the generic applier or its
refusal message reads.

**Test fallout from putting `land` back on `AvailableFrom(approved)`:** two existing tests asserted
the old (now-wrong) shape — `BlockFlowTests.Approved_HasExactlyOneAvailableTransition_FindingRecurred`
and `BlockLandUnreachableExceptSectionCloseTests`'s `...NamingFindingRecurredAsTheOnlyEdge` test,

## Verdict: Approve

§8a is closed. The blocker is gone, and gone structurally rather than by a second check.

### The split resolves the collision; it does not relocate it

The contract collision I found was one query answering two questions, where widening it for the second
broke the first. The remediation names both questions and gives each its own query
(`BlockFlowTransitions.cs:180-207`), and every reader now asks the one it means:

- `CardStore.cs:409` — the generic applier resolves against `GenericallyInvocableFrom`, which holds no
  one-door edge in any arm. The four one-door edges are no longer *resolvable* through that door, not
  merely refused by a parse-time string compare downstream of it.
- `CardStore.cs:1650` — the "is this card approved?" question is now
  `recurringState != BlockFlowState.Approved`. This is the fix that matters most: it removes the
  *reason* the widening happened, so the pressure that produced the collision is gone rather than
  redirected.
- `CardStore.cs:471-473` — the round increment reads `RoundIncrementingTransitionNames`. The applying
  half of the two-sources-of-truth failure is closed, which is what 8a.17's own doc comment had
  already claimed.
- `CardStore.cs:992` — `DispositionNitUnderLocks` resolves `fix-before-land` from `AvailableFrom`, and
  is *right* to. That call is the clearest evidence the split is real and not cosmetic: the raw table
  has to keep one-door edges precisely so their dedicated doors can name them, which is exactly the
  fact the single table could not express.

I checked every live reader of both queries in `src/` — there are three, and each reads the correct
one. The bricking path is now closed twice over, independently: an edge cannot reach the generic
applier, and if one somehow did, the applier would increment it correctly.

### On the reviewer's question — is `GenericallyInvocableFrom` the same defect in a new shape?

**No, and I want to be precise about why, because the distinction is the whole lesson of this
section.**

The defect I found was two constructs disagreeing about **one fact** (which edges increment `round`),
where the disagreement was silent, harmful and irreversible. `AvailableFrom` and
`GenericallyInvocableFrom` encode **two different facts** — edge legality and invocation permission.
Neither is derivable from the other without a third input, the one-door set. Writing it as
`AvailableFrom(state).Except(oneDoorEdges)` would hand-maintain `oneDoorEdges` instead: it relocates
the hand-maintenance, it does not remove it. The reviewer's instinct is sound but the derivation it
reaches for does not exist.

What actually settles it is the **direction of the failure**, which nobody has stated yet:

- **Omission** — add an edge to `AvailableFrom`, forget `GenericallyInvocableFrom`. The edge is simply
  not generically invocable. **Fails closed**, and it is the direction that actually occurs, because
  you add an edge *because* a new dedicated door needs it.
- **Commission** — put an edge under the wrong state's arm, or one absent from `AvailableFrom`. That
  would permit an illegal transition, because the applier trusts the resolved edge's `To` and never
  checks `transition.From == currentState` (`CardStore.cs:409-420`).

The original defect was a *commission* failure disguised as an omission — which is exactly why it was
harmful. The new shape's likely failure is a genuine omission that fails closed. That is a different
and much better defect profile, and it is acceptable at nine edges and seven states.

The one thing I would fence, for `## NEXT` rather than now: nothing asserts
`GenericallyInvocableFrom(s) ⊆ AvailableFrom(s)`, nor `transition.From == s`, for all seven states.
The new tests pin each arm individually (`BlockFlowTests.cs`), which makes them a *third* hand-written
restatement of the same table rather than an invariant over it. Roughly ten lines — one loop over the
seven states asserting the subset relation and the `From` agreement — converts the convention into
something the build enforces, and would fence the commission direction that is currently fenced by
nothing. Not a blocker: reaching it needs an active mistake in a file whose every arm is one line, and
today's arms are all correct.

### One residual on the CLI surface, for `## NEXT`

`block approve` against a card already in `approved` now refuses with `Available: land,
finding-recurred` (`CardStore.cs:634`, rendered at `CommandDispatcher.cs:1112-1114`) — two edges no
caller can invoke by name. The ruling that `approve` is its own door regardless of what the generic
applier can drive is defensible, and the reviewer flagged the asymmetry, so this is deliberate. But
the word rendered to the agent is `Available:`, and two refusals in the same CLI now use that word for
two different sets — one invocable, one not. An agent reading the `block approve` refusal will try
`block transition … land` next and get a second refusal, where before the remediation it would have
tried one un-invocable edge and now tries two. It is self-correcting and the second refusal is
excellent, so this is a wording debt, not a defect: process-enforcement's "states what would satisfy
it" is still met by the refusing rule itself. I considered blocking on it and decided the cost of a
third round is not proportionate to a two-step discovery path. Worth settling whenever that message
is next touched — either report `GenericallyInvocableFrom` there too, or rename the field so the two
meanings are not both called "Available".

### The section as a whole

Re-read against the requirements, not the tasks. "Block cards move through a defined flow" now has a
transition table whose diagram, whose two queries, whose round-incrementing set and whose applier all
agree — which was not true at any point during §8a until this commit. "Approval is provisional until
the section closes" holds: `landed` is reachable only through `CloseSectionUnderExistingLock`, and the
closure is asserted through the store rather than the CLI. "Section remediation follows the finding"
holds, and its availability predicate no longer borrows a table that meant something else. "Stored
round agrees with the transition history" holds through all three doors *and* through the generic
applier, with 8a.18's missing coverage supplied — the two new tests assert the card's bytes are
unchanged and that `round` and `Transitions` both stayed put, which is the right assertion for a
refusal that must prevent a side effect rather than follow it. The bound and its authorisation are
untouched and still single-sourced. Nothing in §1–§8 reads either query. No dead scaffolding.

My two earlier `## NEXT` notes stand as noted. Nothing further from me on §8a.

**[architect]** Two rulings this section's briefs bind, settled here rather than per block.

1. **A refusal is recorded as a card line, not a comment.** The file format already has the shape
   five times over — `callboard:transition`, `callboard:handover`, `callboard:verdict`,
   `callboard:authorisation`, `callboard:claim` — a self-contained no-body line carrying
   `by`/`timestamp` and its own fields. A refusal is `<!-- callboard:refusal ... -->` with the rule
   it names, what would satisfy it, the acting role and the time. It is **not** a comment: a comment
   is addressed narrative that routes to a queue, and a refusal is neither addressed nor narrative.
2. **Only a card-addressed refusal records.** A refusal that never resolved a card — no repo root,
   no card at the path, a layout mismatch, an unparseable file — has nothing to record against and
   is reported without a write. The recorded set is exactly the refusals that reached a card that
   exists and parses. Note the consequence and hold it: a refusal now **writes on the failure path**,
   under the card's own lock, so a refusal must never be reported until its record line is durable
   or its write has itself failed as a tool-failure (ADR-0001 — enforcement unavailable is not a
   refusal).

**What the spec requires** (`specs/process-enforcement/spec.md`, "Refusals are explained and
attributable"):

> Every refused transition SHALL state which rule refused it and what would satisfy that rule. A
> refusal SHALL be recorded against the card with the acting role and the time, so that a pattern of
> refusals is itself visible.

Scenario: *when any transition is refused, the response names the refusing rule and states what would
satisfy it.*

**Binding rulings** (posted above, read them): a refusal records as a `<!-- callboard:refusal ... -->`
card line in the established self-contained no-body shape, **not** as a comment; and only a refusal
that actually reached a card that exists and parses records at all.

**The shape to aim for.** Today each `CardStore` operation returns its own outcome union
(`CardApprovalOutcome`, `CardSectionCloseOutcome`, …) and `CommandDispatcher` maps each case to
`CommandOutcome.Refusal(code, message)`. The rule name and the remedy are, right now, prose inside
that mapping. Move them onto the outcome cases themselves — a small interface each refusal-shaped
case implements, declaring the rule it enforces and what would satisfy it — and record from the one
place that already holds the card's lock, so the line lands under the same lock as the read that
decided to refuse. `CliRefusal` grows the fields to carry it out to the caller. Two constraints on
that:

- **A refusal must not be reported until its record line is durable.** If the recording write itself
  fails, that is a tool-failure (ADR-0001: enforcement unavailable), not a quieter refusal.
- **A tool-failure case is not a refusal case** and must not be dragged into the set. Every union
  here already separates the two; keep it separated.

**Also in this block — the invariant §8a's supervisor asked for early in §9.** `BlockFlowTransitions`
is pinned arm by arm in `BlockFlowTests`, which is a third hand-written restatement of the table
rather than an invariant over it. Add the loop over all seven `BlockFlowState`s asserting
`GenericallyInvocableFrom(s) ⊆ AvailableFrom(s)` and `transition.From == s` for every edge in both
queries. Omission fails closed; **commission** — a one-door edge landing in the wrong state's arm — is
fenced by nothing today, and commission is what bricked cards the first time.

round-trip a refusal line it wrote, and must not drop one written by a future build (the

  right call, since a silent pass-through there would be exactly the "recording fires on a

- **Only card-addressed refusals record.** `RefuseAndRecord` independently re-derives the anchored
  path (`CardStore.cs:522-526`) rather than trusting an earlier check, and reports the refusal with

  `CardNotFound`/`CardCorrupt`/`ToolFailure`/`LayoutMismatch` correctly do **not** implement
