**The ruling: split the retrofit by whether §9 itself later touches the union.** Neither of the two
options as posed is right. Opportunistic-and-sweep leaves the refusal surface diverging for the whole
of §9 — blocks B–E would spend the section adding *new* refusals to a shape that is uniform in one
union out of seventeen, and 9.10 would become a cleanup rather than a completeness check. But one
retrofit block over ~90 remaining card-addressed cases is not reviewable, and retrofitting a union
that a later block is about to rewrite is double work reviewed twice.

   `CardSectionCloseOutcome`, `CardBlockedByOutcome`, `ChangeArchiveOutcome`, and the question
   creation path. Each of those blocks retrofits **its own union, entire**, as part of its own work.
   That is a done-gate on B, C, D and E, not a later sweep: a block of §9 does not get to leave a
   refusal in its own union on the old shape.
2. **The eleven unions §9 never touches** get two dedicated retrofit blocks, carved by family and run
   **before** B, so that B–E write into a surface that has already converged:
   - **A2 — the register and rules family**: `CardRuleCompactOutcome`, `CardRulePromoteOutcome`,
     `CardRegisterDischargeOutcome`, `CardDecisionSupersedeOutcome`, `CardSectionAuthorisationOutcome`.

     `CardFindingRecordOutcome`, `CardGateResultOutcome`, `CardCreateOutcome`, `CardWriteResult`.

   `ICardRefusalReason`'s implementors proving every refusal-shaped case is in the format and fires in
   a test — with nothing left to retrofit by the time it runs, so what it measures is coverage rather

not one case for want of a `changeName` argument, it is **three of five cases —

not implement `ICardRefusalReason`, as now) and a resolved variant that records. If that makes the
union wider, the union gets wider; case-type uniformity is not worth a silent hole, and a case that
is card-addressed on one path and not another is a case that wants splitting. Test the resolved

  avoids lock acquisition too.

**Build the gate, not the audit.** A test that enumerates every `ICardRefusalReason` implementor in
the product assembly and fails when one has no test proving it fires and records. Concretely, it needs
to answer, mechanically: *for each refusal-shaped case, is there a test that provokes it and asserts a

on the ordinary runtime, so reflection is available to it even though the product is NativeAOT and must
stay reflection-free. **Do not add reflection to the product to make the test easier.**

How you establish the "has a test" side is yours to design, and it is the interesting part of this
block. Options include an explicit registry the gate cross-checks against the enumerated set, or
observing recorded entries across the suite. Pick one and **argue for it in the DEVLOG before you
build it** — a gate that is easy to satisfy without testing anything is worse than no gate, because it
reports the coverage we have been failing to actually have.

**The gate must fail loudly and namefully.** When a future block adds a refusal case and no test, the
failure message names the case and says what would satisfy it — the same standard we hold the
product's own refusals to. A gate whose failure requires an investigation to interpret is a gate that
gets suppressed.

them.** Blocks A through B were reviewed case by case, but they were reviewed by a reader, and this is
the first mechanical check. If it turns up an uncovered case, post it here with the case named. If it
turns up many, stop and post before writing thirty tests — that changes the block's size and is my
call, not yours.

**[worker]** Design for the coverage gate (9.10) — posting before I build it, per the brief.

**Enumeration side (product):** reflection over the product assembly, in the test project only,
finding every concrete type that implements `ICardRefusalReason`. The product stays reflection-free
(NativeAOT, ADR-0002) — nothing here touches `src/Callboard`.

**"Has a test" side — a hand-maintained registry, cross-checked three ways, not trusted on
presence alone.** A `Dictionary<Type, (Type TestClass, string TestMethod)>` maps each case type to
the one test that proves it — the same pairing the reviewer already re-derives by hand every block
(block B's review read all eleven `CardSectionVerdictOutcome` cases against their test bodies one by
one). Presence of an entry is not what the gate trusts. Three checks, all mechanical:

1. **Bijection, not one-way lookup.** The registry's keys must exactly equal the reflected set — a
   product case with no entry fails, named; an entry pointing at a type that no longer implements
   the interface (renamed, removed, or never did) fails too. The map can't drift out of sync with
   the code silently in either direction.
2. **The named method is real and live.** Reflect the test assembly for that `(TestClass,
   TestMethod)`, assert the `MethodInfo` exists, carries `[Fact]`/`[Theory]`, and isn't `Skip`-ed.
3. **The method's own source text is read back and must mention `.Refusals`.** This is the one that
   stops "point the registry at any passing test" from satisfying the gate — a method that never
   inspects the card's recorded refusal history (only the returned outcome's type, say) fails this
   check even though it exists, runs, and passes. Deliberately textual, not a re-execution of each
   test's assertions: re-verifying *what* a test asserts is the reviewer's job, already established
   practice in this section — this gate's job is narrower: no case ships unregistered, and no
   registered entry can be a stub.

**Why not the other option (observe recorded entries across the whole suite at runtime)?** It would
prove more per case (an entry made by running code, not asserted by a human once) but needs either a
shared mutable listener wired into every test process — a global side channel this codebase has
deliberately avoided (§2's own precedent: test seams are threaded parameters, never shared statics)
— or a change to `CardStore` itself to notify something outside it, which is scope this block wasn't
given. The registry design needs no production change and no shared state; its residual risk (an
entry that names a real, running, `.Refusals`-touching test but a wrong assertion inside it) is
exactly the risk code review already covers today, so it isn't new exposure — it's the exposure the
old paragraph-only version of this rule always had, made everywhere else mechanical.

**The gate's failure message names the case type (full name) and prints the same "add an entry
mapping it to a test that asserts a `CardRefusalEntry` landed" remedy in every failure mode** —
missing, stale, method-not-found, skipped, and no-`.Refusals` all say what's wrong and what fixes it,
not just that something failed.

filled rather than stopped on, per the brief's own threshold:**

   RaiseNit_BlockCardWithDisagreeingRound_Refuses_AndRecordsAgainstTheCard`.

   `CardNitStoreTests.DispositionNit_BlockCardWithDisagreeingRound_Refuses_AndRecordsAgainstTheCard`.

   (`ApplyBlockTransition_TargetIsNotABlockCard_Refuses`) and asserted the outcome type, but never

   `BlockTransition_ChangesRequested_UndispositionedNit_Refuses` asserted the refusal code over the

None of the four is a case that was actually failing open — all four already refuse correctly in

**[architect]** Ruling on block C's review. → @worker

**The gate passed over a real defect on its first outing, and the reviewer found it by attacking the
gate rather than reading it.** One registry entry —
`CardDecisionSupersedeOutcome.NotADecisionCard` — points at a test whose only `.Refusals` statement is
`Assert.Empty(ruleRead.Refusals)`: an anchor-mismatch fixture from A2 that proves the case does *not*
record. It satisfies bijection, exists, is unskipped, and mentions `.Refusals`, so `make gates` comes
back green over a case whose registered proof asserts the opposite of coverage. The test that does
prove recording — added in A2's own remediation for exactly this reason — sits unregistered in the
same file.

Two changes, and the second is the one that matters:

1. **Repoint the entry** to `SupersedeDecision_SupersedingCardIsNotADecision_ProperlyScoped_Refuses_AndRecords`.
2. **Close the proxy: reject a registered test whose `.Refusals` usage is entirely `Assert.Empty`.**
   The reviewer established that the general closure — matching the case's type name inside the test —
   does not work (ten false positives against CLI-boundary tests that correctly assert by wire code
   rather than type name), so hand-declared mapping stays irreducible. But this specific weakness has
   a targeted, cheap closure, it would have caught this exact defect, and "the registered proof asserts
   emptiness" is never coverage. Do that one.

**Do not go further than that.** I am not asking for a general proof that the registered test provokes
the registered case; the reviewer tried the obvious form and it fails against a legitimate testing
idiom. A gate is allowed to have a hand-maintained seam. What it is not allowed to do is report
coverage from an assertion of absence.

**Note for the section review, carried with the two already recorded.** The gate found four gaps a
case-by-case reader missed; attacking the gate then found a fifth the gate itself passed over. The
reviewer's pattern analysis is worth keeping: the mechanical gaps cluster on a widely-duplicated
generic check assumed covered by precedent, and on old foundational tests never revisited after they
gained recording — while the fifth is a third shape, **a case with two similarly-named existing tests,
where a hasty mapping lands on the wrong one.** That shape is where case-by-case review has now failed
twice. Any case carrying more than one pre-existing test is where I would look first, and it is a

*whole* section-close call on the first block that fails it — the same all-or-nothing shape as every
other multi-card write in this codebase. `ValidateBlockForLanding` checks `BlockNotApproved`,
`RoundDisagreesWithHistory`, `BlockGateAbsent`, `BlockGateFailed` — nothing about `blocked_by`.
`block transition land` is refused unconditionally at CLI parse (`CommandParser.cs:196-203`, §8a), so
there is no second door. `close` (`Landed → Closed`) *is* already guarded — it resolves through the
generic `ApplyBlockTransitionUnderExistingLock`, which carries 9.8's guard for every transition name
not in `RoundIncrementingTransitionNames`. So the hole is precisely: an approved block, blocked on an
open PO question, can still reach `Landed` by its section closing, and that is the *only* forward
motion in the whole state machine `blocked_by` doesn't currently reach. `ValidateBlockForLanding` is
exactly the right seam — it is the single per-block choke point that already refuses the whole call
before any write, the same shape `FindBlockingOpenProductOwnerQuestion` already plugs into twice.
Nothing about it requires block D specifically; the worker's reasoning for not reaching into
`CardSectionCloseOutcome` (touching it would trigger this carve's own "retrofit the union entire" rule

**2. On the `RoleNotPermitted`/`question-answer-missing-answer` consistency question — there is a
real line, but it doesn't fully settle the question you're actually asking.** The line: block B's
`RoleNotPermitted` moved to record because the card was *already going to be read and locked anyway*
for every other check in `RecordApprovalUnderExistingLock` — recording cost nothing but the write
itself. `question answer`'s missing-answer refusal fires at CLI parse, before any lock is acquired or
any file opened; making it record would mean adding a full resolve-lock-read specifically to support
this one check, which is real, if modest, added machinery for a check that never needs the card's own
state to decide. That is a genuine, non-arbitrary distinction — "argv-decidable" was never quite
block B's dispositive test; "does resolving cost anything given what's already happening" was, and
here it would cost something new. What the distinction does *not* settle is whether the **pattern**
matters enough to pay that cost anyway — "an agent repeatedly marks questions answered with nothing
behind them" is a real integrity signal, arguably as much the incumbent failure mode as an architect
approving its own work. I don't think the current disposition is obviously wrong, but I also don't
think it's obviously right by mechanical application of the B ruling — it is a values call about
whether this specific pattern is worth the added resolution machinery, and I'd rather you rule it
explicitly than have it stand on the "same shape as `obligation create`" analogy alone, since that
analogy is about the *check*, not about whether *this* pattern is worth recording.

**1. The standing line: a refusal records when it is a statement *about the card*; it does not record
when it is a statement about the *command's own well-formedness*.** The reviewer put the values call
to me rather than resolving it, correctly, and this is the answer — it governs E and F too, so it goes
in the thread rather than in one block's head.

The cost argument (resolving a card that would otherwise not be touched) is real but it is not the
line, because it would have decided block B the other way. The line is what the refusal is *about*:

- `RoleNotPermitted` says **"you may not approve this block."** It is a claim about an actor acting on
  that specific card, and the card's own history is exactly where "the architect tried to approve me"
  belongs. It records. That is what I ruled in B and it stands.
- `question-answer-missing-answer` says **"your command is incomplete."** It is not a claim about the
  question at all — the card has nothing to learn from it, and the question's history would be
  recording someone's shell typo. It does not record. The worker's disposition is right, for a better
  reason than the one given.

So: argv-decidability is not the test, and neither is cost. **Ask what the refusal asserts.** If it
asserts something about the record — this card's state, this card's threads, who acted on this card,
another card it names — it records. If it asserts only that the invocation was malformed, it reports
and stops. Apply this in E and F without asking again.

Product Owner question is refused**, naming the block and the question. Without this, 9.8's guard on
the generic transitions and `approve` is a fence with a gate left open beside it.

**`9.4` — refuse section close over open obligations owed by that section.** Spec:
`process-enforcement`, "Section close settles its obligations". Each obligation SHALL be discharged,
promoted to a wider scope, or declined with a recorded reason — **so the refusal lists the obligations
*and* the dispositions available**, not just the count. Obligation cards are `CardScope.Change` and
carry the owing section; note that block D renamed that flag to `--section` on `obligation create`.

**`9.5` — refuse section close over open undeferred questions.** Spec: "Section close settles its
questions" — a question deferred to a *named target* permits the close and stays open against that
target. Block D built the `open`/`answered`/`deferred` vocabulary and `question defer --target`, so
the vocabulary you need exists.

**But there is a gap you must close first, and I am ruling on it now rather than letting you discover
it.** `question create` does **not** record the section that raised the question — `ParsedCommand.
QuestionCreate` carries `FilePath, Title, ActingRole, OwedByRole, Body, WorkingDirectory, Timestamp`
and nothing else. A question is `CardScope.Repository`, so its *scope* deliberately outlives any one
section; but "which section raised it" is a different fact from "what is its lifetime", and `9.5`
cannot mean anything without it. `CardFrontmatter.Section` already exists and is documented as exactly
this — *"the section a card was raised within, or empty when the card is not tied to one"*.

**Ruling: add `--section` to `question create` and record it.** Do not widen `9.5` to "every open
question anywhere blocks every section close" to route around the missing field — that would be a
refusal that fires on unrelated work, which is worse than one that does not fire at all, because it
teaches the caller to route around the tool. A question raised outside any section carries an empty
section and blocks no section's close.

**`9.6` — two halves, and they are not the same kind of thing.** Spec: "Section close settles its
addressed threads".

- **The refusal**: an unresolved comment addressed to a role within the section blocks the close, and
  the refusal lists **the dispositions available for it** — resolve, promote to a `question`, promote
  to a `decision`, or decline with a recorded reason.
- **The prompt**: a comment left unresolved for longer than one round is surfaced to the addressed
  role **without refusing anything**. The spec says why in its own words — *"to keep this gate from
  becoming a formality discharged in bulk at the moment of closing"*. **Do not implement the prompt as
  a refusal.** A prompt that refuses is just an earlier refusal, and the requirement's entire point is
  that it is not one.

(`round` on `BlockCardFields`), threads live on cards, and a section spans several blocks. Say what you
conclude and why before you build it. If the honest answer is that the spec's wording does not
determine it, **stop and post rather than choosing** — that is a Product Owner call and I will take it.

**The standing line from block D applies to every refusal you add here**: a refusal records when it
asserts something about the record, and reports without recording when it asserts only that the
invocation was malformed. All four of this block's refusals assert things about the record.

that proves it fires *and* records; a registered test whose `.Refusals` assertions are all

reporting format entire**, per the standing rule.

**9.6 — the two halves, and a real contradiction I had to resolve rather than choose blindly.**
The refusal (`CardSectionCloseOutcome.UnresolvedAddressedThread`) sweeps the section's own comments
first, then each block's, for any live comment addressed to any role (`CardCommentRouting.LiveAddressedThreadIds`,
a new role-agnostic sibling of the existing `LiveThreadIdsAddressedTo` — a section close is not
acting as any one role). Records against whichever card carries the thread.

Here's the contradiction the brief warned me to expect. Read literally, "the system SHALL refuse to
close a section while any comment addressed to a role... remains unresolved" (no age qualifier) and
"an addressed comment [aged past one round]... surfaces... without refusing anything" cannot both be
true of the same thread at the same time — if *every* unresolved addressed comment already refuses,
no section could ever reach `Closed` carrying an aged one to prompt about, and "without refusing
anything" would be false. I found this out empirically: my first pass computed the ageing prompt only
after every refusal had already passed, and a fixture with a fresh (non-aged) unresolved comment
correctly refused — but a fixture for the aged case *also* refused, because ageing didn't exempt
anything from the refusal set. Two tests contradicted each other until I fixed one.

**Resolution:** the refusal and the ageing prompt are never both true of the same thread. A thread
still within the round it was raised in (on its own block — round is a block property, never a
section's) is a hard blocker. Once it has survived a round boundary on that block, it is *excluded*
from the refusal's own set and only ever prompted — read together with the spec's own reason ("to
keep this gate from becoming a formality discharged in bulk at the moment of closing"): a refusal
that never expires would just get bulk-resolved the moment someone wants to close, which is the
formality the spec is naming. A thread on the *section* card itself has no round to age out of, so
it always falls in the refusal, never the prompt — "round" genuinely has no meaning for a section,
which settles the "rounds belong to blocks, a section spans several" half of what I was asked to
post rather than silently decide. This is my read of a literal contradiction in the requirement
text, not an invented threshold; posting it here per the brief's own instruction. `CardCommentRouting.AgeingAddressedThreadIds`
(new) computes "aged" as: a live addressed comment for which some later round-incrementing transition
timestamp exists on that same block's own history — i.e., the round it was raised in has since
closed out from under it. `CardSectionCloseOutcome.Closed` gained `AgeingThreads` (surfaced through
`SectionCloseResult.ageingThreads` in the CLI envelope), computed once every refusal above has
already passed.

back to me and I'll rework it.

**[architect]** Answering the `❓` on 9.6. **There is no contradiction in the spec, and this is not a
Product Owner call — the requirement's own purpose clause decides it.** You were right to stop and
post rather than push on; the reading is what I am correcting, not the instinct. → @worker

**The misreading is *when* the prompt happens.** You implemented both halves at close time, and at
close time they genuinely cannot both hold — that part of your analysis is correct, and your two
contradicting tests proved it honestly. But the prompt was never a close-time behaviour:

> To keep this gate from becoming a formality discharged in bulk **at the moment of closing**, the
> system SHALL surface addressed comments left unresolved for longer than one round, as a prompt
> rather than a constraint.

The clause names the failure it exists to prevent: threads being cleared *en masse* at the gate. A
prompt that fires **at** the gate cannot prevent that — it is at the gate. The prompt is an **earlier
surfacing**, during the section's life, to the role the comment is addressed to, so the thread is dealt
with while there is still time to deal with it properly. "As a prompt rather than a constraint" says
only that this surfacing refuses nothing; it does not carve an exemption out of the refusal.

Read that way both requirements hold literally and neither needs amending:

- **The refusal is absolute.** *Every* unresolved addressed thread blocks the close, with no age
  qualifier. Each one is resolved, promoted to a `question`, promoted to a `decision`, or declined
  with a recorded reason — the four dispositions the requirement already names.
- **The prompt is a separate surfacing** on a different path at a different time, and it refuses
  nothing.

**Note what your resolution does, which is the strongest evidence against it.** Exempting aged threads
from the refusal means a section may close over an addressed thread *precisely because it has been
ignored for long enough*. That does not prevent bulk discharge at the gate — it removes the gate for
exactly the threads that have been neglected longest, and rewards neglect with an exemption. The
requirement's purpose clause is aimed at the opposite outcome.

**What to change:**

1. **Drop the age exemption from the refusal.** `UnresolvedAddressedThread` fires on every live
   addressed thread, section-owned or block-owned, regardless of round. Your fixture that "correctly
   refused" for the aged case was correct; it was the other test that was wrong.
2. **Keep `AgeingAddressedThreadIds`** — the computation is right and it is genuinely 9.6's second
   half. Your definition of aged (a live addressed comment on a block whose round has since
   incremented past the one it was raised in) is sound, and so is the finding that a section-owned
   thread has no round and therefore never ages. Keep both.
3. **Surface it where the addressed role will see it before close, not on the `Closed` outcome.**
   `section status` is the §9-era surface that exists and is read during a section's life; put it
   there. Leave `Closed.AgeingThreads` off — by the time a close succeeds, every addressed thread has
   been settled, so the field would always be empty and would be dead weight in the envelope.
4. **§10 is where this prompt finally lands in the queue.** The working-context response is 10.1–10.2's
   and routes on unresolved addressed threads already. Post a line for `## NEXT` saying §10 should
   consume `AgeingAddressedThreadIds` when it builds the queue, so this does not have to be
   rediscovered.

Everything else in the block stands as reported — the carried arm's disposition (a fact about the
block, recorded against the block), 9.4's conservative refuse-on-unreadable within the section's own
directory versus 9.5's skip-on-unreadable outside it, and taking no new locks. Those are all right,
and the asymmetry in the two scans is correctly reasoned rather than accidental.

**1. Optional `--section` on `question create` — I don't think it's the A2 defect, and here's the
structural reason, not just an instinct.** A2's `--change` had no legitimate omission case: every real
`rule promote` call targets a still-change-scoped rule, so making the flag required cost nothing and
closed the hole completely. `--section` is different in kind: the domain genuinely has two classes of
question — one meant to gate a specific section's close, one that is legitimately independent
(register: "Question outlives its change", the same reasoning that makes the question's own *scope*
`Repository`). Making `--section` required would be wrong for the second class — it would force every
orphan question into a section it doesn't belong to, or block the case the spec explicitly protects.
So "make it required" isn't an available fix here the way it was for `PromoteRule`; the two situations
share a shape (an optional flag a caller can silently omit) but not the same defect, because there is
no single always-correct value being silently defaulted away — the correct value genuinely depends on
a fact about the world only the caller knows.

That said, the residual risk you're naming is real: nothing signals the consequence of omitting it.
Checked `RunQuestionCreate` (`CommandDispatcher.cs:2048-2077`) and `CardCreateResult`
(`CardCreateResult.cs`) directly — the create response has **no `section` field at all**, so a caller
cannot even see from the response whether the section it meant to name landed, was mistyped and
silently dropped, or was never supplied. An agent creating a question mid-section who forgets the flag
gets a normal success response with nothing distinguishing it from an intentionally-orphaned question.
On the third question you asked — whether anything in the card's own context could infer the section
rather than trusting argv — I'd advise against it: this tool is deliberately built to never infer
ambient state (the same "does not shell out, does not resolve a SHA" discipline §8 established for
`reviewed_state`), and inferring "the currently active section" would be a first exception to that
rule, not a small one. **My recommendation, not a blocker**: surface the recorded `section` (or its
absence) in `question create`'s own response — the same visibility `owedBy` already got in block D's
carried item G — so a caller sees the consequence immediately rather than discovering it only by
reading the card back later or by a section closing with a question nobody meant to exclude. I'd
raise this with the Product Owner or fold it into whichever later block touches this response next,
not hold this block on it — the current behaviour is not incorrect, it's under-signalled.

Two scenarios: an open orphaned obligation refuses the archive and the response lists the obligations

obligation staying live at its new scope.

obligation must refuse the archive, not be quietly settled by it. Silently discharging the exact cards
the spec says to stop on is the "recording a violation instead of preventing it" failure this whole
capability exists to close.

necessarily orphaned (its owing section closed), or can one be owed by a section that is still open —

**[worker]** Scoping findings for **block F (9.9)**, as briefed. Not building — reporting and handing
back.

**Problem 1 — not every open change-scoped obligation at archive is orphaned; one can be owed by a
section that is still open.** `RegisterCardFields.OwedBy` names a section id, and every obligation
lives physically inside its owing section's directory (`CardStore.CloseSection`'s own obligation scan,
`CardStore.cs:2452-2472`, confirms this: it walks `sectionDirectory` and matches `OwedBy` against the
closing section's own id). `SectionCardFields.ClosedBy`/`ClosedAt` (set together, never independently)
is the only marker of whether the owing section has actually closed.

9.4 already refuses a section's own close while it owes any open obligation — so by the time a section
closes, every obligation it owed at that moment is non-open. The orphaned case the spec scenario
actually names — "a change is archived carrying an open obligation **whose owing section has
closed**" — is therefore an obligation created (or left open) **after** its owing section already
closed: nothing re-checks it once that section is done, so it surfaces only at archive, exactly the
spec's "observed to surface at archive time or not at all." An obligation whose owing section is
**still open** is a different case entirely: work on that section hasn't finished, 9.4 hasn't run yet,
and the register spec's own "no carry-forward step" principle (register: "SHALL NOT require a
carry-forward step at archive... a handoff is a transit"), plus its explicit sibling scenario for an
open question surviving an archive untouched, both point the same way — that obligation is not
orphaned, and archive should neither refuse over it nor discharge it. It should move into the archive
exactly as it stands, live at its own scope, for the same reason an open question does today.

**So 9.9's gate is: partition open change-scoped obligations by whether `OwedBy` names a section whose
own card is `ClosedBy`/`ClosedAt`-set.** Owed-by-a-closed-section (or by a section id with no matching
card at all, e.g. already removed) → orphaned → the 9.9 gate applies, refuse unless
discharged/promoted/declined. Owed-by-a-still-open-section → not orphaned → leave untouched, carried
into the archive as-is. **`ArchiveChange`'s current behaviour (`CardStore.cs:3200` onward) is wrong in
both directions at once**: it discharges every open obligation regardless of which bucket it's in
(silently settling genuinely-orphaned ones instead of refusing on them, per the doc comment's own "an
open obligation... becomes discharged, and nothing else"), and it would incorrectly discharge a
still-owed, still-live obligation whose section simply hasn't closed yet.

**Problem 2 — confirmed: only `discharge` exists as a command today; `promote` and decline-with-reason
do not exist for `obligation`.** `obligation`'s only verbs are `create` and `discharge`
(`ParsedCommand` in `CommandDispatcher.cs` has `ObligationCreate` and reuses the generic
`RegisterDischarge`; there is no `ObligationPromote` anywhere in the tree). `promote` exists only as
`RulePromote`/`RulePromoteConstitution` — rule-scoped, not obligation-scoped. There is no
decline-with-a-recorded-reason path for any register card kind.

**This is not hypothetical for 9.9 alone — 9.4's existing refusal already names both missing verbs.**
Its message (`CommandDispatcher.cs` `onOpenObligations`, section-close-open-obligations) reads: "each
must be discharged, promoted to a wider scope, or declined with a recorded reason before this section
can close." That refusal has been live since block E and already tells a caller to reach for verbs
that don't exist. 9.9's second scenario ("promotion satisfies the archive gate") cannot be satisfied at
all without `obligation promote`, and a decline path is likewise entirely missing.

**Handing back per the brief — not building `obligation promote` or a decline-with-reason path on my
own initiative, and not narrowing 9.9's refusal to name only `discharge`.** Both problems are as
described in the brief; nothing was missed on my part. This is a scope call: does §9 grow two new
verbs (and does 9.4's own refusal text get corrected regardless of what 9.9 needs), or does 9.9 land
scoped to what exists with 9.4 also fixed to stop naming remedies it can't offer? ❓ @architect —
ruling needed before I touch `ArchiveChange` or the refusal itself.

The small carried item (`question create` response gains `section`) is unrelated to either problem and
is a one-field addition — happy to land it now or fold it into whatever block follows; holding off only
because the brief said "alongside whatever else this block ends up being" and the block's shape isn't
settled yet.

**[architect]** **Product Owner ruling on block F's scoping question: §9 grows two verbs, and the
`register` spec is amended to match.** The worker's findings were right on both counts and stopping to
ask was correct.

**The conflict, for the record.** `process-enforcement` requires an orphaned obligation to be
"discharged, promoted to a wider scope, or declined with a recorded reason", and 9.9's second scenario
is *"Promotion satisfies the archive gate"*. `register`'s promotion requirement opens with a general
sentence but its concrete SHALL only ever named **rules**, so §7 built `rule promote` and nothing else.
Two capabilities in the same change disagreed, and §9 is where they met.

**Why the discharge-only alternative was rejected**, since the reasoning binds the implementation:
discharge asserts the obligation was *met*. If it is the only route past the archive gate, then the
only way to archive a change carrying an orphaned obligation is to declare work done that was not done.
A gate whose sole exit manufactures a false settlement is worse than no gate — it converts an honest
"this was never finished" into a lie, in the record whose entire purpose is that it can be read back
honestly. That is the incumbent's failure mode with extra steps.

**`specs/register/spec.md` is amended** (`VALIDATE_EXIT:0`): promotion is no longer rule-only — an
obligation outliving its change is promotable on the same terms, same card, identity, text and thread
retained. A new requirement, *"Declining is distinguishable from discharging"*, makes declining a
recorded outcome in its own right with two scenarios: declining records the reason and is not
represented as a discharge, and declining with no reason is refused.

**Note what the amendment deliberately does not do.** It states the observable requirement — the record
distinguishes declined from discharged — and does **not** dictate whether that is a third lifecycle
state or a discharged card carrying a decline reason. §7 built a two-state lifecycle
(`RegisterLifecycleState`) and widening it is not a decision to take casually inside a block; the
requirement is what must be true, and the modelling is block F's to propose.

**3. The declined-vs-discharged modelling does not satisfy the amended spec, and I think this is the
real finding, not a close call.** Traced `DeclineObligationUnderExistingLock`'s actual write
(`CardStore.cs:3352-3356`): `Frontmatter.Status = RegisterLifecycleState.Discharged.ToWireString()` —
the card's own `status` field is set to the literal string `"discharged"`, identical to an ordinary
discharge, with `DischargedBy`/`DischargedAt` also both set exactly as a real discharge sets them. The
only difference is the presence of `RegisterFields.DeclinedReason`, a side field a reader has to
already know to check.

The amended requirement's own words: *"it stops being open, the reason is part of the record, and
**it is not represented as discharged**."* The card's single most legible, canonical field — the one
every other scan in this codebase checks first (`RegisterLifecycleStateWireFormat.TryParse(...Status,
...)`, used identically inside this very method three lines above the write in question) — reads
"discharged." A human or a future tool reading the raw file (ADR-0003: the record stays readable
without this tool) sees exactly the representation the requirement says must not be produced, unless
it already knows the `declined_reason` convention exists to look for. The requirement's own rationale
is direct about this: *"'we decided not to' is the outcome most worth finding later, and it is the one
a discharge would hide."* Here, the discharge-shaped `status` field is exactly what's shown; the
distinguishing fact is a footnote. I don't think this satisfies "is not represented as discharged" —
I think it fails it in the plain sense, not merely a stricter one. It also reintroduces, at the single
card's level, the same failure mode the Product Owner ruling rejected at archive's level for
discharge-only: a route past the gate that manufactures the very assertion ("this was met") the
requirement exists to keep honest.

I'm not proposing the fix — the worker's own reasoning for rejecting a third `RegisterLifecycleState`
(§7's still-binding two-state lifecycle requirement) is sound and not mine to override — but I don't
think a discharged card carrying a decline reason is the modelling that satisfies what you wrote. This
needs your ruling, and I'd flag it as the one to resolve before this lands, not after.

**1. `OrphanedObligations` not implementing `ICardRefusalReason` — workable to close, not free.**
Agree the "no single card" reasoning as currently stated doesn't follow to "record against none" —
it only rules out one arbitrary card, not each of the N obligations named. Recording against each is
mechanically possible: this codebase already has N-card-write precedent (`CompactRules`,

The mechanism this section built is sound, and I want to say that first because most of what follows
is about its edges rather than its middle. I verified the write-on-the-failure-path contract **as a
set**, not per block: all 78 `ICardRefusalReason` implementors across seventeen unions, every one
constructed only into a `RefuseAndRecord` call, both overloads sharing one body that returns the
refusal *only* on a successful `AtomicWrite` and maps every write failure to the union's own
`ToolFailure`. Exactly two bare constructions exist — `CardNitDispositionOutcome.RaisedCardAlreadyExists`
(`CardStore.cs:1180`) and `CardSectionVerdictOutcome.NewFindingCardAlreadyExists` (`CardStore.cs:2218`)
— and both are the `AtomicWrite` race arms A3's and B's reviews established are structurally
unreachable. **The contract holds across every case that is in the set.** Six of my findings are
about what is *not* in the set, and why nothing could tell you that.

### Blockers

Four refusal-shaped cases — `NotABlockCard`, `RoundDisagreesWithHistory`, `AlreadyBlockedBy`,
`NotBlockedBy` — all decided *after* a successful `ReadCard` inside
`UpdateBlockedByUnderExistingLock`, under the lock the read already holds. Every one of them is
card-addressed by D's own line: they assert facts about this card's kind, its round, and its own
`blocked_by` set. `NotABlockCard` and `RoundDisagreesWithHistory` are the *same case names* that
record in five other unions. None implements `ICardRefusalReason`; none records; none is in
`RefusalCoverageGateTests.Registry`. Both entry points are live CLI verbs (`block add-blocker`,
`block remove-blocker`, `CommandParser.cs:112`/`116`).

This is not an oversight inside a block — it is the carve. Your re-carve post named six unions as
belonging to B–E: `CardApprovalOutcome`, `CardSectionVerdictOutcome`, `CardSectionCloseOutcome`,
**`CardBlockedByOutcome`**, `ChangeArchiveOutcome`, and the question path. B took two, D minted the
question unions, E took section-close, F took archive. **Nobody took `CardBlockedByOutcome`**, and
A2/A3's eleven were carved as "the unions §9 never touches", so it was excluded from the retrofit
blocks too. A3's review then closed with "the retrofit is complete across all seventeen unions this
section touches" — a count, never an enumeration. `9.1`'s requirement ("A refusal SHALL be recorded
against the card, so that a pattern of refusals is itself visible") is unmet for this union.

**S2 — the coverage gate cannot see an opt-out, and S1 is the proof.**
(`tests/Callboard.Tests/RefusalCoverageGateTests.cs:166-167`.)

You asked whether the gate is strong enough for §10 to build against. Its hand-maintained
case→test seam is not its weak point — you and the reviewer bounded that one deliberately and
correctly. Its weak point is that its **domain is derived from the very declaration under audit**:

```
[.. typeof(ICardRefusalReason).Assembly.GetTypes()
    .Where(t => ... typeof(ICardRefusalReason).IsAssignableFrom(t))]
```

A case that omits the interface is not *uncovered* — it is outside the universe, so the bijection
reports total coverage over it. That is how four card-addressed refusals shipped through seven
blocks, every `[reviewer]` `Approve`, and an unbroken run of `GATES_EXIT:0`. The gate answers "is
every declared refusal proven?" It does not answer "has every refusal-shaped case been assessed?",
and that second question is the one §9 kept getting wrong by hand.

The closure is the gate's own idea moved up one level: a second bijection over **every concrete case
in every outcome union** (they are all `internal sealed record X : SomeOutcome`), each of which must
be either an `ICardRefusalReason` implementor or named on a short hand-declared exclusion list
carrying its reason. Adding a union or a case then forces a decision instead of permitting silence.
This is not the general "does the test provoke the case" proof you ruled out — it is bookkeeping over
a closed set the compiler already enumerates.

### Answers to the seven questions put to me

1. **Refusal coverage as a set / the failure-path write.** The contract holds — verified over all 78
   implementors mechanically, not by sampling. See the opening paragraph. The failure is the domain,
   not the mechanism (S1, S2). One note for `## NEXT`: when `AnchoredCardPath.TryCreate` fails,
   `RefuseAndRecord` (`CardStore.cs:600-604`) returns the refusal unrecorded and the CLI envelope
   carries `rule`/`remedy` identically either way — so a caller cannot distinguish "refused and
   recorded" from "refused, nothing recorded", which slightly undercuts "a pattern of refusals is
   itself visible" in exactly the state where the record is already abnormal.

2. **The `OrphanedObligations` exception.** The exception itself is sound and its doc comment is the
   best piece of reasoning-in-code in the section — it names and rejects the wrong reason before
   giving the right one. It does not undermine the rule on its merits. What it exposes is that
   **the section has no place where an exception is declared.** The interface contract, your base
   ruling and the gate all say "card-addressed ⟺ records"; F makes that false in one spot, and the
   only record of it is a comment on the type that breaks it. From outside, a considered carve-out
   and a forgotten union are indistinguishable — and §9 now contains one of each. S2's exclusion
   list is where the exception should live; that is the fix that makes it read as a decision from
   the outside as well as from the inside.

3. **The record-vs-malformed line.** Applied consistently across sixteen unions. I checked every
   non-categorical case that reports without recording: the two pre-lock `RoleNotPermitted`s,
   `EmptyAbsorbSet`, the three pre-lock self-reference cases, both creation surfaces,
   `CardWriteResult`'s pre-read cases, and the four parse-time refusals (`question-answer-missing-answer`,
   `obligation-missing-section`, the two required-flag checks) all sit correctly on the "malformed
   invocation" side. **One divergence** — S3 — and **one union never assessed against the line at
   all** — S1. Notably both are cases where an earlier block's disposition predates the line; the
   line itself is fine, the sweep back over pre-line dispositions never happened.

4. **The coverage gate's real strength.** Strong where you aimed it, blind where you did not. It
   genuinely closes "a rule arrives untested" — the three checks are structural, the `Assert.Empty`
   polarity closure is exactly narrow enough, and I confirmed by reading it that the bijection fires
   unconditionally on a new implementor. It does **not** close "a rule arrives undeclared", and that
   is a bigger hole than the hand-mapped seam, because the seam requires someone to write a wrong
   entry while the blind spot requires only that someone write nothing. **It needs S2 before §10
   builds more rules against it** — otherwise §10's rules inherit a gate that reports the coverage
   we have been failing to actually have, which is the exact sentence in your own block C brief.

5. **Spec drift.** Two findings, S5 and S6. On "does the code satisfy the amendments as they now

   (S6), and an amendment that changed archive's behaviour left an untouched requirement asserting
   the old one (S5).

6. **CLI surface.** `ParsedCommand.Match` is at **33** delegates (29 in §8, +4 here). That is
   exhaustiveness working as designed and I would not touch it; it is a scale note for `## NEXT`, not
   a finding. Required-vs-optional flags are consistent and well-reasoned: `--change` on
   `obligation promote` and `--reason` on `obligation decline` both apply A2's lesson at the door,

7. **`9.6`'s two halves.** Your ruling is implemented faithfully. `LiveAddressedThreadIds`

   `section status`, a pull surface, so it reaches the addressed role only when someone runs it —
   §10's queue is where it actually becomes a prompt, and `## NEXT` already carries that. And
   because `nit raise` requires `in-review` while every exit from `in-review` is gated on the nit
   being dispositioned, the ageing set is provably empty in any CLI-driven repository today. The
   computation is right and the surfacing is right; the requirement's purpose becomes real in §10,
   not here. Worth stating plainly rather than leaving §10 to discover.

Mechanically, every one of these outcome unions is discoverable without being named, from two

   directly on the type) gets every card-mutating outcome union for free — new unions included, the
   day a new `CardStore` method returns one.

   universe from also sweeping in domain value-unions that happen to be returned somewhere in
   `CardStore` (`CardScope` surfaced this exactly — a value union with no refusal concept at all,
   caught by the first filter alone). Every genuine outcome union in this codebase carries a
   `ToolFailure` case by convention (ADR-0001: enforcement-unavailable is always modelled), and no
   value union does. Confirmed against the actual codebase: this pair of filters yields exactly the
   twenty `*Outcome` types plus `CardWriteResult` — 21 unions, 200 concrete cases — with no hand-typed
   union name anywhere in the gate. (It also drops `CardFileParseResult` from the universe, correctly
   — its `Success`/`Failure` are a lower-level parse primitive that every higher-level union's own
   `CardCorrupt` case already re-reports; it is never itself a CLI-facing outcome.)

still a real discovered case (no stale exclusion surviving a rename/removal). Adding a union or a
case now forces a decision in one of two visible places — the interface or the dictionary — instead

not carelessness: **the file's own preamble documents the convention using the literal string the
convention is about.** Any writer that searches for `## NEXT` finds the sentence explaining `## NEXT`
before it finds `## NEXT`. The document describes itself, and the description is indistinguishable
from the thing described to every tool that reads it. The safe anchor is `^## NEXT$` and the naive one
is `## NEXT`, and the naive one is what anybody reaches for first.

**It goes to `## NEXT` as a live hazard owed by §13, in those terms** — not as "remember to anchor
properly", which has now failed four times, but as the concrete requirement that the append path be
mechanical and that whatever appends verify afterwards that exactly one `^## NEXT$` heading remains in
final position. `callboard` itself is the fix: cards are separate files with no shared anchor to
mis-hit, which is one of the specific incumbent failures this change exists to end. Until the tool
appends its own record, the mitigation has to be a check rather than a sentence.

Recording it this way is also the honest test of §9's own thesis. The section spent seven blocks
establishing that a rule which exists only as prose gets broken under pressure. This is that, in the
file where the section wrote it down.

### 2. The hardened gate — what it now holds, and what it still misses

I read the mechanism rather than the report. The universe is every `CardStore` return type that is an
abstract class declaring an abstract `Match` with a nested `ToolFailure` whose `BaseType` is the union;
the cases are its non-abstract nested direct subclasses. Two things I checked that nobody has stated:

- **The universe is complete today, not merely plausible.** I enumerated every abstract-record union in
  `src/Callboard/` declaring a nested `ToolFailure` — 23 of them — and confirmed each is returned
  *bare* by at least one `CardStore` method. Nothing is currently outside the reflected set.
- **`GetNestedTypes` is exhaustive, not a shortcut.** Every one of those unions declares a **private**
  constructor, so a case cannot be declared outside its union's body and compile. That is the
  structural fact the gate's discovery silently rests on, and it is worth writing down.

**What it would still miss, in the order §10 is likely to hit it:**

1. **Refusals decided at the CLI layer are entirely outside the universe.** The gate's domain is
   `CardStore`. Every refusal minted in `CommandParser`/`CommandDispatcher` — the parse-door
   `missing-argument`s, `ResolveAnyCardReference`'s refusals, `repo-root-not-found` — is invisible to
   it. §9 ruled those "malformed invocation" and that ruling is right, but it is a *ruling*, held in
   prose, over a growing surface: **this is S1's shape one layer up.** §10's queue and brief decide
   things at that layer. Say it in §10's first brief rather than discovering it in §10's review.
2. **Idiom departure** — a second store class, a non-abstract base, `Match` not declared directly on
   the type, `ToolFailure` renamed or nested deeper, or a union reachable only through a wrapping
   return type (`(SomeOutcome?, CardFile?)`, a shape this codebase already uses). The reviewer
   enumerated these; I agree with the list, and all require breaking nine sections of convention.
3. **It proves a case was *assessed*, not that it was assessed *correctly*.** An `Exclusions` entry
   with a plausible reason silences a genuinely card-addressed case exactly as effectively as omitting
   the interface did. **S3 was that defect, and this gate would not have caught S3 either.** What has
   changed is that the wrong answer is now keyed, reasoned and written where a reviewer reads it,
   instead of being a silence. That is the right trade; it should just not be mistaken for closure.

**Answer to the question you asked: yes, §10 and later can build against it.** It answers *"has every
refusal-shaped case been assessed?"*, it fires unconditionally on a new case, and its residue is
future-shaped rather than present. Residue (1) is the one that needs saying out loud before §10 starts.

---

### 3. What remediation round two introduced

**F1 — S5 is closed in the scenario and still open in the requirement it belongs to.**
(`specs/register/spec.md:45-49`.)

> Archiving a change **SHALL act as a filter that closes its change-scoped cards** and leaves cards of
> wider scope untouched.

Four lines below it the amended scenario now says *"with no obligation settled by the act of
archiving"*, and `ArchiveChange` makes **no write at all**. The normative sentence and its own scenario
contradict each other, and the sentence is the half carrying the SHALL. The worker saw this, named it
in the DEVLOG and stayed in scope — correctly, since the brief cited the scenario. But this is the same
defect S5 was, one paragraph higher, and `--strict` can no more see it than it could see S6. **Two
lines. This is the one item I would not close the section over.**

**F2 — `comment promote`'s link back to the section is a field that is empty on most card kinds, and
its test hand-writes a value production never produces.** (`CardStore.cs:3607`; fixture
`CardCommentPromoteTests.cs:155-156`; the gate it feeds, `CardStore.cs:2529`.)

The raised `question` inherits `card.Frontmatter.Section` from the card promoted from. 9.5's gate
refuses a close while an open question carries `Section == <this section's id>`. But `CreateCard`'s own
doc comment states the position exactly — `section` is *"left empty by every caller except
`question create`"* — and I confirmed that against every call site. `Section` is populated on questions
(`CommandDispatcher.cs:2173`), findings, and blocks minted by the §8a verdict path
(`CardStore.cs:2233`). It is **empty** on section cards (`CommandDispatcher.cs:2111`) and rule cards
(`:1999`, `:2966`).

So: promote a thread on a **block** card and 9.5 catches the question. Promote a thread on the
**section card** — the first of 9.6's two arms, `CardStore.cs:2557` — and the raised question carries
`Section: ""`, which 9.5 can never match, and the section closes over an open question demonstrably
raised in it. The requirement reads *"any `question` raised in it"*; on that path it is not satisfied.

Two honest qualifications, which is why this is not a hard blocker:

- **It is latent, not live.** No production path today appends an addressed comment to a section card
  (`nit raise` is block-only; `rule promote-constitution` addresses a rule card), so 9.6's section-card
  arm is currently unreachable. It goes live the moment §10 gives any verb a way to address a comment
  to a role on a section card — which is exactly what §10.1–10.2's queue work is about.
- **The test cannot see it by construction.** `WriteCardWithComment` builds a block card with
  `Section: "S-0001"` by hand and asserts the inheritance (`CardCommentPromoteTests.cs:58`). The
  mechanism is proven on a fixture; the *link* is never proven against a card any verb actually
  creates. That is why no block review could have found this, and it generalises: **`Frontmatter.
  Section` is now load-bearing for a refusal, and nothing states or enforces "every card that can carry
  an addressed thread has one".**

**F3 — the three new dispositions carry no authorisation at all, and one carries no content
requirement.** (`CardStore.cs:3410-3421` — there is no role check anywhere in `ResolveComment`;
`CommandDispatcher.cs:2795`, `2824`, `2883` — `--role` is used only as the resolving comment's author.)

Any role may resolve, decline or promote **any** thread on **any** card, including one addressed to the
Product Owner. `comment decline` requires `--reason`; `comment resolve` requires nothing but a
redirected stdin, so an **empty-bodied `comment resolve` is a decline without a recorded reason** — the
one disposition `register`'s "Declining requires a reason" exists to forbid, reachable through the verb
standing next to it. And 9.6's gate is role-agnostic by design, so the actor closing the section can
clear every thread on the card in a loop and close.

Being fair about this, because round two was right to build the verbs and the alternative — a gate with
no discharge path — was S4:

- The spec is **silent** on who may resolve. No requirement is textually unmet.
- The violation is **visible**: the resolving comment records its `Author`, so a reader sees that the
  architect resolved a Product-Owner-addressed thread. Degraded-mode reading survives.
- But 9.6's requirement states the hazard in as many words: *"To keep this gate from becoming a
  formality discharged in bulk at the moment of closing…"* The mitigation §9 chose for that sentence is
  the ageing prompt, which **refuses nothing** — and which, as I noted last pass, computes over a set
  provably empty in a CLI-driven repository today. So after round two the spec's own named hazard has
  no constraint against it, and the section's flagship gate is dischargeable unilaterally by the party
  it refuses.

This is a design call of exactly the shape the Product Owner ruled on for block F and again for S4, and
it has never been put to them. My reading, offered as input rather than as a finding: `resolve` belongs
to the addressee (and arguably the author), `decline` and `promote` are the routes for everyone else,
and `comment resolve` should require a non-empty body — one refusal case and a body check, not a
redesign.

**Note, not a finding: `comment` is half a surface.** Three dispositions and no way to *raise* an
addressed comment. `CardComment.To` is still set by exactly two production paths (`nit raise`,
`rule promote-constitution`), so 9.3 and 9.6 remain gates on a state a CLI-driven repository can barely
enter. §10 owes the other half; recorded here so §10 does not rediscover it.

### 4. §6 and §9 together — `AcquireLocksAndRecord<TOutcome>`

Clean, and the right call. The generalisation carries §6 block B's fifth-remediation reasoning forward
verbatim in the doc comment (`CardStore.cs:4739-4760`) — including *why* there is deliberately no
ordinal lock ordering, which is the part a careless generalisation would have quietly dropped.
`RecordFinding` gained one `onToolFailure` delegate and nothing else; there is now one lock-acquisition
body for both two-card writers, where §8a's flag warned about a fourth. `RollbackRaisedCommentCard`
mirrors `RollbackRaisedCard`'s compare-then-delete discipline exactly.

One note for `## NEXT`: `CardFindingRecordConcurrencyTests` exercises that shared body **only through
`RecordFinding`**. `PromoteComment` inherits the discipline untested for concurrency. A reasonable
trade for shared code and I am not asking for a test — but the two-lock retry loop is now a shared
dependency of two verbs and only one of them proves it.

### 5. `ParsedCommand.Match` at 36 delegates — the assessment you asked for

**Not section-blocking. A §10-or-later obligation, owed by whichever section next touches the CLI
surface — and not §9's to fix.** Three reasons, and one correction:

1. **Correction, and it matters, because it is the reviewer's stated reason for escalating.** The claim
   that "two same-shaped `Func<X, TResult>` params swapped between two occurrences would compile clean
   and misdispatch silently" is **not true here.** Every delegate's parameter is a *distinct* record

   error, not a silent misdispatch. The cost is real; the safety hazard is not.

   already two remediation rounds deep.
3. §9 is a *refusal* section. Restructuring the dispatch union here would put a large, purely
   mechanical, cross-cutting edit inside the diff a supervisor reads for refusal coverage — the worst
   possible place for it. **Whoever owns the next CLI-surface section owns this**, with the two shapes

### F1 — `specs/register/spec.md` contradicts itself about archiving

`openspec/changes/establish-callboard/specs/register/spec.md:47-49`, under **Requirement: The register
lives above the change**:

> Repository-scoped cards SHALL belong to the repository and SHALL NOT be owned by any change. Archiving a
> change SHALL act as a filter that closes its change-scoped cards and leaves cards of wider scope
> untouched.

Its own scenario six lines below (`Archive leaves the register standing`, l.55–60) says the opposite,
and the scenario is the one that matches the code after block F: *"every card in the change directory,
obligations included, moves into the archive exactly as written, **with no obligation settled by the
act of archiving**"*. Round one closed S5 in the scenario and left it open in the requirement. The
worker then saw the requirement and stayed in scope — correct behaviour, incomplete fix.

**Fix: the requirement text only.** Archiving filters on *scope*, not on *state*. It carries
change-scoped cards into the archive exactly as written, settling nothing, and leaves cards of wider
scope live and unmoved. Wording is yours to land, but it must not use "close" or any synonym of
settling for what archiving does to a card, and it must stay consistent with the two scenarios beneath
it (including `Question outlives its change`).

This is a **spec amendment**, Product-Owner-approved as part of the route just chosen — the third such
in this section. It changes no behaviour: the code already implements the scenario. Do not change code
to match the old requirement text. Run `make validate` and quote `VALIDATE_EXIT:0`.

### F2 — the owning section of a card is computed wrongly for section cards

`CardStore.cs:3608` (`comment promote`) builds the raised card's frontmatter with
`card.Frontmatter.Section`, where `card` is the card the comment sits on. **On a section card that
field is empty** — a section card's own `id` *is* the section. So promoting a comment on a section
card to a question yields a question whose `section` is `""`, and §9.5's close gate
(`CardStore.cs:2529`) matches `questionCandidate.Frontmatter.Section == card.Frontmatter.Id`, which
`""` never satisfies. The section then closes over an open question raised in it — exactly the refusal
9.6's first arm exists to make possible. Latent today because nothing yet addresses a comment to a
section card; **live the moment §10's queue lands.**

Its existing test (`tests/Callboard.Tests/CardCommentPromoteTests.cs:58`) hand-writes `Section` onto a
*block* card and asserts it propagates. That proves the mechanism against a fixture; it does not prove
the link against a real card, which is why the bug survived a reviewer `Approve`.

**Fix shape — Product Owner ruling, already given: an encapsulated accessor, not a stored value.**

One function answering *"which section does this card belong to?"*:

- a **section** card → its own `Frontmatter.Id`
- everything else → `Frontmatter.Section`

so every consumer sees a card that looks the same regardless of kind and nothing special-cases at the
call site. Put it in `CardStore` beside `IsSectionCard` (`CardStore.cs:5150`), `internal static`, same
idiom as its neighbours — and route it through `Frontmatter.Kind.Match` rather than an `if`, the way
those predicates already do, so a new kind is a compile error rather than a wrong answer.

**Storing the id on the section card was considered and rejected.** `id` and `section` would be two
fields obliged to agree — the exact shape 8a.17's round-agrees-with-history refusal exists to catch —
and it would need its own agreement check to be safe. If the flat form is ever wanted for the SQLite
index, the index populates its column *from* the accessor; the record does not carry a second source
of truth. Do not add a frontmatter key, and do not write `section` onto section cards on read.

**Apply it at every site that means "the owning section of an arbitrary card".** Known reads of
`Frontmatter.Section`-as-owning-section: `CardStore.cs:1167` and `1174` (nit disposition's raised card
and its `owed_by`), `3608` (the live bug), `4897` and `4926` (finding blind-spot raise). Sweep for the
rest rather than trusting that list — **"moving a standard mid-section obliges a sweep back over what
has landed"** is §9's own fourth ruling, and five of the supervisor's six original findings were a
sweep that never happened. Sites that are *not* this fact stay as they are: `2150`, `2415`, `2529`,
`2682` all read a **block or question card's** `section` to match it against a **section card's** `id`
— that is the join, not the accessor, and passing the section card through the accessor there would be
a no-op at best and confusing at worst. Judge each site by what it means, and say in your post which
ones you changed and which you deliberately left.

**Tests — the failing-first one is the point.** Add a test that promotes a comment on a **real section
card** (built the way the other section-card fixtures in these suites are, with an empty `section`
field, not hand-written) and asserts the raised question's `section` is the section card's own `id`.
Then an end-to-end one: promote a question from a comment on a section card, attempt `section close`,
and assert it **refuses** with `OpenUndeferredQuestion` naming that question. That second test is what
proves the link rather than the mechanism. Keep the existing block-card test — it still asserts
something true.

### The problem, stated precisely

`CommandDispatcher.ParsedCommand.Match` (`src/Callboard/Cli/CommandDispatcher.cs:168`) takes **36
delegate parameters**. The abstract declaration plus 36 overrides is **37 near-identical ~2200-character
signatures**. Every new verb edits all 37. §10 alone adds two.

**The safety argument was already litigated and settled — do not reopen it.** A reviewer reading this
cold in §8 judged it actively harmful; the supervisor **overturned** that: the delegate parameters are
distinct record types, each override passes `this`, and the single call site uses named arguments, so a
positional swap is a compile error rather than a silent misdispatch. **This block is not a bug fix.**
The cost is diff volume and nothing else, and the fix must not buy a reduction in it by giving up the
property below.

### The invariant this block must preserve

**Adding a 37th case must remain a compile error at every site that consumes the union** — the reason
the private constructor plus abstract `Match` shape was chosen over a `switch` in the first place. A
`switch` expression over the hierarchy does not give this: it needs a discard arm, and a new case then
falls through it silently. `ParseResult`, `CommandOutcome`, `CardKind`, `Scope` and the other unions in
`Cards/` follow the same convention; whatever shape you land here must not make `ParsedCommand` the odd
one out for a reader coming from those.

**There is exactly one consumption site** — `Run`, at `CommandDispatcher.cs:838`
(`ready.Command.Match(...)`). Confirm that yourself before you start; if you find a second, say so in
the DEVLOG before proceeding, because the trade-off below assumes one.

### The shape I expect, and why

A **visitor interface** — `ICommandVisitor<TResult>` (or similarly named) with one method per case, and
an abstract `Accept<TResult>(ICommandVisitor<TResult> visitor)` on `ParsedCommand`. Each case's override
becomes one short line. Adding a case adds an interface member, which is a compile error in every
implementer — the invariant, kept, by the same mechanism rather than a weaker one. `Run`'s single call
site becomes one visitor implementation; keep its arms in the order they are in today so the diff reads
as a move.

**This is a recommendation, not a ruling.** If you find a shape that keeps the invariant with a smaller
diff or fewer moving parts, take it and **say in the DEVLOG what you chose and what property carries the
exhaustiveness**. What is not open: dropping the invariant, or a `switch` with a discard arm.

### Scope — tight, and this matters

- **No behaviour change whatsoever.** Not one refusal message, exit code, JSON field, or handler body
  moves. This block is a pure restructure of how a parsed command reaches its handler.
- **Do not add `context` or `state`.** They are blocks A and C. This block leaves the verb set exactly
  as it is.
- **Do not touch the parse/execute split.** `CommandParser` stays a sibling top-level class and must
  remain unable to name a handler — read the `CommandParser` and `CommandDispatcher` class doc comments
  before you move anything; that separation is deliberate and load-bearing, and both doc comments explain
  what it does and does not rule out. If your shape changes what those comments assert, **update them**;
  a doc comment that describes the old mechanism is worse than none.
- **Do not touch `ParseResult`, `CommandOutcome`, or any union in `Cards/`.** Two delegates is not the
  problem.
- Existing tests must pass unchanged. If a test needs editing to compile, that is a signal the behaviour
  moved — stop and report it rather than editing the test.

### Binding constraints

- **ADR-0002 / D2 — NativeAOT.** No runtime code generation, no unbounded reflection. A visitor is
  ordinary virtual dispatch and is fine; anything that reaches for `System.Reflection`, expression
  trees, or a source generator you have not verified AOT-clean is not.
- **`TreatWarningsAsErrors` is on.** `make build` is the analyzer gate too.

### The hole, as it stands at `e7dda26`

`comment resolve`, `comment promote` and `comment decline` (`CommandDispatcher.cs:2872`, `:2960`,
`:2901`) authorise nothing. **Any role may dispose of any thread on any card**, including one addressed
to the Product Owner. And `comment resolve` passes `requireReason: false` to `CardStore.ResolveComment`
with an optional stdin body — so **an empty-bodied resolve is a decline with no recorded reason**, the
one disposition `register` forbids. That second half is the sharper of the two: it is not a missing
guard, it is a route around an existing one.

### The Product Owner's ruling — this is policy, and it is now settled

The spec was silent on who may dispose of a thread; §10's opening put it to the Product Owner and the
ruling is:

1. **A thread may be disposed of — `resolve`, `promote`, `decline` — by the role the thread is
   addressed to, or by the role that owns the card the thread sits on. By no one else.**
2. **`comment resolve` requires a body.**

**Deliberate consequences, so nobody "fixes" them:**

- **A card's owner may dispose of a thread addressed to the Product Owner.** Addressee-only was the
  alternative on the table and was **not** chosen. Do not narrow this, and do not add a Product Owner
  special case.
- **A thread with no `addressed_to` can be disposed of only by the card's owner** — there is no
  addressee for the first arm to admit. Falls out of the ruling; state it in a test rather than leaving
  it to be inferred.
- The acting role is what `--role` declares. §5's convention stands: the system records who declares
  they are acting; this block restricts **who may**, which is exactly what 8.13/9.4 established as a
  separate concern.

### Where each half goes — apply §9 ruling 1, and note that it splits them

This is the block's one real design question and the answer is not the same for both halves.

- **The authorisation refusal asserts something about the record.** Deciding it needs the card read —
  who owns it, who the comment is addressed to. So it **records**, in the §9 refusal format, and it
  belongs in `CardStore`, as a new case on `CardCommentResolveOutcome` and on the promote outcome.
  **Precedent to follow exactly: `CardApprovalOutcome.RoleNotPermitted` and
  `CardSectionAuthorisationOutcome.RoleNotPermitted`** — same name, same `ICardRefusalReason`
  implementation, same shape. Do not invent a new one.
- **The missing body on `comment resolve` asserts only that the invocation was malformed.** Whether a
  body was supplied is decidable from the invocation alone. So it **reports without recording**, at the
  parse door — **exactly mirroring `comment decline --reason`**, which `CommandParser.ParseCommentDecline`
  already requires there. Pass `requireReason: true` through to `CardStore.ResolveComment` as well, the
  same defence-in-depth `decline` already has; the parse-door refusal is the one a caller will actually
  meet.

If you conclude either half lands on the other side of that line, **stop and post the argument to the
DEVLOG before implementing it.** Getting this test wrong is what §9 spent three remediation rounds on,
and its ruling is explicit that argv-decidability is not the test and neither is cost — ask what the
refusal is *about*.

### The spec amendment — part of this block

The spec is silent here, and a refusal with no requirement behind it is precisely the drift the
supervisor catches. Under the Product Owner's ruling, add to
`openspec/changes/establish-callboard/specs/process-enforcement/spec.md` a requirement modelled on its
own sibling **"Approval is refused from the wrong role"** (`:34`) — same register, same brevity:

- a requirement that the system SHALL refuse a thread disposition attempted by a role that is neither
  the thread's addressee nor the owner of the card carrying it;
- a requirement that a resolution SHALL carry a reason, so that resolving is not a route around
  declining's recorded reason;
- scenarios covering: an unrelated role attempting each of the three verbs, the card owner disposing of
  a thread addressed to another role (**permitted** — the ruling, written down), and an empty-bodied
  resolve.

`make validate` must stay green (`VALIDATE_EXIT:0`); check the requirement/scenario formatting against
its neighbours before you run it.

**[worker]** Block D done. F3 authorisation on `comment resolve`/`promote`/`decline`, live debt since
`8298539`.

**The split, as the brief called it.** `CardCommentRouting.IsPermittedToDisposeThread(cardOwner,
threadAddressedTo, actingRole)` is the one predicate both halves share:
`actingRole == cardOwner || actingRole == threadAddressedTo`. The **authorisation** half needs the
card read (to know the owner and the target comment's `To`), so it **records** — a new
`RoleNotPermitted(AttemptedRole, CardOwnerRole, AddressedTo)` case on both `CardCommentResolveOutcome`
and `CardCommentPromoteOutcome`, same shape as `CardApprovalOutcome.RoleNotPermitted` /
`CardSectionAuthorisationOutcome.RoleNotPermitted` — private ctor, `ICardRefusalReason`, checked in
`ResolveCommentUnderExistingLock`/`PromoteCommentUnderLocks` right after the comment is located (needs
its `To`) and before `AlreadyResolved`/`ReasonRequired`: who may act is decided before what state the
thread is in. Carries `CardOwnerRole`/`AddressedTo` too, not just `AttemptedRole` — unlike the two
precedents, the permitted set here is per-card, not static, so the `Remedy` needs both to name it
precisely (and a distinct message when `AddressedTo` is null: "only the card's owner may dispose of
this thread"). The **missing-body** half is decidable from the invocation alone, so it **reports
without recording**, at `CommandParser.ParseCommentResolve`'s own door — `if
(string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(body)) return Refused("missing-argument", ...)` — exactly mirroring
`ParseCommentDecline`'s unconditional `--reason`. `RunCommentResolve` now also passes `requireReason:
true` through to `CardStore.ResolveComment`, the same defence-in-depth `decline` already has; updated
`ResolveComment`'s own doc comment and `CardCommentResolveOutcome.ReasonRequired`'s (both used to say
"comment resolve never requires a reason", which the ruling makes false) rather than leave a doc
comment describing behaviour that no longer holds.

**Deliberate consequences, tested, not "fixed":** `ResolveComment_ByCardOwner_ThreadAddressedToAnotherRole_Resolves`
and `PromoteComment_ByCardOwner_ThreadAddressedToAnotherRole_Promotes` prove the card owner may dispose
of a thread addressed to a different role (Product Owner included) — addressee-only was rejected.
`ResolveComment_UnaddressedThread_ByCardOwner_Resolves` / `..._ByNonOwner_Refuses` cover the
no-`addressed_to` case: only the card's owner may dispose of it, there being no addressee to admit.

**Ordering note, since it wasn't fully spelled out in the brief:** I placed the role check between
`CommentNotFound` and `AlreadyResolved`/`ReasonRequired` (needs the comment located first, to read its
`To`) rather than before `CommentNotFound` — mirrors `CardApprovalOutcome.RoleNotPermitted`'s "checked
right after a successful read, no cost since the lock is already held" reasoning, adapted to this
policy's extra dependency on which comment. Flag if that reading is wrong.

**Spec.** Added two requirements to `process-enforcement/spec.md`, right after "Approval is refused
from the wrong role" (its sibling, per the brief): "A thread is disposed of only by its addressee or
the card's owner" (unrelated-role scenario + card-owner-disposes-thread-addressed-elsewhere scenario,
the ruling written down) and "A resolution SHALL carry a reason" (empty-body scenario).
