**Priority item — the `RegisterLifecycleState.Open` inline-check pattern, assessed on its own, not as
a blocker here.**

The divergence is real, and I demonstrated it by running the CLI, not just by reading:
`CardLifecycle.IsRegisterDischarged` (`CardLifecycle.cs:59-60`) is `TryParse && == Discharged` — an
unparseable `status:` fails to `Discharged`, so `IsClosed` returns `false` (treated **live**). The
inline checks (`RuleCitations.cs:162,211`; `WorkingContext.cs:161`; `CardStore.cs:4092`;
`CommandDispatcher.cs:3483`) are all `TryParse && == Open` — the same parse failure fails to `Open`,
so the card is treated as **not live**. Opposite fail-behaviour for the identical failure mode
(readable frontmatter, unparseable per-kind status), assigned by which formula happens to run over
that card.

**Reachability, traced and then run.** A card's `status:` is a free string (`CardFrontmatter.Status`
in `CardFrontmatter.cs:37`) — nothing validates it against a kind's enum at parse time, so a
`kind: obligation` or `kind: rule` card with `status: bogus` parses as `onSuccess`, not `onFailure`;
it never reaches `ArchiveChange`'s own fail-closed `CardsUnreadable` gate (`CardStore.cs:4104-4109`),
which only catches parse failure of the whole file, not an invalid enum value inside a parsed file. I
built the CLI (`make build`, clean) and ran it against two hand-written cards in a scratch repo:
`O-0001` (`kind: obligation`, `status: bogus`, `owed_by: S-0001`) and `R-0001` (`kind: rule`,
`status: bogus`), both otherwise well-formed. Results:
- `context --role architect`: `O-0001` appears in `queue`, becomes `topItem`, `halted: false` —
  treated as a fully live, actionable obligation. `liveRules` is `[]` — `R-0001` does not appear
  anywhere in the response (not in `liveRules`, not in the queue): it is silently and completely
  excluded, with nothing in the response flagging that a rule card exists with an unreadable status.
- `state`: `liveObligations` contains `O-0001` (`owedBySectionId: "S-0001"`, a section that doesn't
  even exist in the fixture) — same live treatment.
- `rule review`: `liveRuleCount: 0`, `uncitedOpenRules: []` — `R-0001` is invisible here too, matching
  `context`'s treatment of it.

**Is it "the same asymmetry" from the ruling under `## 11.`?** Not the identical shape. That ruling
was about one predicate (`FindBlockingOpenProductOwnerQuestion`) disagreeing with itself depending on
*which kind of failure* hit the same blocker id. What I found here is different in shape but the same
defect *class*: liveness for the register lifecycle is derived by at least five independent call
sites using two different formulas that disagree on the unparseable-status case, and the split falls
along **card kind** — obligation/decision go through `CardLifecycle.IsClosed` (fails open on
corruption), rule/hazard go through the inline `==Open` checks (fails closed on corruption) — not
along which command is asking. Within any *one* response, a rule/hazard card and an obligation/
decision card never collide on the same card (kind dispatch is exclusive), so there's no
single-predicate self-contradiction the way the ruling described. But it is still a real, reachable,
demonstrated defect: an architect running `context` or `state` today gets an obligation with a
corrupted status reported as live and actionable, while a rule with the identical corruption vanishes
without a trace — both wrong, in opposite directions, and neither is a stated, deliberate ruling the
way the `blocked_by` asymmetry was before this session settled it. It also means `CardLifecycle`'s
own doc comment claim of being "the one place 'closed' is defined per kind" is not true in practice —
`RuleCitations`/`WorkingContext`'s rule/hazard branch/`CardStore.ArchiveChange`/the compaction-propose
check in `CommandDispatcher` all re-derive register liveness with a different formula, which is
exactly the "sixth reader" §10 S2 and this block's own brief warned against, except there turn out to
already be several, predating this block and out of its scope to fix.

There is a second-order consequence worth naming: `CardStore.ArchiveChange`'s own obligation gate
(`CardStore.cs:4085-4089`) uses the fail-closed-on-corruption formula, so a corrupt-status obligation
is *not* counted as open there — meaning `change archive` would not flag it as orphaned and would not
block on it, while `state` simultaneously reports the same card as a live, owed obligation. A change
could archive clean by this gate's reckoning while `state` insists an obligation is still owed against
it.

**Verdict on this finding: real, not blocking this diff.** It predates block D (block D changed no
implementation and was explicitly briefed to confirm `rule review`, not touch it), and none of the
five call sites are new here. I'm posting it as a finding for the section and for whoever picks this
up next, since it sits squarely in the territory §10 S2 and this session's `blocked_by` ruling both
just closed for other predicates. Recommend the architect treat this as a `## NEXT` carry-forward for
a future section (or a targeted remediation) rather than something owed inside §11: it touches
`RuleCitations`, `WorkingContext`, `CardStore.ArchiveChange`, and `CommandDispatcher`'s compaction
path, none of which block D's brief authorised touching.

### Blocker — the export emits references into a namespace it never prints

`RecordExportRenderer.AppendThread` (`src/Callboard/Cards/RecordExportRenderer.cs:399-448`) renders
every comment's `To`, `ReplyTo`, `Resolves`, nit metadata and `Disposition` — but **never the
comment's own `Id`**. `CardComment.Id` (`src/Callboard/Cards/CardComment.cs:50`) is the only handle
those three fields refer by, and block B decided it is part of "in full": `card show` emits it
(`Cli/CardShowResult.cs:116`).

So an exported document contains lines of the form

```
**[worker]** 2026-08-27T09:00:00.0000000+00:00 (replies to c-2) (resolves c-2) [disposition: fix-before-land]
```

where `c-2` appears nowhere else in the document. Two consequences, both against 11.4's own central
claim:

1. **The "nit + its disposition" row of the 11.4 table is rendered but not reconstitutable.** The
   table (block C's post) homes the pair as `IsNit`/`Required`/`Sites` **plus** a later comment's
   `Resolves`/`Disposition`. The export emits both halves and destroys the link between them. In a
   three-comment fixture adjacency makes it guessable; in the 31,000-line DEVLOG this export exists to
   replace — where a nit is disposed rounds later, among dozens of threads — it is not recoverable at
   all. `record-retrieval` requires every class to be *"reconstitutable by this export"*, and this
   class is not.
2. **Same for the thread's reply structure** (`ReplyTo`). The incumbent DEVLOG carried reply structure
   in prose and position, unambiguously. The export replaces that with an identifier it withholds — a
   net loss against the log it is specified to approximate, and a degraded-mode regression: a human
   reading the exported artefact cannot resolve a reference the tool itself put there.

`RecordExportTests.SectionExport_RendersEveryContentClass_InReadingOrder`
(`tests/Callboard.Tests/RecordExportTests.cs:110-189`) asserts `[NIT, sites: ...]` and
`[disposition: fix-before-land]` each appear. It never asserts they can be **paired**, which is why
this passed block C's audit and its re-audit.

**Why block review could not catch it.** Block B's reviewer checked `CardShowResult` field-for-field
against `CardFile`/`CardComment` — correct, nothing dropped. Block C's reviewer checked the 11.4 table
row-by-row against the *model* and confirmed the renderer reads every group — also correct. Nobody
compared **B's output to C's**, because no single diff contains both. `RecordExportRenderer` sits in
`Cards/` and renders from `CardFile`; `CardShowResult` sits in `Cli/`. The layering is right; the
agreement was never established.

### The same divergence, secondary, to settle in the same block

`card show` emits, and the export drops: `unknownFrontmatterFields` (`CardShowResult.cs:57`),
`unknownHeaderFields` (`:149`), every sequence entry's `unknownFields` (`:166,229,245,258,301,318,449`),
and `CardApprovalClaim.Id` (`:236`).

The unknown-field groups are not incidental. `CardFile`'s own doc comment
(`Cards/CardFile.cs:12-20`) makes preserving them the extensibility rule §2 owns for the format,
explicitly on ADR-0003's degraded-mode footing — *"a record humans are expected to hand-edit"*. The
export is the **archival** artefact, and it silently discards the one category of content the record
goes out of its way never to lose. Block C's reviewer noticed one instance
(`SectionVerdictEntry.UnknownFields`) and reasoned it away per-field; the section-level view is that
this is a uniform, undecided divergence across seven sites, not a per-field judgement call.

I am not prescribing that it must be emitted — an archival document reasonably declines to carry
forward-compat wire debris. I am blocking on it being **decided and recorded** rather than left as
drift between two renderers, because "what does a full rendering of a card include" is now answered
twice, differently, in one codebase.

### Suggested remediation shape — one fix block, no new `N.M` numbers

- `RecordExportRenderer.AppendThread`: emit each comment's own `Id` on its header line, so `ReplyTo`
  and `Resolves` resolve within the document.
- One test asserting the **pairing**, not the presence: from the exported text, locate the
  disposition's `resolves` target and assert the comment bearing that id is the one carrying
  `[NIT, ...]`. A test that only asserts both strings appear is what let this through.
- State the unknown-fields boundary in `RecordExportRenderer`'s class doc comment, one way or the
  other, and say which in the DEVLOG. If the answer is "emit them", it is a `### unknown fields`
  block per card and per comment; if "deliberately not", the reason belongs beside the claim that
  every content class has a rendering.
- Optional, and I would take it: `RecordExportAssembler.ReadingOrderDescription`
  (`Cards/RecordExportAssembler.cs:34`) is a `const` referenced by **nothing but a `<see cref>`** in
  another file's doc comment (grepped `src` and `tests`). Emitting it into the exported document's
  header would turn near-dead scaffolding into the thing that makes the artefact self-describing to a
  reader with no tool — which is the property this whole capability is for.

### ❓ @architect — the liveness split is a Product Owner ruling, not a `## NEXT` carry

Block D's reviewer found and demonstrated it. I am escalating its placement, and I found one site it
did not.

`CardLifecycle.IsRegisterDischarged` (`Cards/CardLifecycle.cs:59-60`) is `TryParse && == Discharged`,
so an unparseable `status:` reads **live**. Five inline checks are `TryParse && == Open`
(`Cards/RuleCitations.cs:162,211`, `Cards/WorkingContext.cs:161`, `Cards/CardStore.cs:4092`,
`Cli/CommandDispatcher.cs:3483`), so the identical failure reads **not live**. The reviewer's
demonstration stands.

**The sixth site, which changes the severity: `CardStore.cs:2691` — `section close`'s obligation
gate.** An obligation owed by the section whose `status:` does not parse hits `continue` and is never
counted as open, so **the close is not refused**. Six lines above it, in the same loop, a card that
fails to *parse* refuses the whole close (`CardCorrupt`) — the comment there even says "conservative
... an unreadable card anywhere in this directory refuses the whole close". So one loop fails closed
on a corrupt file and open on a corrupt status value, which is the identical asymmetry the ruling at
the top of this section settled for `blocked_by`.

That means the divergence is not confined to report paths. It reaches **two refusal doors**:

- `section close` (`CardStore.cs:2691`) — closes a section with an unsettled obligation.
- `change archive` (`CardStore.cs:4092`) — archives a change while `state`
  (`Cards/DerivedState.cs:88` → `IsClosed`) simultaneously reports that same obligation live and owed.
  Two enforcement answers about one card, contradicting.

And it is reachable without corruption: `CardFrontmatter.Status` is a free string, nothing validates
it against the kind's enum at parse time, so a hand-edited card — which ADR-0003 explicitly invites —
gets there. A typo, again, not a disk fault.

**My recommendation: put it to the Product Owner now, before §12 opens.** Not a §11 remediation block
— §11 neither introduced nor worsened it, and no block was authorised to touch those files. But not a
`## NEXT` carry either: a `## NEXT` carry is precisely how the identical defect class survived §10's
four blocks and two audits, and it was only closed because it became a Product Owner ruling at the top
of this section. Repeating the weaker mechanism for a **worse** instance — one that reaches refusal
doors rather than a read path — would be a knowing regression in process.

It needs a decision, not an implementation, and the decision is not §11's: whether to fail closed at
all six sites, or to **validate `status:` against the kind's enum at the parse door** — the one place
all six converge, and the answer that makes the class unreachable rather than handled six times — or
to state a deliberate per-site policy. That spans §5, §7, §9 and §10. If the ruling is "fix", block A
of this section is the precedent for where it lands: out-of-section, no `N.M`, ticks nothing.

Also worth acting on whatever the ruling: `CardLifecycle`'s class doc comment claims to be "the one
place 'closed' is defined per kind", and that is not true of the shipped codebase.

### The DEVLOG splice incident — the carry is sufficient, with one sharpening

The architect's verification was the right one and I am not re-opening it: `git diff --numstat` showing
407 added / 0 removed proves no committed line was altered, and exactly one `^## NEXT$` remains in
final position (I re-checked both). Making this a §11 finding would push a tooling obligation into a
section that does not own the tooling; §13 already owes the anchor check and this widens it correctly.

The sharpening: **append-only is not the property that needs the mechanism.** `--numstat` against
`HEAD` catches deletion of committed lines, which is the failure that did not happen. It would not
catch an auditor *appending* foreign content that then gets committed — which is the failure that
nearly did. The check §13 owes should be about the shape of what was appended (attribution prefix
present, no unexpected `^## ` heading introduced, the anchor still last), not about line arithmetic.

  real: `section export` resolves through `ResolveRecordDirectories` and therefore works on a card in
  an **archived** change, while `change export` gates on `Directory.Exists` under the live changes root
  only (`Cli/CommandDispatcher.cs:4147-4153`) and cannot export an archived change at all. The refusal
  text says *"no live change named ..."*, which is accurate but names a distinction the surface offers
  no way to cross. Given §13 owns archival, decide it there rather than leaving it as an accident.
- `--out` is resolved relative to **repo root**, not the caller's working directory
  (`Path.GetFullPath(Path.Combine(repoRoot, parsed.OutputPath))`, `CommandDispatcher.cs:4100,4155`).
  Absolute paths behave; a relative `--out out.md` typed from a subdirectory lands somewhere the caller
  did not point at. §12's human view will be the second command to take an output path — settle the
  convention once, there, and make both obey it.
- Block C's reviewer's note that `CardsForChange` reads `ReadAllCards(changeDirectory)` twice. Correct
  as written, not worth complicating today.

**[architect]** Supervisor findings answered — one remediation block, one Product Owner ruling.

### The blocker is real. I verified it before acting.

`RecordExportRenderer.AppendThread` emits `(replies to …)`, `(resolves …)` and `[disposition: …]`, and
emits no comment's own `Id` anywhere in the document. The referents point at nothing. The supervisor's
reading of why two audits passed it is right and worth keeping: `SectionExport_RendersEveryContentClass_
InReadingOrder` asserts both strings **appear**, never that they can be **paired**. A test can cover a
content class and still not cover the thing that makes it content.

### The boundary the supervisor asked me to decide, decided

It declined to prescribe whether `unknownFrontmatterFields`, `unknownHeaderFields`, the sequences'
`unknownFields` and `CardApprovalClaim.Id` should be exported, asking only that the boundary be **stated
rather than left as drift**. It is this:

> **The export is complete with respect to reference-closure and content classes. `card show` is complete
> with respect to the record.**

Two renderers, two jobs. The export is *"a single readable document approximating the shape of the log it
replaces"* — a human archival artefact, so it emits every DEVLOG content class, and it emits anything
another emitted element refers to, because a document that names an identifier it never defines is
broken **as a document**. `card show` is the machine-facing quotable path and stays complete with respect
to the record, unknown fields verbatim included.

Applied: **comment `Id` is emitted** (a referent of `ReplyTo`/`Resolves`, so reference-closure demands
it). **`CardApprovalClaim.Id` is emitted only if another exported element refers to it** — check, do not
assume. **The `unknown*` groups are not exported**: they are forward-compatibility capture, not a DEVLOG
content class, and `card show` already preserves them. Put this in `RecordExportRenderer`'s doc comment
so the next reader inherits the rule rather than the outcome.

### ❓→ Product Owner: answered. Register liveness closes at the parse door.

The supervisor escalated the six-site split and argued it needed a ruling now rather than a `## NEXT`
carry, because a `## NEXT` carry is exactly how the identical class survived §10. It also found a
**sixth** site the block reviewer missed — `CardStore.cs:2691`, `section close`'s obligation gate, six
lines below a `CardCorrupt` branch that fails closed on the same loop — putting the divergence on two
**refusal doors** and making it reachable by a hand-edited `status:` rather than by corruption.

**Ruling: validate `status:` against the kind's enum at the parse door.** A card whose status does not
parse never gets constructed; it reports as a corrupt card, the path that already exists. All six sites
converge on the parser, so the divergence becomes **unreachable** rather than aligned — the class dies
instead of six instances being fixed. `record-retrieval`'s damage-containment already expects per-card
failure, so a corrupt card reporting as corrupt is the intended shape.

**Placement: an out-of-section block at the head of §12**, the same shape block A took this morning — no
`N.M` numbers, ticks nothing. §5, §7, §9 and §10 are all closed, so there is no remediation slot, and it
must not be folded into §11's remediation: that would reach into four closed sections from inside a
remediation block, and hand the supervisor a re-audit range containing work its own findings never
covered. **This is not §11's to fix, and §11 does not wait on it.**

### The splice carry, sharpened

The supervisor accepted my `## NEXT` carry with a correction I am adopting: append-only is not the
property that needs a mechanism. `--numstat` catches the failure that **did not** happen. §13's check
should be about the **shape of what was appended**, not the fact that nothing was removed.

### The boundary as recorded — one clarification worth making before it is inherited

The rule now in the class doc comment (`RecordExportRenderer.cs:29-46`) is the right one and I would
not change what it *does*. But as worded it over-claims, and it is now the thing a future block will
read as the rule:

> it emits anything another emitted element refers to — a document that names an identifier it never
> defines is broken as a document

Applied literally that is not satisfiable, and not satisfied today. The export emits nine other
id-shaped referents: `blocked by` (`:166`), `finding key` (`:171`), `raised as` (`:246`), `owed by`
(`:289`), `supersedes` (`:294`), `superseded by` (`:299`), `earned from` (`:304`), `absorbs` (`:309`),
`answer (decision)` (`:341`), `deferred to` (`:356`). A section export can and routinely will name a
blocker question, a superseded rule or an answering decision that is not in the export's scope.

That is **correct behaviour**, and the distinction is the part worth writing down: a comment id is
**document-local** — it addresses nothing outside the document, so a document that withholds it
withholds the only handle there is. A card id is a **globally resolvable identity** — `card show <id>`
retrieves it, and `CardIdentityResolver` finds it anywhere in the record including the archive. Naming
one is a citation, not a dangling reference.

Suggested wording for whoever next touches that doc comment, not owed as a fix: *the export closes
every **document-local** reference; a card identity it names is resolvable against the record by
identity and is deliberately not inlined.* One sentence, and it stops a later block either trying to
inline transitively-referenced cards or concluding the rule was already broken and ignorable.

### The two reviewer notes, weighed

**The `definedIds` regex is unscoped — worth acting on, in `## NEXT`, not now.** The reviewer is right
that it matches anywhere in the document rather than inside `### thread`, so a comment *body*
containing literal `**[role token]**` would register a false definition and could let a real regression
pass. I want to record that this is **not hypothetical**, because that changes how it should be
weighted: this very remediation thread is the counter-example. The posts under this heading contain
`**[reviewer c-2]**`-shaped text as illustration; the moment such a post is a card comment — which is
precisely what §11.4 homes it as — an export of that card carries a false definition in a body. It
fails in the direction that matters: the test passes when it should fail, which is the "test that
cannot fail" hazard the architect made blocking in block C.

It does not block today: the fixture is fully controlled and contains no such body, and the shipped
renderer is correct regardless of the test's extraction. But the fix is cheap and should not wait for
someone to be bitten — scope the extraction to the `### thread` sections, or better, take the defined
ids from the `CardFile` the fixture already holds rather than by regex over rendered prose, so the
test's notion of "defined" cannot be spoofed by content at all.

**The whitespace assumption — low, and it fails safe.** `(\S+)` for a definition against `([^)]+)` for
a referent is asymmetric, so an id containing whitespace would be captured whole as a referent and
truncated as a definition: the assertion fails. A false negative, not a false positive. Noting the
asymmetry alongside the item above, since one fix addresses both.

**[architect]** Product Owner ruling, carried into §12 from §11's `## NEXT` — **register liveness closes
at the parse door.**

The parked finding was six divergent derivations of "is this register card live?", disagreeing about
which way an unparseable `status:` falls:

- `CardLifecycle.cs:59-60` — `IsRegisterDischarged` fails **open**: a status that will not parse is not
  `Discharged`, so the card reads as live.
- `RuleCitations.cs:162`, `RuleCitations.cs:211`, `WorkingContext.cs:161`, `CardStore.cs:4092`,
  `CommandDispatcher.cs:3483` — inline `== RegisterLifecycleState.Open` checks, all failing **closed**: a
  status that will not parse is not `Open`, so the card reads as discharged.
- The supervisor's sixth, **`CardStore.cs:2691`** — `section close`'s obligation gate, where an
  unparseable status hits `continue` and the close is **not refused**, six lines below a `CardCorrupt`
  branch that fails closed in the same loop.

Two of the six are **refusal doors** — `section close`, and `change archive` at `:4092`, which disagrees
with `state` about whether the same obligation is owed. And none of this needs corruption to reach: a
hand-edited `status:` gets there.

**Ruling: validate `status:` against the kind's enum at the parse door.** A card whose status does not
parse is **never constructed** — `CardFileParser` returns `CardFileParseResult.Failure` and the card
reports as corrupt on every path that already knows how to say so. The six derivations then converge on
the parser and the split becomes **unreachable** rather than merely aligned. This is the same move §11
block A made for `blocked_by`: close the hole at the door, and leave the read-path predicates saying what
they already document.

Rejected, so a later reader does not relitigate it: **aligning the six by hand** leaves six sites that can
drift again and a seventh that can be added unguarded — the same shape as §10's "call site 34" finding,
and the reason that one is still open. **A shared `IsLive` predicate** is better than six inline checks
but still fails somewhere by choice; the parse door removes the choice.

this in would have reached back into four closed sections and handed the supervisor a range its findings
never covered. So it lands as **block A of §12**, out-of-section: **no `N.M` numbers, ticks nothing**, the
shape §3c.3 gives a remediation block. `@supervisor` — when you audit §12 on `5f7919d..HEAD`, block A is

**The envelope-category finding — `investigate`, not `park` and not yet `fix-before-land`.**

The worker is right that the 18 `onCardCorrupt` → `throw` sites are pre-existing and uniform, and right

reachability is this block's. That is an observable regression caused here, at the exact door this block

And the category is not a nicety. A tool-failure envelope asserts **enforcement was unavailable**. That is
false here: the record was read, it is definitively bad, and the tool knows exactly which field and which
values. §9.1 says a parse-door refusal reports without recording — the worker is right that nothing is
recorded either way, but "reports" is not satisfied by reporting the wrong thing. The tool that says
*I could not check* when it means *I checked and you are wrong* is the incumbent's failure mode with a
JSON envelope on it.

**What the fix must assert.** `onCardCorrupt` returns a `CommandOutcome.Refusal` carrying
`corrupt.Reason` verbatim, not an `InvalidOperationException`. The category is the point: a tool-failure
envelope asserts **enforcement was unavailable**, and that is false — the tool read the record, the
record is definitively bad, and the tool knows the field, the value and the recognised values. §13.2's
"the loop proceeds unenforced when the tool cannot run" is about the tool not running; a corrupt card is
the tool running and refusing. Do not preserve `EXIT:2` for these paths — the exit-code category moving
from tool-failure to refusal **is** the fix, not a side effect of it.

has no jurisdiction here. So it gets **direct tests**: at least one per command family, asserting the
envelope's `ok:false` + refusal shape, the exit code, and that `corrupt.Reason` reaches the caller intact
with field, value, kind and recognised values still in it. A refusal whose message survives but whose
envelope lies is the failure this item exists to remove; test the envelope, not just the string.

right — that site is a finding: post it here and leave it alone. Do not make it uniform by force.

all three rewritten tests (`CommandDispatcherBlockGateTests`, `CommandDispatcherBlockTransitionTests`,
`CommandDispatcherBlockedByTests`) — each now asserts `RefusalExitCode`, `ok:false`,
`refusal.code == "card-corrupt"`, a non-empty message, and *empty* stderr (flipped from the old
non-empty-stderr assertion, correctly — a refusal is not a thrown exception). None weakened; each
flips to assert the opposite, correct disposition. The three new CLI-level family tests
(`CommandDispatcherRegisterTests`, `CommandDispatcherSectionTests`, `CommandDispatcherQuestionAnswerTests`)
check the envelope shape and exit code, not just that the message string survived — each asserts
`refusal.code`, the exit code, and `Contains` on the offending value/kind/recognised-values inside
`message`. This is what item 3 asked for.

**The new question — established, not fixed, with actual envelopes and exit codes.**

**1. Is it true? Yes — driven end to end, envelopes quoted.**

`rule promote --id R-9001` against a repository-scoped rule card at `status: briefed` (unparseable):
```
$ callboard rule promote --id R-9001 --role architect --change establish-callboard
{"ok":false,"command":"rule promote --id R-9001 --role architect --change establish-callboard","refusal":{"code":"card-id-unresolvable","message":"'--id' names id 'R-9001', but 1 card file(s) elsewhere in the record could not be read, so its presence cannot be confirmed or ruled out: <path>/r-9001.md."}}
EXIT:1
```

`obligation decline --id O-9001` against a repository-scoped obligation card at `status: briefed`:
```
$ callboard obligation decline --id O-9001 --role architect --reason test
{"ok":false,"command":"obligation decline --id O-9001 --role architect --reason test","refusal":{"code":"card-id-unresolvable","message":"'--id' names id 'O-9001', but 1 card file(s) elsewhere in the record could not be read, so its presence cannot be confirmed or ruled out: <path>/o-9001.md."}}
EXIT:1
```

Both a `refusal` envelope (not `tool-failure` — the exit code stays `1`, `RefusalExitCode`), but the
wrong refusal: `card-id-unresolvable` asserts "I could not confirm or rule out this id exists", not
"I found the card and it is corrupt." Neither envelope carries the field, offending value, kind, or
recognised values that `card-corrupt` would have — the message the Product Owner needs to fix the file
is gone, replaced by "go check every unreadable file in the record."

**2. Does id resolution distinguish "no file" from "a file that will not parse"? Partially — it has
the fact, but throws away the reason.** `CardIdentityResolver.Resolve` (`src/Callboard/Cards/
CardIdentityResolver.cs:57-93`) and `NitResolver.Resolve` both already return a distinct
`CardIdentityResolution.Unreadable`/`NitResolution.Unreadable` case, separate from `NotFound`, exactly
when zero matches were found and at least one file in the searched directories failed to parse — so
"no file" and "a file exists but won't parse" are not collapsed into one case at the type level. But
the loop that builds that list discards the parse failure itself: `card = result.Match(onSuccess: ...,
onFailure: static _ => null)` — the `_` throws away `Failure.Reason`, keeping only the file path. So
`Unreadable` can name *which* file(s) couldn't be read, never *why*. Upgrading `card-id-unresolvable`
to carry `card-corrupt`-quality detail (when exactly one candidate id could plausibly be the unreadable
file) is a real fix but a different, larger one than the mechanical nineteen-site replacement this round
made — it needs `CardIdentityResolver`/`NitResolver` to start carrying `Reason` strings forward, not
just paths.

**3. How many of the nineteen `onCardCorrupt` arms are genuinely reachable via a single CLI
invocation? Nine — not thirteen (19 − 6).** I checked all nineteen call sites directly, not on the
worker's list: each handler either resolves its target with `ResolveFilePath` (a caller-supplied path,
reachable) or `ResolveCardReference`/`ResolveAnyCardReference`/`NitResolver.Resolve` (an id, intercepted
earlier by that resolver's own `Unreadable` branch, unreachable via a single call).

Reachable (9): `RunBlockTransition`, `RunBlockGate`, `RunBlockRemoveBlocker` (blocked-by family),
`RunSectionVerdict` (main section target — the `--finding-recurred` ids it also resolves are a separate,
auxiliary `ResolveCardReference` call, not this arm), `RunSectionClose`, `RunSectionAuthorise`,
`RunQuestionAnswer` (main question target — `--decision` is likewise auxiliary), `RunQuestionDefer`,
`RunRegisterDischarge`.

Unreachable via a single CLI call (10): `RunNitRaise`, `RunNitDisposition`, `RunDecisionSupersede`,
`RunRulePromote`, `RunObligationPromote`, `RunObligationDecline`, `RunCommentDecline`,
`RunCommentPromote`, the shared `ResolveRuleCompactOutcome` arm — **and `RunBlockApprove`**, which the
worker's round-two post did not name among the six families it flagged.

**`RunBlockApprove` is a genuine gap in the worker's own disposition, not a difference of judgement.**
`block approve` resolves its target via `--id` through `ResolveCardReference`

$ callboard block approve --id B-9001 --role reviewer --claims structural-soundness --state "the diff at abc123" --change establish-callboard
{"ok":false,"command":"block approve --id B-9001 --role reviewer --claims structural-soundness --state the diff at abc123 --change establish-callboard","refusal":{"code":"card-id-unresolvable","message":"'--id' names id 'B-9001', but 1 card file(s) elsewhere in the record could not be read, so its presence cannot be confirmed or ruled out: <path>/b-9001.md."}}
EXIT:1

Same shape, same gap. The worker's "block gate / block transition / block add-blocker" tests all cover

**[architect]** Brief — §12 **block B**, tasks **12.1–12.3**. This is §12's actual deliverable.

**Spec:** `specs/record-retrieval/spec.md` — "Human view of the board" and both its scenarios. **Binding
ADR: D5** — a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, emitted by `callboard` itself. No server,
no npm, no build step, no hosting, no authentication. D5 states the accepted trade-off explicitly: **the
view cannot offer interactive filtering.** Do not add any, and do not reach for the vanilla-TS-plus-Vite
convention the rest of my stacks use — D5 departs from it deliberately, and a second toolchain here would
mean a second full gate set and a second worker agent for a read-only render.

**The verb, which the spec does not name — I am ruling it:** `view --out <path>`. `--out` is
**required**; the command never writes to a location the caller did not name. The command's own output
stays the project's one-JSON-line envelope, with the written path in the result — `view` is a command
like any other, not an exception to the CLI contract. Follow the surrounding idiom for result types
(`ICommandResult`, source-generated JSON, no reflection — this ships AOT).

**What the view must show,** from the spec's first scenario — cards **by column and owner**, **what is
blocked and on what**, and **the open questions with who owes each answer**. Read the data the way the
read paths already do: §10's ruling 1 is binding — **the read paths read card files, not the index.**
`state` is your closest existing relative; look at what it assembles before you assemble anything new,
and reuse rather than growing a second derivation of the same facts. A blocked relationship must name
*what* it is blocked on, not merely that it is blocked; an open question must name *who owes the answer*,
not merely that it is open.

**12.3 splits, and I flagged this when I opened the section.** Two halves, and only one of them is yours
to close:

- **"The view alters no state" is yours and must be gated.** Assert it, don't assume it: generating the
  view leaves every card file byte-identical and touches no index; and the emitted HTML contains no
  mechanism by which a reader could alter anything — no `<form>`, no `<script>`, no `<input>`, no
  `<button>`, no external fetch of any kind. That last one is also D5's self-contained requirement, so it
  is one assertion doing two jobs. A `file://` page with no script and no form cannot mutate the record,
  and that is the property the second scenario is asking for.
- **"It renders correctly in a browser" is not yours and not mine.** It is §4's human-in-the-loop case.
  End your post with a **copy-pasteable block for the Product Owner**: the exact command to run, the exact
  path it writes, how to open it, and a short numbered list of what she should see — one line per thing
  the spec's first scenario names, so she can check them off. **12.3 is not ticked until she confirms**,
  so do not report the block as complete; report it as complete-pending-confirmation.

**Design latitude, and its limit.** The HTML is a deliverable a human reads, so make it legible — clear
column structure, owners visible at a glance, blocked and open-question relationships readable without
cross-referencing. Inline CSS only. No web fonts, no CDN, no images fetched from anywhere. Everything in
the one file.

**Watch for:** a card with no owner, a column with no cards, a question with no addressee, a card blocked
on a card that is closed, and an empty board. Each of those is a render case, and an empty board should
produce a valid page that says so rather than a broken one.

**[architect]** Product Owner ruling on what a **column** is. The worker ruled this one itself and
documented the reasoning in `BoardViewColumn`'s doc comment — the reasoning was sound and the ambiguity
was real, but §4 makes an ambiguous spec the Product Owner's call, not the implementer's. Raising it is
the move; the code comment was the right instinct one step short. Noting it once, here, so it is on the
record rather than repeated per-block.

**The ruling: a column is a flow state, and the register gets its own area.** Not card kind.

"Board" and "column" together mean the states a card moves through, and the view's job per the spec's
first scenario is to answer **where is everything** — which is a question about position, not about
taxonomy. Grouping by kind produces an inventory: correct, complete, and silent on the thing a board
exists to show. A card's flow state would appear only *on* the card rather than *in* its position, which
is precisely the information a glance is supposed to carry.

**The complication the ruling has to absorb** — and the reason the kind reading was tempting — is that
register cards **SHALL NOT occupy flow states**. Four of the eight kinds have nowhere to stand in a
kanban. So the structure is **lanes by flow vocabulary, columns by that vocabulary's states**:

- **Blocks** — columns are `BlockFlowState`, in flow order. This is the primary lane; it is where the
  work moves.
- **Sections** — columns are `SectionFlowState`.
- **Questions** — columns are `QuestionStatus`. Ruling 2 from §10 binds the reading of this lane: **not
  answering is itself a halting state**, so a deferred question sits with the open ones, not in a softer
  third place. Closed means answered and nothing else.
- **Findings** — a finding never closes (`CardLifecycle`'s `onFinding: static () => false`), so this lane
  is a single column. Do not invent a second state to make it look symmetrical with the others.
- **The register** — obligations, rules, hazards, decisions — is **an area, not a lane**, grouped by kind
  and showing open against discharged. It is rendered below the flow lanes, visibly a different kind of
  thing, because it *is* one: the register is what constrains the work, not work in progress.

**Owner grouping stays** — the spec says "by column and owner", and that half was right. Owners group
within each column, in the fixed order you already established.

**Keep, unchanged:** `AllKinds`/`AllOwners` as fixed-order lists rather than `Dictionary.Values`; the
reuse of `DerivedStateAssembler.Build` for blocked cards and open questions; reading live card files and
never the index; the atomic write; and both 12.3 assertions. **Empty columns still render** — that was
right and it matters more now: an empty `in-review` column is information, and a board that hides its
empty columns hides exactly the fact that nothing is in review.

**The two facts a board must not merely list.** A blocked card must show *what it is blocked on* in a
place a reader will find it while looking at the card, and an open question must show *who owes the
answer*. `DerivedStateAssembler` already yields both; the ruling here is only that they must not be
exiled to a footer the eye never reaches while it is looking at the lane.

`@worker` — rework the grouping to this shape, keep everything named above, and re-post the
copy-pasteable confirmation recipe with the numbered list updated to the new structure. **12.3 stays
complete-pending-confirmation** — the Product Owner has ruled on what the view *is*, which is not the
same as having seen it render.

**Re-posting the recipe in full**, not as a diff — this replaces the copy-pasteable block from my

```
REPO=/Users/rendle/github/daemonicai/callboard
SCRATCH=$(mktemp -d /tmp/callboard-view-demo.XXXXXX)
CB() { dotnet run --project "$REPO/src/Callboard" -- "$@"; }

cd "$SCRATCH"
git init -q

# A section (Section lane).
echo "Demo section for the board view recipe." | CB section create callboard/changes/demo/s-0001.md \
  --role architect --title "Demo section" --change demo

# A block (Block lane) — the one CLI door that mints a block card is a section's own
# "request changes" verdict, naming a new finding via a small manifest file.
mkdir -p manifests
cat > manifests/finding-1.md << 'EOM'
---
key: demo-finding-1
new-card-file: callboard/changes/demo/b-0001.md
title: Demo block for the board view
---
Demonstration finding body.
EOM
CB section verdict callboard/changes/demo/s-0001.md --role supervisor --verdict request-changes \
  --range-from abc111 --range-to abc222 --finding-new manifests/finding-1.md --change demo

# An open question (Question lane), owed by the Product Owner.
echo "Should the demo board show closed cards too?" | CB question create callboard/register/q-0001.md \
  --role architect --title "Demo open question" --owed-by product-owner

# Block the block on the question — a visible blocker, and it halts too (the question is
# open and Product-Owner-owned).
CB block add-blocker callboard/changes/demo/b-0001.md Q-0001 --role architect --change demo

# A finding (Finding lane, its own single column).
echo "A demo finding for the board view recipe." | CB finding record callboard/changes/demo/f-0001.md \
  --role reviewer --title "Demo finding" --section S-0001 --change demo --blind-spot none

# Register cards: an open rule, an open hazard, and an obligation created then discharged
# (both open and discharged represented).
echo "Demo rule, stays open." | CB rule create callboard/register/r-0001.md \
  --role architect --title "Demo open rule" --scope repository
echo "Demo hazard, stays open." | CB hazard create callboard/register/h-0001.md \
  --role architect --title "Demo open hazard" --condition "the demo repo still exists" --cadence "every review"
echo "Demo obligation, will be discharged." | CB obligation create callboard/changes/demo/o-0001.md \
  --role architect --title "Demo obligation to discharge" --change demo --section S-0001
CB obligation discharge callboard/changes/demo/o-0001.md --role architect --change demo

# Render the board.
CB view --out /tmp/callboard-board-demo.html
open /tmp/callboard-board-demo.html
```

**[architect]** A gap surfaced by block B's confirmation recipe, and the Product Owner's ruling on where
it goes. Recording it now so it is not lost between here and the section review.

**There is no CLI verb that creates a task-implementing `block` card.** Verified directly, not taken from
the worker's report: `card` has exactly one subcommand, `show`. `block` has `transition`, `gate`,
`add-blocker`, `remove-blocker` and `approve` — every one of them operating on a card that already
exists. No path writes a fresh block card at `drafting`.

The one door that creates a block card is `section verdict --finding-new`, which is what block B's recipe
had to use to get a block onto the board at all. That door is spec'd deliberately: `work-lifecycle`'s
"Section remediation follows the finding, not the verdict" requires a supervisor's first-time finding to
create a new block card carrying the finding as its brief. So the **remediation** path can mint a card.
The ordinary path — the Architect carves a section into blocks and briefs one — has none.

I can find no requirement in any spec under this change that says a work card can be created through the
tool. So today a block card comes into existence only by hand-authoring a Markdown file, which is the
practice `callboard` exists to replace. That is why this is worth a ruling rather than a note.

the section whole and reads the specs rather than the tasks, and it is the one agent positioned to say
whether this is a spec omission or a deliberate design in which the brief card is hand-authored and the
tool only ever routes what already exists. It also may find a creation path I have not looked in the
right place for. Nothing is decided until then, and nothing is built on the assumption either way.

### What holds, so the blockers are not read as wider than they are

**Block B satisfies its spec requirement.** `record-retrieval`'s "Human view of the board" asks for cards
by column and owner, what is blocked and on what, and the open questions with who owes each answer, with
no server, no authentication and no hosting. `BoardViewAssembler.Build` (`BoardView.cs:66-122`) delivers
all three from live card files, and `BoardViewRenderer` (`BoardViewRenderer.cs:38-63`) emits one
self-contained document. Both rulings are structurally realised, not merely asserted: a column **is** a
flow state (four flow lanes, register as its own area, `BoardView.cs:126-203`), and an empty column
renders (`BoardViewRenderer.cs:73-76`, driven by `BuildColumn` producing a column for every declared
state regardless of card count). §10 ruling 1 holds — no index reference on the new path. D5 holds. The
second scenario is gated, not assumed. Per the Product Owner's note I have judged structure and rulings,
not polish, and "the view is plain" is not a finding here.

**Block A's core is sound and I am not reopening it.** The parse door converges the six divergent
derivations, `CardStore.cs`'s section-close `continue` is unreachable by construction, the six deleted
`InvalidStatus` cases leave `RefusalCoverageGateTests`' bijection balanced with no exclusion key added
(the Registry diff removes exactly six entries and adds none), and the nineteen-site envelope fix was the
right scope call — "the code is old; the reachability is this block's" is the correct test, and it was
applied honestly. The `unreachable:` throws and the seven naming comments are genuinely at kind-confirmed
sites. That work is not what I am blocking on.

**Gate coverage is intact.** The section added no project, package or stack; `Makefile` is unchanged in
range and every constituent exit line is quoted in-thread for both blocks and both remediation rounds.
The human-in-the-loop half of 12.3 carries the Product Owner's recorded confirmation (`0aa940b`), so the

### Blocker 1 — block A turned five read paths into silent droppers, and block B built the sixth

This is the finding no block review could make, because it needs both blocks and the pre-`5f7919d`
behaviour in view at once.

**Before `a0974bb`, `status:` was unvalidated.** The worker's own round-one report establishes it: *"dozens
of pre-existing tests across the suite hand-built cards with a placeholder `status: "open"` regardless of
kind (a block card with `"open"`, never a legal block status even before this block — the field was simply
unvalidated)"*, and `CardShowTests` carried a block card at `"in_review"` that parsed fine. So before this
section, **an out-of-vocabulary status still produced a constructed `CardFile`**. The card was present in
every read path. The six inline `TryParse` sites disagreed about how to *classify* it; nothing made it
disappear.

**After `a0974bb`, the same card fails to parse — and five read paths respond by silently discarding it:**

- `Cards/BoardView.cs:80` — `view`, added by block B **after** block A, in the same section
- `Cards/DerivedState.cs:86` — `state`
- `Cards/WorkingContext.cs:144` — `context`
- `Cards/RecordExportAssembler.cs:59`, `:90`, `:109`, `:126` — `section export` and `change export`

Each is `onFailure: static _ => null` followed by `if (card is null) continue`. No count, no path, no
reason, no marker on the output. A card that is on disk, that the tool read, and that the tool knows
precisely what is wrong with, is rendered as **absent**.

Three things make this a blocker rather than a §13 note:

1. **The reachability is wholly this section's, not merely widened by it.** The Architect's own ruling on
   the envelope regression — *"The code is old; the reachability is this block's ... no other change made
   that input land there"* — applies here with more force, because before block A this class of parse
   failure **did not exist**. Nineteen CLI sites were swept on exactly this argument. Consistency of
   ruling requires the same disposition for these.
2. **It reaches a closed section's shipped contract.** `change export` is §11's archival document, and
   §11's `Approve` was given on a build where a hand-edited `status:` could not remove a card from it.
   `a0974bb` changed that, in my range, and nobody looked: block A's thread enumerates only the six
   *predicate* sites and the *refusal doors*. The silent-drop read paths appear nowhere in the brief, in
   either worker post, or in either reviewer audit. That is the union hole — every rule individually
   correct, the set incomplete.
3. **Block B then built a sixth one, on the Product Owner's only surface.** `view` is the artifact whose
   whole job per the spec is to answer *where is everything*. It will answer incompletely and say
   nothing. Block A's stated premise is that such a card *"reports as corrupt on every path that already
   knows how to say so"* — §12 then added a path that does not know how to say so, and did not teach it.

Note that block A made the message quality excellent for exactly this purpose (`Failure.Reason` names
field, value, kind and recognised values) and every one of these six sites has that string in hand at the
discard site and throws it away.

**This is not a fail-open on enforcement** — nothing is wrongly permitted, and the refusal doors
(`section close`, `change archive`) were verified closed. It is a fail-open on **record fidelity**: the
tool's rendering of the record is silently incomplete, which is the incumbent's failure mode with better
formatting.

### Blocker 2 — `CardKindWireFormat.AllKinds` ships the overturned design as current documentation

`src/Callboard/Cards/CardKind.cs:118-131`. Its doc comment reads *"§12 block B's board view reads this to
name one column per kind"*. That is block B's **first** implementation — the one the Product Owner
overturned with *"a column is a flow state, not a card kind"*. The board names no column per kind. The
member's only consumer is `RegisterKinds` two lines below (`:139-143`), which filters four of the eight
and discards the rest; nothing else in `src/` or `tests/` references it.

Ordinarily a stale comment is the reviewer's business and I would leave it. It is a blocker here for one
specific reason the Architect put on the record in `0aa940b`: the view's visual design is deferred to a
follow-on change, and *"two things must survive any such restyle, because they are rulings rather than
taste: a column is a flow state, and an empty column renders."* The one place in the codebase a later
implementer will look for the column vocabulary now asserts, in `src/`, that columns are kinds. The
ruling survives in `BoardView.cs`'s doc comments and in this thread; it is contradicted in `CardKind.cs`.
Shipping the superseded design as live documentation is the dead scaffolding this review exists to catch.

### The change-level question — is the missing block-creation verb a spec omission or a design?

Reported separately, as instructed; it is **not** a §12 finding and does not bear on the verdict above.

**It is a spec omission, and the evidence is stronger than the CLI surface alone.**

*The surface.* Confirmed independently. Every card kind with a creation door has one — `section create`,
`question create`, `rule create`, `hazard create`, `obligation create`, `decision create`, `finding
record`, `nit raise`. `block` has `transition`, `gate`, `add-blocker`, `remove-blocker`, `approve`, all
operating on an existing card. `card` has only `show`. The sole minting path is `CardStore.cs:2413-2420`
(`section verdict --finding-new`), which allocates a `CardKind.Block` identity at
`BlockFlowState.Briefed`.

*The decisive evidence — the flow's entry state has no producer.* `grep -rn "BlockFlowState.Drafting"
src/ --include=*.cs` returns **zero matches**. `work-lifecycle`'s "Block cards move through a defined
flow" makes `drafting` the leftmost node of its own diagram, and nothing in the tool can put a card
there. A spec that defines a state its implementation cannot create is not describing a deliberate
design; it is describing a door nobody built. I read all seven capability specs under this change and
found no requirement anywhere stating that a work card is created through the tool — which is precisely
the omission, not evidence of intent.

*Why it is not benign.* Hand-authoring a block card does not merely bypass a convenience — it bypasses
`CardIdentityAllocator`, whose own doc comment says the counter file exists because *"an identity SHALL
NOT be reused"* and explicitly rejects deriving the next number by scanning filenames. A hand-authored
`b-0007.md` does not advance the counter, so the next `section verdict --finding-new` can allocate
`B-0007` again. `VerifyCounters` reconciles only at `index rebuild`, and `CardIdentityCounterViolation`
is explicitly *"never produced as, or turned into, a refusal"`. So the gap is not "the Architect types
some YAML"; it is **card-model's identity guarantee being unenforceable for the one kind that carries the
work**, because the guarantee is only enforced on the path the tool mints.

*The shape of the omission.* The remediation path can mint a card because `work-lifecycle`'s "Section
remediation follows the finding, not the verdict" required it; the ordinary path has no requirement
because none was written. The asymmetry tracks which requirement happened to force a creation door, not a
decision that briefs are hand-authored. And a design in which the Architect hand-writes the brief card
would have to say so somewhere — it says so nowhere, in any spec or ADR.

Two adjacent gaps found while checking, offered because they are the same shape and the ruling should
probably cover them together:

- **There is no verb that appends an ordinary addressed comment.** `comment` has only `resolve`,
  `promote`, `decline`. The only writers of `CardStore.AppendComment` are `nit raise` and `rule
  promote-constitution` (`CommandDispatcher.cs:3545` calls itself *"the first CLI verb to reach that
  surface"*). So the ordinary in-thread post — `❓ @architect`, `→ @reviewer`, the whole substance of this
  file — has no door either, while `card-model`'s "Append-only addressed comment threads" is the
  mechanism the routing depends on.
- **`--base` has no recording door of its own**, though "Blocks carry their brief context" requires it
  *"recorded before the block is briefed"* — consistent with the block card having no pre-`briefed`
  existence the tool can create.

`callboard` today can route, refuse and close work it did not create. That is a coherent half of a tool,
and the missing half is the half that replaces the practice the tool exists to replace.

### For `## NEXT` — not blocking, and not for the fix block

1. **Six recorded refusals became one unrecorded report, and §9.1's criterion now has an unwritten
   exception.** §9.1 says a refusal records when it asserts something about the record. Four of the six
   deleted cases recorded (their test names carry `_AndRecords` / `_AndRecordsTheRefusal`). The parse-door
   replacement records nothing. The Architect's *"this is a parse-door refusal: it reports, it does not
   record"* is correct as engineering — you cannot append a `CardRefusalEntry` to a card you cannot parse
   — but it is not what §9.1's criterion says, since a corrupt-card refusal plainly asserts something
   about the record. The exception is real and forced; it should be written down before someone applies
   §9.1 literally to the next door. Net effect worth naming: attempting to discharge a bad-status register
   card used to leave a durable trace on the card and now leaves none anywhere.
2. **`view` refuses with `export-target-exists`** (`CommandDispatcher.cs:4176`) though it is not an
   export; the message says "the view is derived and regenerable" while the code a machine keys on names
   another command family. Small, but this section spent a whole remediation round establishing that the
   refusal *code* is the contract and a code naming the wrong thing is the defect.
3. **Lane names are sourced two ways.** Flow lanes hard-code `"Block"`/`"Section"`/`"Question"`/
   `"Finding"` (`BoardView.cs:131`, `:157`, `:174`, `:185`); register lanes use `kind.DisplayName()`
   (`:199`) — the helper introduced to avoid "hand-listing a second time" is used for half the lanes and
   hand-listed against for the other half.
4. **`ValidateStatus`'s `finding` arm hard-codes the single literal `open`.** Correct today
   (`CardLifecycle`'s `onFinding` never closes), but it is the one kind whose vocabulary is a literal
   rather than a wire format. If a finding ever gains a second state, the parse door refuses every
   existing finding card before anything else runs — a forward hazard worth a line in `## NEXT` rather
   than a discovery.

**[architect]** **Product Owner ruling on the three missing verbs: amend the spec, build them in §13.**

The spec is wrong, not merely silent, so it moves — §10's ruling 4 in force again: *where the spec and
shipped behaviour contradict, one of them moves, deliberately, and the Product Owner decides which.* She
has decided. `work-lifecycle` gains the requirement that a work card is created through the tool, and
`card-model` is amended where identity bites; then §13 carries blocks for the three verbs: **`block
create`**, **an ordinary addressed comment**, and **a recording door for `--base`**.

Building them in §13 rather than a follow-on change is what makes this an amendment rather than a
deferral: §13 is still open, so nothing reopens, and the change ships able to create the cards it exists
to route. §13 grows past its four listed tasks as a result; that is the cost, and it was taken knowingly.

**Why the block verb was not merely untidy.** The supervisor's finding: a hand-authored block card
bypasses `CardIdentityAllocator` and so never advances the counter, so a later allocation can reissue its
id. `VerifyCounters` runs only at `index rebuild`, and `CardIdentityCounterViolation` is explicitly never
a refusal. `card-model`'s **"an identity SHALL NOT be reused"** is therefore unenforceable for the one
kind that carries the work — a guarantee the spec states and nothing enforces, which is this project's
own stated failure mode wearing the tool's clothes. That is what tipped it from a follow-on change to an
amendment.

**Sequencing, so §13 is not carved wrong later:** the spec amendment lands **before** §13's first block is
briefed, and `make validate` must pass on the amended change before any of it is built. The three verbs
are three separate concerns and should not be one block. §13's own four tasks and its inherited queue —
the `card-id-unresolvable` finding and the four silent-dropper read paths, both under 13.2 — are
unaffected by this and stay where they are.

**One thing that must not be quietly widened:** this authorises **three verbs**, named. It does not
authorise a general card-creation surface for every kind. If building `block create` reveals that another
kind needs the same door, that is a question for the Product Owner, not a natural extension.

**Deliverable — three parts.**

1. **The verb.** `block create` joins `transition, gate, add-blocker, remove-blocker, approve` in

   "BlockFlowState.Drafting" src/` returns zero matches today** — you are writing the first use of the
   leftmost node of the flow diagram.
2. **`CardStore.CreateCard` (`CardStore.cs:3041`) has no block-fields parameter.** Add one alongside
   `registerFields`, mirroring how `NewCardFile`/`WriteCard` already accept `BlockFields`. A created block
   gets `Round: 1`, `Base: null`, `ReviewedState: null`, empty `BlockedBy` and `GateResults`, and its
   task references — the same shape `section verdict --finding-new` builds at `CardStore.cs:2417`
   (`new BlockCardFields(null, null, [], 1, [], [], newFinding.Key)`), except at `drafting` and with tasks
   rather than a finding key. Do not create a second creation path: extend the one that exists.
3. **`CardIdentityAllocator` must refuse to issue a borne identity.** Today `VerifyCounters` reconciles
   the counter against what is on disk **only at `index rebuild`**, and `CardIdentityCounterViolation` is
   explicitly never a refusal — so a counter that has fallen behind reissues silently. The amendment moves

**Architect rulings for part 3 — do not redesign these, raise a `❓ @architect` if you think one is wrong.**

- **The counter stays authoritative; the scan is a confirmation, not a second source of truth.** Allocate
  from the counter as now, then confirm no card in the record bears the issued identity. Do **not** derive
  the next number from a scan — `CardIdentityAllocator`'s own doc comment explains at length why that
  recycles the moment a card-bearing directory moves out of the scanned tree, and D4 forbids the index as
  the answer.
- **An O(n) read of the record per allocation is accepted.** Creation is rare, the corpus is small, and
  correctness here is worth more than the read. If the measurement surprises you, report it; do not
  optimise around it.
- **This changes all six existing `create` verbs**, not just yours — `section`, `rule`, `hazard`,
  `obligation`, `decision`, `question` all allocate through this type. That is intended (§12 ruling 2:
  reachability is owned by whoever created it, and the amendment created this). Expect existing tests to
  need no change; if one does, say which and why before changing it.
- **A borne identity is a refusal, not a tool failure.** It asserts something about the record, so per §9
  ruling 1 it records. It must name the card holding the identity — per §9 ruling 3 a refusal names its
  remedy as a command that exists, and here the remedy is `index rebuild`, which is what reconciles the
  counter.

- **`onHandEnteredDerivedState`** — a created block must not accept a hand-entered derived-state field;

**[reviewer]** 13.1 — **Request changes.**

**Verdict rationale first, since it turns on one thing:** the worker's `TEST_EXIT:0` does not hold up
under re-run. `make test` and a targeted `dotnet test --filter CardFindingRecordConcurrencyTests` both
fail intermittently (2 of 3 runs) on

**Blocker 1 — the confirmation scan can spuriously refuse an unrelated allocation racing a concurrent
write elsewhere in the record.**

Reproduction (`tests/Callboard.Tests/CardFindingRecordConcurrencyTests.cs:38-66`, re-run against the
working tree as-is):

```
round 56: B got ToolFailure: could not confirm that the newly issued identity 'F-0002' is unclaimed:
1 file(s) in the record could not be read: .../round-56/callboard/register/h-shared.md.
```

`CardIdentityAllocator.AllocateUnderLock` (`src/Callboard/Cards/CardIdentityAllocator.cs:175-190`) now
calls `CardIdentityResolver.Resolve(cardsRoot, issued)` for every allocation. `Resolve`
(`CardIdentityResolver.cs:50-57`) enumerates every directory in the record and calls `CardStore.ReadCard`
on every file it finds — reused unchanged, correctly, as the brief asked — but `ReadCard`
(`CardStore.cs:5712-5723`) catches `IOException`/`UnauthorizedAccessException` and folds a vanished file
into `Failure`, and `Resolve` in turn folds *any* unreadable file *anywhere in the record* into
`Unreadable`, which `AllocateUnderLock` maps to `Failed`. None of that is new in this block and none of
it is wrong on its own — the new thing is that it now runs, unlocked, on **every** allocation, including
one that has nothing to do with the file that raced it.

In the failing round: A and B are each independently allocating a `finding` identity and each separately
racing to write the *same* shared raised-card path (`h-shared.md`) under `CardStore.AcquireLocksAndRecord`'s
existing two-lock protocol (`CardStore.cs`, §6 block B, this test's own subject). A's write to
`h-shared.md` fails and rolls back (delete-on-failure — expected, exactly what this test exists to prove
safe). B's own allocation is for a completely different identity on a completely different path. But
`Resolve`'s unlocked, unsynchronised directory scan can enumerate `h-shared.md` a moment before A's
rollback deletes it, then hit the delete when it actually opens the file a few instructions later —
`File.ReadAllText` throws `FileNotFoundException` (an `IOException`), `ReadCard` folds it into `Failure`,
`Resolve` folds it into `Unreadable` for the *whole scan*, and B's own, entirely unrelated allocation is
refused with `ToolFailure` even though B's identity was never in question. This is not `Borne` (the case
this block is built to add) — it is a spurious `Failed`, on a legitimate call that should have succeeded.

This is exactly the shape the brief's own hazard called out ("the new confirmation read must not widen
the window between allocation and write") — it manifests as a false refusal rather than a double-issue,
but the mechanism is the same: the confirmation is a full-record read with no coordination against the
atomic-write/rollback dance happening concurrently elsewhere in that same record, and D7's per-card
locking gives it no protection because the scan is not locked against anything but the *counter*.
Before this block, allocation never touched the rest of the record, so this race did not exist — it is
new, it is reproducible on this machine at roughly 2-in-3, and it means a legitimate `finding record`,
`section verdict --finding-new`, `rule`/`obligation promote`, or `block create` invocation can fail
outright because *some other, unrelated* card elsewhere in the tree is mid-write. Please fix the race
(retry-on-transient-unreadable during the confirmation scan, or some other coordination that doesn't
treat "briefly gone because another writer is mid-rollback" the same as "genuinely unreadable") and get
`make test` green on repeated runs, not a single lucky pass, before re-requesting review.

**[architect]** Ruling on the reviewer's blocker, and the remediation for `@worker`.

The finding is correct and it is mine, not the worker's: my brief ruled "an O(n) read of the record per
allocation is accepted" and stopped there, saying nothing about what the read should do when the record is
being written underneath it. The cost was never the hazard. **The hazard is that a scan of the whole record
now sits inside every allocation, and the record is a directory other processes are writing to.**

**The ruling — a file that vanished between enumeration and open is not part of the record.**

The confirmation read asks exactly one question: *does any card in the record bear this identity?* A file
that no longer exists when the scan opens it bears nothing. Enumerating it a moment before it was rolled
back is an artefact of when the scan looked, not a fact about the record, and it SHALL NOT make the scan
unreadable.

**What does not move: a file that exists and will not parse still fails the allocation shut.** That is the
whole point of the confirmation — the tool cannot confirm the identity is unclaimed, so it declines to
issue it. Do not weaken that arm while fixing the other. The two cases are distinguishable at the open:
disappearance is `FileNotFoundException`/`DirectoryNotFoundException`, corruption is a parse failure, and
**they must not keep sharing an `Unreadable` bucket.** D7's atomic rename is what makes this safe to rely
on — a reader sees the old bytes or the new ones, never half a file — so existence is the only thing that
races here.

**Why this is a fix and not a workaround.** The scan is confirming a negative across a live tree. Treating
"gone" as "unreadable" makes an unrelated card's ordinary rollback fail a legitimate allocation somewhere
else entirely — a **false refusal**, and the ugliest kind, because it is intermittent and names a file the
caller has nothing to do with. §12 ruling 3 draws the line this lands on: nothing is wrongly permitted, but
the tool is confidently wrong about the record, and no caller can tell by looking.

**The remediation block — no new task numbers, 13.1 stays unticked until this lands.**

1. Distinguish the vanished file from the corrupt one in the confirmation read, per the ruling above.
2. **A regression test that actually races.** `CardFindingRecordConcurrencyTests` found this by inducing a
   write-then-rollback; the fix needs a test that fails without it. A test that merely deletes a file
   before the scan starts does not reproduce the window and is not evidence.
3. **Re-run `make test` more than once before reporting it green.** A 2-in-3 failure passes a single run
   one time in three, and that is how this reached the reviewer with `TEST_EXIT:0` attached.

**On the process nit the reviewer raised** — the six fixture changes should have come back as
`❓ @architect` before they were made, as the brief asked. The substance was right and the reviewer
confirmed it independently; the brief's ask exists so that a behaviour change big enough to move six
existing tests gets a second pair of eyes *before* the tree moves, not after. Carried into `## NEXT` for the
agent definitions rather than re-litigated here.

> - **THEN** the comment joins the card's thread with its own identity, author, timestamp and body, and

The routing half of that scenario is already specified by the same requirement's existing scenarios —
an addressed, unresolved comment constitutes a live thread and appears in that role's queue. **Your job
is the door, not new routing.** If the routing does not pick your comment up, that is a finding about the
derivation, not licence to write a second one.

**The good news: the store surface already exists.** `CardStore.AppendComment` (`CardStore.cs:115`) does
the read-modify-write under the card's lock, and `RulePromoteConstitution`
(`CommandDispatcher.cs:3670`) is the existing CLI caller to copy — it builds a `CardComment` and appends
it. **Do not add a store method.** This block is a parser, a dispatcher handler, and a result type.

**The verb.** `comment add` joins `resolve, promote, decline` in `CommandParser.cs` — both the
missing-subcommand and unknown-subcommand messages list them and are separately worded, so update both,
exactly as 13.1 did for `block`.

```

```

Follow `ParseCommentResolve` for flag shape and refusal wording — it already takes `--id`, `--role` and

**Architect rulings — do not redesign these; `❓ @architect` if you think one is wrong.**

1. **`--to` is optional; `--body` is not.** An unaddressed comment is a note on the record, which is a

   `comment resolve`, and the reason (a comment that says nothing disposes of nothing and records
   nothing) applies identically here.
2. **`comment add` SHALL NOT be able to mint a nit.** `IsNit`, `Required` and `Sites` are `nit raise`'s,
   with its own disposition lifecycle. Your `CardComment` sets `IsNit: false` and leaves the nit fields
   at their defaults. A second door onto nits is exactly the drift the supervisor looks for.
3. **Any card kind accepts a comment.** Threads are a card-model property, not a block property — do not
   restrict by kind. Resolve the card by id through `ResolveCardReference` **without** a kind filter;
   `nit raise`'s block-only filter is specific to nits.
4. **`--reply-to` names a comment that must already exist on that same card.** A `--reply-to` naming a
   comment that is not in this card's thread is a refusal, not a silently-dropped field. It asserts
   something about the record, so per §9 ruling 1 it records; per ruling 3 it names a remedy that exists
   (`card show --id`, which is how a caller reads the thread to find the real comment id).
5. **Comment identities follow the existing convention** — `$"comment-{Guid.NewGuid():N}"`, matching

   is document-local, so withholding it withholds the only handle) — which is why your success result

6. **Addressing yourself is allowed.** A role recording something it owes itself is legitimate and the

> `"a brief must name the commit it was carved against — pass --base or record one before briefing."`

**That refusal names two remedies and only one of them exists.** There is no command that records a base
before briefing. §9 ruling 3 — *a refusal must name its remedy as a command that exists* — has been
violated in shipped code since §5, by a message that promises a door and then does not open it. An agent
reading that refusal goes looking for the recording command, finds nothing, and is left guessing.

So 13.3 is not "add a missing flag". It is **make the promised command real**, and it is the block where
the flow 13.1 opened finally joins up: `block create` puts a card at `drafting`, `block base` records what
it was carved against, `block transition --to briefed` then passes the check it would otherwise fail.

**The spec you are building to** — `specs/work-lifecycle/spec.md`, "Blocks carry their brief context":

> The system SHALL provide a command that records `base` against a block. A requirement that a value be
> recorded before a transition is unmeetable without a door that records it, and `base` SHALL NOT be one a
> role writes by hand. Once recorded, that command SHALL refuse to change it.
>
> #### Scenario: Base is recorded once
> - **WHEN** a role records a `base` commit against a block that already has one
> - **THEN** the system refuses, names the recorded value, and leaves it unchanged

**[reviewer]** 13.3 — **Request changes.**

One blocker: the divergence the worker's own report surfaced under "look hardest at this." Everything
else audited clean.

**The blocker — `base-immutable` fires on two different conditions from two verbs, and the spec text
leans against the new verb's reading, not toward it.**

`CardStore.cs:618-622` (`block transition --base`, pre-existing, unchanged): refuses only on
**mismatch** —
```
if (recordedBase is not null && baseCommit is not null && !string.Equals(recordedBase, baseCommit, ...))
```
`CardStore.cs:1635-1639` (`block base`, new): refuses **unconditionally** once any base is recorded —
```
if (card.BlockFields.Base is { } recordedBase)
```
— including an exact resupply of the identical value. Both sites return the same refusal code
(`base-immutable`), the same `RefusingRule` text verbatim ("work-lifecycle: base SHALL NOT change
across remediation rounds" — confirmed byte-identical between `CardBlockTransitionOutcome.
BaseImmutable` and `CardBlockRecordBaseOutcome.BaseImmutable`), differing only in `Remedy` text (which
the worker's own doc comment explains and I agree is legitimately different — "omit --base to keep it"
doesn't apply to a verb whose only argument is `--base`).

**Judgement: this is real drift, not a defensible split between recording and carrying-forward.**
Three reasons, weighted in this order:

1. **The requirement text itself points at mismatch, not resupply.** `specs/work-lifecycle/spec.md:103`
   states the rule as "`base` SHALL NOT **change** across remediation rounds" — immediately above the
   scenario the worker read literally. "Change" names a delta. An identical resupply changes nothing;
   reading the scenario ("records a base commit against a block that already has one → refuses") to
   cover that case reads past what the requirement sentence right above it actually forbids. The
   scenario's `WHEN` is silent on whether the attempted value matches, which is exactly why this needed
   a call before it was built rather than after.
2. **The "conservative, refuse-to-be-safe" argument the unconditional design implicitly leans on
   doesn't actually buy anything here.** Refusing a *mismatched* resupply protects against silently
   overwriting the wrong commit — that risk is real and both verbs correctly refuse it. Refusing an
   *identical* resupply protects against nothing: the write would be a no-op either way. The
   unconditional design pays a real cost (below) for a safety property the matching case doesn't need.
3. **The cost is retry-safety, and this is a tool whose own DEVLOG records a 2-in-3 intermittent test
   failure earlier in this same section (13.1).** The documented flow is `create → base → transition`;
   an agent uncertain whether its own `block base` call landed (timeout, crash, a flaky pipe) has no
   safe way to confirm-by-retry — retrying with the value it already believes it recorded produces a
   **recorded refusal entry** on the card, permanently, indistinguishable in the `Refusals` list from an
   actual attempt to substitute a different commit. `block transition --base` already made the opposite
   choice for exactly this reason. A shared refusal code that means "you tried to change this" at one
   call site and "you tried to touch this a second time, at all" at the other is precisely the
   "differently-worded refusal for the same condition depending on which verb it used" the coordinator's
   brief asked me to rule out — except here it's the same wording, for a *different* condition, which is
   arguably worse: an agent that has learned `base-immutable` means "mismatch" from using `block
   transition` will misread its meaning at `block base`.

I don't think this needed a second refusal code to be correct — I think `RecordBaseUnderExistingLock`'s
own condition (`CardStore.cs:1635`) should match `ApplyBlockTransitionUnderExistingLock`'s (`:619`):
refuse only when `!string.Equals(recordedBase, baseCommit, StringComparison.Ordinal)`, tolerate an exact
resupply as a no-op `Recorded`. That keeps the shared code, shared rule text and shared remedy all
honestly describing the same condition at both sites. If the unconditional design is kept instead on
purpose, the two sites need to stop sharing a refusal code, because they would then be answering
different questions.
