**[architect]** Stopping on 13.3 and putting it to the Product Owner. WIP stays uncommitted, 13.3 unticked,
nothing reverted.

**The reviewer is right, and the defect is in the spec I drafted.** Its blocker: `block base` refuses an
exact resupply of the identical value, while `block transition --base` refuses only a mismatch — both
emitting the same `base-immutable` code and the same rule text for two different conditions.

**Read the requirement against its own scenario** (`specs/work-lifecycle/spec.md`, "Blocks carry their
brief context"). The prose says **change**, twice:

> `base` SHALL be recorded before the block is briefed, and SHALL NOT **change** across remediation rounds.
>
> Once recorded, that command SHALL refuse to **change** it.

The scenario I added underneath it says something broader:

> **WHEN** a role records a `base` commit against a block that already has one — **THEN** the system refuses

**An identical resupply changes nothing**, so the two sentences permit it and my scenario forbids it. The
worker implemented the scenario literally, which was the correct thing for it to do: it is the more
specific statement, and a worker should not quietly prefer the prose it finds more reasonable.

**This is the spec being wrong, not the code** — CLAUDE.md §4's stop-and-ask, and it is a wording the
Product Owner read in full and approved before it was committed, which is why I am not fixing it on my own
authority.

**The reviewer's third argument is the one that decides it for me.** Retry-safety: this is a tool whose
callers are agents, and an agent that cannot tell whether its `block base` call landed has no safe way to
find out. Under the unconditional reading its retry both fails **and** writes a permanently recorded
refusal indistinguishable from a genuine attempt to overwrite. That is a tool punishing a caller for the
tool's own uncertainty — and this section has already spent a remediation round on an intermittent that
made exactly that uncertainty real.

Two rulings this touches, noted for whoever reads this later:

- **§10 ruling 4** — where a spec and shipped behaviour contradict, one of them moves, deliberately, and
  the Product Owner decides which. This is the same shape one level in: **a spec contradicting itself.**
- **§12 ruling 6** — an ambiguous spec is the Product Owner's call, not the implementer's, even when the
  implementer's reading is sound and documented. It was sound here, and it is still not the implementer's
  call.

**[architect]** **Product Owner ruling: the scenario moves, not the code's condition.**

Put to the Product Owner as a spec-contradicts-itself call; she ruled that **the scenario is reworded to
match on *change***, which is what the requirement's own prose said twice all along. `block base` tolerates
an identical resupply. The amended requirement now carries two scenarios where it carried one:

> #### Scenario: Base does not change once recorded
> - **WHEN** a role records a `base` commit that **differs from** the one a block already carries
> - **THEN** the system refuses, names the recorded value, and leaves it unchanged
>
> #### Scenario: Recording the same base again is not a change
> - **WHEN** a role records the `base` commit a block already carries
> - **THEN** the system **does not refuse**, and the recorded value is unchanged

`VALIDATE_EXIT:0` on the amended change.

**The second scenario is the point, and it is why the reword is not just a narrowing.** The original said
what must be refused and left what must be *permitted* to inference — and inference is exactly what
diverged, silently, between two verbs sharing one refusal code. **A spec that only ever states its
refusals will grow a divergence at every door it does not mention.** The permitted case is now written
down, so the next verb that touches `base` cannot quietly pick the other reading.

**Retry-safety is the reason this mattered**, and it generalises past this block: the callers of this tool
are agents, and an agent that cannot tell whether its call landed must be able to ask again without being
punished for asking. Under the old reading the retry failed *and* left a permanently recorded refusal
indistinguishable from a real attempted overwrite. **Carry this into `## NEXT`** — it is a property the
whole CLI should be audited against, not a fact about `block base`.

Credit where it is due: the worker implemented the scenario literally rather than the prose it might have
preferred, which is what surfaced the contradiction at all; and the reviewer refused the invitation to
soften a real finding into a nit.

**The defect.** `RecordExportTests.SectionExport_EveryThreadReferent_ResolvesToADefinitionInTheSameDocument`
(`tests/Callboard.Tests/RecordExportTests.cs:202`) builds its set of *defined* comment ids by regex over
the **rendered document**:

```csharp
var definedIds = Regex.Matches(text, @"\*\*\[[a-z][a-z-]*\s+(\S+)\]\*\*")
```

Any text anywhere in the export matching that shape counts as a definition — **including a comment body**.
So a body containing the literal `**[reviewer c-2]**` manufactures a definition of `c-2` that no comment
provides, and the test's central assertion passes on it. **It passes when it should fail**, which is worth
less than no test at all, because it is read as coverage.

**It is reachable today and this is not hypothetical.** 13.2's worker reproduced it end to end through the
CLI and established that **`comment resolve` has taken an unconstrained stdin body since §9** — so this has
been live in shipped code for four sections. `comment add` widened the door; it did not open it.

**What the test is actually for**, from its own comment, and it is a property worth keeping:

> A reader with no tool and no other file open must be able to find the definition of every name the
> document uses.

**Architect rulings.**

1. **Defined ids come from the `CardFile`, never from rendered prose.** The fixture knows exactly which
   comments exist; that is the truth, and prose cannot be allowed to add to it. This is `## NEXT`'s stated
   fix and it also retires the `(\S+)` whitespace-in-an-id assumption on the definition side.
2. **Do not lose the half the regex was doing honestly.** Taking ids from the card proves referents point
   at real comments, but no longer proves the **document renders a definition for each**. Both halves must
   hold: for every comment the card carries, assert its definition actually appears in the exported text;
   then assert every referent the document uses is one of those ids. Dropping the second half would trade
   a false pass for a blind spot.
3. **Add the fixture that proves it.** A comment whose **body** contains a `**[reviewer c-9]**`-shaped
   string, plus a referent naming `c-9` where no comment `c-9` exists. **Verify both directions and say so
   in your post**: it must fail against the current test and pass against the fixed one. 13.1's remediation
   set that bar and it is the bar here — a regression test nobody has watched fail is a guess.
4. **The referent side still reads the document, and that is correct** — what the document says is the
   whole point. But note its scan is likewise unscoped (`## NEXT`: "unscoped to `### thread`"), so a body
   containing `(replies to c-2)` registers a false *referent*. That direction makes the test **stricter**,
   not weaker, so it is not a false pass — **scope it if it is clean to do so, and if it is not, say so

**Item 3 — the `ThreadSections` premise holds structurally, not only for this fixture's shapes.**
Read `RecordExportRenderer.AppendCard` (`:64-88`) directly: the call order is

for every card kind — this is a hard structural guarantee, not an accident of what block/section
cards happen to render. More: `grep -n '"## \|"### '` across the whole renderer file shows exactly

output (two cards, two `### thread` blocks) confirms this empirically too: `ThreadSections` returned
exactly two sections, each holding exactly that card's own two comments, correctly bounded at the
next `## ` heading and at end-of-file respectively.

everything the *renderer* emits, but a comment **body** that happens to contain a literal line
starting `## ` would still terminate `ThreadSections`'s non-greedy capture early, silently dropping
whatever follows in that card's own thread from the scanned text — a referent hiding after such a
line would go unchecked, not because it resolves, but because the scope truncated before reaching
it. This is narrower and differently-shaped than the defect this block fixes (it would drop coverage,
not manufacture a false definition), and it does not affect this block's own fixture or its actual
correctness — but it is the same class of risk (prose forging document structure) landing on the new
boundary instead of the old one. Worth a line in `## NEXT` for whoever next touches this test; not
worth reopening this block for.

back, as the worker reported.

**[architect]** 13.4 — implemented by me, not by a worker, at the Product Owner's direction. The block's
only file is `.claude/hooks/dmons-guard.sh`, which the guard denies to every agent by its own
`*/.claude/*` rule: a worker cannot write it, and lifting the rule for the duration would disable the
very boundary the block extends. Same carve-out as the `Makefile`. The reviewer still audits the diff and
the gates still ran; only the authorship moved.

**What the boundary now denies.** Two rules, one message, one shared path pattern:

- **File-write tools** (`Edit`/`Write`/`MultiEdit`/`NotebookEdit`) on any path under the card store.
- **Anything that can run a shell** (`Bash`, the `ctx_*` tools) where a *mutating* command names a store
  path — `>`/`>>` redirects, `rm rmdir unlink mv cp tee touch truncate mkdir install dd ln chmod chown
  shred`, and `sed`/`perl`/`ruby`/`python`/`ed`/`patch` invoked in-place.

**Reads are untouched, deliberately.** `cat`, `grep`, `sed -n`, `ls` over a card file all pass. 13.6 rests
on a card's status, owner, scope and history being determinable from the file alone, and 13.5 on the
record staying readable when the tool cannot run — a boundary that blinded an agent to its own record
would refute both. The store is `callboard`'s to *write*; it was never `callboard`'s to *show*.

**The trap this repository sets, and the pattern that avoids it.** The naive rule is `callboard/`. This
repository **is** `callboard`, so every source file under it carries `callboard/` in its absolute path and
that rule denies the whole tree — `src/Callboard/Cards/CardLayout.cs` included. The pattern matches the
five directories `CardLayout.cs` and `IndexPaths.cs` actually name (`register decisions changes identities
.index`) **as a path tail**, the way `AnchoredCardPath` matches one. That is also what makes it right for
a store rooted outside this repo rather than merely right here.

**Segment-splitting, not whole-string matching.** The existing git rule joins every string in the tool
input and matches across the lot. Reused here that would condemn `cat callboard/register/rule-0001.md ; rm
/tmp/scratch` — a legitimate read sentenced by an unrelated deletion. The store rule splits on `; & | \n`
first and requires the path and the mutation in the *same* segment. Fixture case 13 is that case.

**The refusal names verbs that exist** (§13 ruling 5): `callboard comment add`, `block create`,
`block base`, `block transition` — all four verified present in `CommandParser.cs`. It closes by naming
the gap-reporting route, because a boundary with no exit is one an agent routes around: *if no verb records
what you have, that is a gap to report to the Architect, not to route around.*

(`$TMPDIR/guard-fixture.sh`, scratch; not committed):

```
ok    deny   redirect into a card                  ok    allow  grep the store

ok    deny   ctx_execute mv a decision             ok    allow  read a card, rm elsewhere
ok    deny   append into a card                    ok    allow  ordinary build
ok    deny   perl -pi a card                       ok    allow  sed reading a card (no -i)
ok    deny   still denies git commit               ok    allow  still allows git diff
                                                   ok    allow  grep -i over the store
```

The first pass was **18/19**: `sed -i '' …` slipped through. The `-i` pattern required a space *before*

not a guess because the fixture ran before the claim.

Nothing landed: `ls callboard/ 2>&1` → `ls: callboard/: No such file or directory` — no file, and no parent
directory silently created either. **The block's central claim holds: the rule is live against a real
agent's real tool call, not only against a fixture.** Two further live confirmations fell out of the

**What I verified clean, so it is not re-litigated later.**

1. **The directory list is exact.** `CardLayout.cs:17,18,19,31` gives `register/ decisions/ changes/

   `changes/` and therefore covered by it; `IndexPaths.cs:12` gives `.index/`. Five directories, five

   `callboard/**/*.lock` and `callboard/**/*.tmp-*` also live under those five, so the lock and temp-file
   surface is covered without a sixth alternative.
2. **Tail-matching is the right shape and matches `AnchoredCardPath`'s caution about it.** Note the
   asymmetry is deliberate and correct: `AnchoredCardPath` *rejects* mere tail-matching because it is
   deciding where a write may land under one known root; the guard has no known root, so a tail is all it

   `sed -n`), which is what 13.5 and 13.6 rest on.
4. **The loop runs in the current shell.** `done <<<"$(…)"` (:92) is a here-string, not a pipe, so
   `deny`'s `exit 2` at :33 actually exits the hook. Had this been `… | while`, every store denial would
   have silently not blocked. Worth having got right.
5. **`tr ';&|\n' '\n\n\n\n'` loses nothing** — a 1:1 character map; `&&` merely yields an empty segment.
   And `<<<` re-appends the newline that `$( )` stripped, so the final segment is still read.
6. **All four named verbs parse.** `CommandParser.cs:45 → :3053 ParseCommentAdd`; `:35 → :111 create`,

### Blockers — the rule fails open on ordinary commands

I re-implemented `STORE_PATH_RE` and the three mutation patterns verbatim, including the `tr`/`while`
split, and ran 22 payloads through them. The controls behave (`rm` a card file, `>` redirect, heredoc
redirect, `dd of=`, `awk`'s internal `>`, `find … -exec rm`, and `cat card ; rm /tmp/x` correctly
*allowed* — fixture case 13's separation works). These did not:

**B1 — `STORE_PATH_RE` requires a trailing `/`, so naming the directory itself escapes.**
`dmons-guard.sh:28` ends `(register|decisions|changes|identities|\.index)/`. A path that stops at the
directory never matches, so the whole rule is skipped by the `|| continue` at :86:

- `rm -rf callboard/register` → **allowed**
- `mv callboard/register /tmp/x` → **allowed**

This is the plainest destructive command in the set, and it deletes more than any single-card write could.
It is the same shape as the `sed -i ''` defect the fixture caught: the elaborate case passes, the obvious
one walks through. Suggest making the trailing `/` optional with a boundary — `(…)(/|$|[^[:alnum:]_.-])`.

**B2 — the store root itself is not covered.** `rm -rf callboard` matches nothing at :28 and is
**allowed**. That removes the entire record. A separate alternative for the root (bounded so that
`src/Callboard/…` still cannot match) is needed, or B1's fix generalised.

**B3 — splitting on `|` defeats a pipeline; splitting is what does it.** `:92` turns `|` into a newline,
so path and verb land in different segments and neither segment satisfies both halves:

- `ls callboard/register/*.md | xargs rm` → **allowed**
- `cat /tmp/x >| callboard/register/a.md` → **allowed** (the `>|` noclobber-override redirect is split
  apart before `:87`'s redirect pattern ever sees it)

The `;`-splitting fix for fixture case 13 is right; splitting on `|` as well buys nothing (a pipeline is
one command) and costs both of these.

**B4 — `find … -delete` is not in the verb list.** `:88` has no `find`. Even with B1 fixed,
`find callboard/register/ -name '*.md' -delete` names no listed verb and is **allowed**. (`-exec rm`
happens to be caught, but only because `rm` appears — which is luck, not coverage.)

**B5 — an interpreter payload carries no shell verb at all, and this is the agents' busiest path.**
`:89` matches `python3`/`perl`/`ruby` **only when followed by `-i`/`--in-place`**. Everything else is
open:

- `python3 -c "open('callboard/register/a.md','w').write('x')"` → **allowed**
- `python3 -c "import os; os.remove('callboard/register/a.md')"` → **allowed** (the `;` split also
  separates the two halves here)
- `node -e "require('fs').writeFileSync('callboard/register/a.md','x')"` → **allowed**

And the sharpest form: the guard deliberately covers `ctx_execute` because "those run commands too"
(:52–54) — but `ctx_execute` takes a `language` parameter, and a call with `language: "python"` or
`"javascript"` and body `fs.writeFileSync('callboard/register/a.md','x')` contains **no shell text
whatsoever**. `:88`–`:89` are shell-verb patterns applied to a non-shell payload; the store path is
right there in `CMD` and nothing matches it. Given how routinely these agents reach for `ctx_execute`,
this is the bypass most likely to be taken by accident rather than by intent.

I do not think a `PreToolUse` regex can ever be a sandbox, and I am not asking for one. B1, B2 and B5
are not exotic — they are what an agent types when it is tidying up or scripting a fixture. A boundary
whose header says it "Fails CLOSED" (:17) should catch those.

segment containing a store path, so *prose* that names both is denied. Confirmed:
`printf 'the guard denies rm, mv, cp under callboard/register/' >> …/DEVLOG.md` → **denied**. Writing a
DEVLOG post about the store through a Bash heredoc is blocked. It only misses me because I am posting via
`Edit`, whose check at :119 looks at `file_path` alone. Low harm, but it is the boundary refusing the
hand-back it demands.

**N2 — a worker's scratch fixture store is denied.** `rm -rf $TMPDIR/callboard/register/` → **denied**,
because the pattern is root-agnostic by design (:26–27). That trade is defensible and I would keep it,
but it is worth stating in the header, since a worker building a temp store to test against will hit it
and needs to know the denial is intended.

**N3 — the refusal message is duplicated at :90 and :120 and the two copies have already drifted**: :90
ends "Reading card files (`cat`, `grep`, `ls`) is fine", :120 ends "Reading card files is fine". Same
message, two literals, no shared variable — the next edit will drift them further. `STORE_PATH_RE` was
hoisted for exactly this reason; the message deserves the same treatment.

**[architect]** 13.4 remediation — all five blockers fixed, both remaining nits addressed or ruled, and
the fixture grown from 19 cases to 38. **All five were real**, and four of them shared one shape: the
pattern matched the *form of the write I had pictured* rather than the *set of ways to write*.

- **B1 — the trailing slash.** `STORE_PATH_RE` ended at `/`, so `rm -rf callboard/register` — which
  destroys the whole directory — walked past a rule that stopped `rm callboard/register/rule-0001.md`.
  The directory name now ends at any non-path character. **This is the `sed -i ''` defect a second time,
  in the same block**: a pattern that catches the elaborate case and misses the blunt one.
- **B2 — the store root.** `rm -rf callboard` was uncovered and could not be covered by the path pattern,
  because a bare `callboard` token is far more often *the binary being invoked* than a directory being
  destroyed. It needed its own rule, matching the root only as the **argument of a destructive verb**:
  `callboard block create` passes, `rm -rf callboard` does not. Two fixture cases pin that distinction,
  including `rm -rf bin obj && callboard block create`, where both readings appear in one command.
- **B3 — splitting on `|`.** A pipeline is *one* command, and splitting it put `ls callboard/register/*.md
  | xargs rm` into a segment whose only verb was `ls`. Splitting on `;` and `&` was the part that earned
  its keep; `|` bought nothing and cost this. Now split on sequencing operators only.
- **B4 — `find`.** Added `-delete`, `-exec` and `-execdir`.
- **B5 — interpreters, and the sharpest case in the review.** `python3 -c "open(p,'w').write(x)"` was
  allowed because the rule wanted `-i`. Interpreters are now matched on *any* flags — `python node ruby
  perl php deno bun osascript` — while `sed`, `awk` and `jq` stay out deliberately, since each needs a
  `-i` or a redirect to write and both are already caught, which is what keeps `sed -n` a legal read.
  **And the form with no shell text at all**: a `ctx_execute` with `language: "python"` carries code, not
  a command line, so there was nothing for a verb rule to match — on the agents' busiest path. Non-shell
  code is now judged before the verb rules and **fails shut on any mention of a store path**. There is no
  verb vocabulary to read in Python: `open(p,'w').write(x)` and `open(p).read()` differ by one character.
  Nothing is lost — reading a card is `cat`.

**N3 — the duplicated refusal — was right, and it had already drifted** between its two copies within one
block. Extracted to `deny_store()`. **A refusal stated twice is a refusal that will eventually say two
different things**, and this one managed it before the block was even committed.

**N1 stands as a documented cost.** Prose naming a store path in the same Bash segment as the word `rm`
is denied, so a DEVLOG post *about* the store cannot be written via a heredoc. The route is the `Write`
tool, which is allowed on `DEVLOG.md` — this very post took it. Narrowing the rule to catch only verbs in

convenience. **N2** (`$TMPDIR/callboard/register/` denied) is intended: the pattern matches a store *tail*

### Blockers

**R1 — the store root fails open whenever the verb does not sit next to the word.**
`.claude/hooks/dmons-guard.sh:38`. `STORE_ROOT_TARGET_RE` is ordered: verb, then tokens, then
`callboard`. Every destructive shape that puts the path *before* the verb, or names it to a tool that is
not in the verb list, passes:

```
allow   ls -d callboard | xargs rm -rf
allow   find callboard -delete
allow   find callboard -name '*.md' -delete
allow   tar -xzf backup.tgz -C callboard
allow   rsync -a --delete /tmp/x/ callboard/register/
```

The first is exactly the shape B3 was raised on, one directory higher. The `xargs` fix works for the
*path* pattern (`ls callboard/register/*.md | xargs rm` → `DENY(verb)`, confirmed) because there
`STORE_PATH_RE` matches anywhere in the segment and any verb anywhere then denies — order-free. The root
rule did not get that treatment, so the store's most destructive command is the one that passes. B4 has
the same asymmetry: `find` with `-delete` is inside the `STORE_PATH_RE`-gated branch, so it catches
`find callboard/register -delete` and not `find callboard -delete`. The last line is a fifth verb gap
that is not about the root at all — `rsync` writes *into* the store, through the path pattern, and is
absent from the write-verb list at line 124 along with `tar` and `unzip`.

The same hole reaches through the new language gate. Lines 106–111 fail shut on `STORE_PATH_RE` only, so
a non-shell tool aimed at the root is not judged at all:
`ctx_execute(language:"python", code:"import shutil; shutil.rmtree('callboard')")` → allowed. (The `;`
splits it, and neither segment carries a store *path* or a listed verb.)

**R2 — `patch` and `ed` write in place with no flag, and are guarded as if they needed one.**
`.claude/hooks/dmons-guard.sh:130`. The predicate requires `-i`/`--in-place` before it fires. That is
right for `sed` and wrong for the other two: `patch`'s `-i` names the *patch file*, not in-place editing,
which is its default; and `ed` has no `-i` at all — it writes when told `w`. Both are present on this
machine:

```
allow   patch callboard/register/rule-0001.md < fix.diff
allow   printf '1d\nw\n' | ed callboard/register/a.md
allow   ex -sc '%d|x' callboard/register/a.md
```

That is a card file rewritten wholesale, past every refusal, with a tool the guard already names.
(`ex` is the third of the family and is not listed at all.)

**R5 answer, folded in — the interpreter list.** Naming only what this environment genuinely has and
what genuinely writes: `dotnet fsi` (F# interactive ships with the .NET 10 SDK this repo already
requires) — `dotnet fsi w.fsx callboard/register/a.md` → allowed. Plus `patch`/`ed`/`ex` above. I did
**not** raise `swift`, `lua` or `Rscript`: I have no evidence any of them is installed here, and padding
a denylist with absent binaries makes it read as more complete than it is. `xargs -I{} python3 …` needs
nothing — the interpreter predicate is position-free and already catches it. `awk`'s exclusion is
correct as documented: `print > "callboard/register/x.md"` is caught by the redirect predicate.

### Notes under the changes requested

**N-A — `STORE_ROOT_TARGET_RE`'s greedy middle denies ordinary work.**
`([[:space:]]+[^[:space:]]+)*` spans the whole segment, and B3 removed the `|` split, so the rule now
reads: *any* destructive verb anywhere in a pipeline plus *any* bare `callboard` token anywhere after it.
Confirmed false positives:

```
DENY   rm -rf obj bin | grep callboard
DENY   truncate -s 0 log.txt | grep callboard
DENY   cp bin/Release/net10.0/osx-arm64/publish/callboard /usr/local/bin/
DENY   chmod +x ./callboard
DENY   dotnet tool install --global callboard
DENY   ln -s "$PWD/bin/callboard" ~/bin/cb
```

The first two are unrelated cleanup that happens to mention the tool downstream. The last four are the
*built binary*, which is textually identical to the store root — that ambiguity is inherent and cannot be
regexed away, and I am not asking for it to be. I am asking that it be **stated in the comment at
lines 34–37**, which currently says only that `callboard block create` passes. A worker who hits
`chmod +x ./callboard` and reads that comment will conclude the guard is broken; a worker who reads
"the binary and the store share a name, so verb-shaped commands naming the binary are denied — report
it, do not route around it" will do the right thing. Same standard the file sets for itself at
lines 13–15.

**N-B — B3's cost, also worth writing down.** Reads that pipe into a write-named tool are now denied:
`cat callboard/register/rule-0001.md | tee /tmp/x.md` → `DENY(verb)`. Fail-closed, so not a defect — but
the comment at lines 96–99 promises "`cat`, `grep`, `ls` and `sed -n` … is fine and is not blocked", and
that promise is now conditional on what follows the pipe. One clause.

**N-C — B1 in the other direction: clean.** I checked the widened terminator `(/|[^[:alnum:]_.-]|$)`
against the near-misses. `callboard/register.bak` and `callboard/changes-old` are correctly **not**
matched (`.` and `-` are inside the excluded class), so a sibling file is not mistaken for the store. One
over-match: a URL matches, because `[^[:space:]]*/` swallows the scheme and host —
`https://x/callboard/changes` satisfies `STORE_PATH_RE`. Harmless alone (`curl -sO …` → allowed); it only
bites combined with N-B, where `curl -s https://x/callboard/changes | tee /tmp/p.json` → `DENY(verb)`.
Not worth a pattern change; worth knowing it exists.

**N-D — the language gate is sound in the dangerous direction.** `case` is exact-match, so `Shell`,
`SHELL`, `shellscript` and `sh -c` all fall to `*)` and fail shut. That is the safe side, and the cost is
only a denied read. Nothing lands in the pass-through arm carrying non-shell code: `''` is reachable from
exactly two tools, `Bash` and `ctx_batch_execute`, and both carry shell; `ctx_execute` and
`ctx_execute_file` both mark `language` **required**, so neither can reach `''` by omission. The
`[.tool_input | .. | strings]` sweep reaches everything that matters — `..` recurses through
`ctx_batch_execute`'s array of `{label, command}` objects, and `ctx_execute_file` marks `code` required,
so there is no shape where executable text lives outside `tool_input`. The gap in this arm is R1's, not
the arm's.

**N-E — one thing that is right and easy to break later.** The loop at line 117 is fed by a here-string
(`done <<<"$(…)"`), so it runs in the current shell and `deny_store`'s `exit 2` actually blocks. Had it
been `… | while read`, every store denial in rule 2 would have exited a subshell and the guard would have
returned 0 — a refusal that fails open while reading as if it fires. Worth a comment saying so, because
the pipe form is the one someone reaches for.

**R1 — the root rule was ordered, so it failed open wherever the verb did not sit beside the word.**
`STORE_ROOT_TARGET_RE` matched verb→argument, so `ls -d callboard | xargs rm -rf`, `find callboard

stop asking the regex to do two jobs. **The root is now matched as a plain token, and the distinction
between the tool and the store is drawn separately, by position**: a `callboard` at the head of a segment,
a pipeline stage or a substitution is the binary being invoked — the one thing entitled to write the
store — and is blanked out before the token match runs. Whatever `callboard` survives that is a path.

the other side of it: `callboard block create`, `cat body.md | callboard comment add`, `ID=$(callboard
block create)`, `./callboard index rebuild`, and `rm -rf bin obj && callboard state` — the last one being
both readings in a single command. `rsync`, `tar`, `unzip` and `zip` joined the verb list.

**The strip itself is sound in both directions**, which is what you asked me to audit. Direction 1 — the
routes that do *not* reach the modelled command position (`xargs callboard comment add`, `env FOO=1
callboard block create`, `bash -c "callboard block create"`, `exec callboard state`, `command callboard
state`) all land on `allow` anyway, because none of them carries a write verb; the strip missing them
costs nothing. `sudo`/`env`/`time`/`nice`, `./`, pipeline heads and `$( )` heads all strip as intended,
and all five of your controls pass. Direction 2 — I could not find a segment where the strip eats a token
that was a path *and* that segment would otherwise have denied. It only fires on a `callboard` at the
head of a segment, stage or substitution followed by whitespace-or-end, and in every case I could

### Blocker

**R3 — a backslash line continuation splits the verb from the path, and the store deletes.**
`.claude/hooks/dmons-guard.sh:149`. The segment split is `tr ';&\n' '\n\n\n'`, which treats **every**
newline as a sequencing operator — including one the shell does not, the escaped newline. A continued
command therefore arrives as two segments: one with the verb and no path, one with the path and no verb.
Neither denies. Confirmed on the harness:

```
allow   rm -rf \
        callboard/register
allow   rm -rf \
        callboard
allow   rm -rf \
          callboard/register/rule-0001.md
DENY    rm -rf callboard/register        (same command, one line — control)
DENY    rm -rf callboard                 (control)
```

That is the whole store, destroyed by a single ordinary shell command, past a guard whose one job is that
this cannot happen. It is not evasion-shaped — a long `rm` broken across lines is a formatting habit, not
a trick — and the guard is what stands between an agent and the record. (The strip is only incidental
here: on the bare-root form it blanks the surviving `callboard`, but the `…/register` form is not
stripped at all and passes on the missing verb alone. So this is the split, not this round's change, and
it has been open since the rule was written — which is why I am blocking rather than noting it.)

Fix is one line, in bash, no fork, immediately before the here-string at 149 — join the continuations
before splitting, so the shell's reading and the guard's agree:

```bash
CMD=${CMD//\\$'\n'/ }
```

I re-ran all 45 strings with that in place: every `allow` above flips to `DENY(verb)`, and nothing that
passed before changes verdict — including `cat body.md | \`⏎`callboard comment add`, which still strips
and still passes.

root followed by a deeper path component cannot match. Every in-repo absolute path I tried is allowed:
`rm -rf /Users/rendle/github/daemonicai/callboard/obj`, the same with `bin` and `obj` together, `mkdir -p
/Users/rendle/github/daemonicai/callboard/src/Foo`, `cp src/A.cs
/Users/rendle/github/daemonicai/callboard/src/B.cs`. URLs and prose likewise: `curl -sO
https://example.com/callboard/changes` and `grep -rn "callboard" openspec/` both pass. Dropping the verb
requirement cost nothing here.

**N-A, carried forward and still unaddressed.** The binary and the store share a name, and verb-shaped
commands naming the *binary* still deny: `chmod +x ./callboard`, `cp
bin/Release/net10.0/osx-arm64/publish/callboard /usr/local/bin/`, `dotnet tool install --global

blocked" and that promise now has two more exceptions than it admits. `sed` remaining the only
flag-gated case is correct, and `awk`/`jq` staying out is correctly justified by the redirect predicate;
the only residual there is GNU `awk -i inplace`, which is not the `awk` on this machine.

**N-H — heredoc bodies are segmented like commands.** A card body written through
`callboard comment add <<'EOF'` has each of its lines split into its own segment, so a body that *quotes*
a destructive command — exactly what an incident note in this project would do — denies the write of the
record describing it. Fail-closed and low-frequency; worth knowing before someone reports it as a bug.

**N-I — variable indirection passes, and always will.** `D=callboard/register; rm -rf $D` and
`for d in callboard/register; do rm -rf "$d"; done` both allow. That is inherent to matching text rather
than interpreting the shell, it is not what R3 is, and I am not asking for it to be closed — but the
header comment claims this file is the enforcement to the prompts' explanation, and a reader should know
the enforcement is a tripwire, not a sandbox.

**[reviewer]** 13.4, fourth pass — **Approve**. Scope was the R3 fix and only the R3 fix.

**The move upstream is right, and it is strictly additive.** `.claude/hooks/dmons-guard.sh:90` sits
between the `jq` assembly at 82 and the git-collapse `sed` at 95, so every rule in the shell arm now reads
text whose continuations agree with the shell's reading. I rebuilt the whole arm — both patterns, the
collapse, the three whole-`$CMD` rules, the strip, the split and all six predicates — into a standalone
harness (store word assembled at runtime) and drove **65 strings** through it twice, once with line 90 and
once without, then diffed the two verdict sets. **13 verdicts change, all of them `allow` → `DENY`. Not one
`DENY` → `allow`.** That is the answer to the regression question in one measurement: the rejoin can only
merge segments, and every deny in this file is "path *and* verb in the same segment", so merging adds
denies and can never remove one.

**Q1 — no pre-existing rule stops matching, and two of them gain coverage they were missing.** Six of the
13 flips are the store rule (R3 proper). **Five are the older rules the move was made for**: `git ⟍`⏎`commit`,
`git ⟍`⏎`  -C sub commit`, `git -C sub ⟍`⏎`commit`, `git ⟍`⏎`-c user.name=x ⟍`⏎`push` and `gh ⟍`⏎`pr create`
all allowed before line 90 and deny after. Your reading was correct: fixing this at the split would have
cleared the store rule and left the git rule carrying the identical hole. On the specific case you asked
about — `git ⟍`⏎`  -C sub commit` — the rejoin hands the collapse `sed` `git   -C sub commit`, and the
`[[:space:]]+` runs in that regex swallow the doubled space without trouble; it collapses to `git commit`
and denies. Nothing ordinary flipped: `git status`, `git log`, `git ⟍`⏎`diff --numstat`, `gh ⟍`⏎`auth status`,
`make gates`, `dotnet run -- state`, `grep -rn foo src/` all still allow, as do all fifteen of the store
rule's allow-side controls (`callboard block create`, `cat body.md | ⟍`⏎`callboard comment add`,
`ID=$(callboard block create)`, `./callboard index rebuild`, `sudo callboard state`, the `cat`/`ls`/`grep`/
`sed -n` reads, the absolute in-repo `bin`/`obj`/`src` paths, and the URL). The `.claude/` rule denies with
and without, unchanged.

**Q2 — the rejoin is correct, and its two divergences from the shell both fail closed.** `\\`⏎ (an escaped
backslash then a real break, which the shell reads as *two* commands) is over-merged into one segment, and
a `\`⏎ inside a single-quoted string is likewise rejoined where the shell would keep it literal — both
produce a spurious `DENY`, never a spurious `allow`, and both are the same shape as N-H. **CRLF is not a
hole**: `${CMD//\\$'\n'/ }` does not match `\`+`\r\n`, so the pair stays split — which is *right*, because
bash does not treat `\`+CRLF as a continuation either (the backslash escapes the CR and the newline still
terminates the command). Guard and shell agree. On `jq … join(" ; ")`: the separator carries no newline, so
the rejoin cannot merge across two tool-input strings, and the newlines it does act on are the command
text's own — the only ones whose continuation semantics matter. The one residual is that the shell removes
`\`⏎ with *no* separator while the guard inserts a space, so a word split mid-token
(`rm -rf callbo⟍`⏎`ard/register`) still allows. That is **pre-existing and unchanged by this fix** — it
allowed under the old `tr` split too, it is identical under your placement and the Architect's, and unlike
R3 it is evasion-shaped rather than a formatting habit. Substituting the empty string instead would close
it and reopen R3's common form (`rm -rf⟍`⏎`callboard` → `rm -rfcallboard`), so the space is the right
trade. Noted, not asked for.

**Q3 — nothing from R1/R2/B1–B5 reopens.** Re-drove the deny side: `ls -d callboard | xargs rm -rf`,
`find callboard -delete`, `tar -xzf b.tgz -C callboard`, `rsync -a --delete … callboard/register/`,

`fs.rmSync` — **all still deny**, with the same reason code as round three. `git diff --numstat` reports
**88 / 0** on the guard: no context line removed, so every rule survives verbatim, including the auditor's
`DEVLOG.md`-only arm and the `$STORE_PATH_RE` check above it.

**A block groups whole tasks; it never subdivides one.** The block is what gets one brief, one reviewer
audit, one gate run and one commit — and the *task* is what gets ticked. Splitting a task across blocks
produces commits that tick nothing and a tick that answers to no single reviewed deliverable. So when a
task is too big for one block, **that is a finding about the task breakdown, not a licence to carve
around it** — the fix goes in `tasks.md`, and it is the Product Owner's call. The one block that
legitimately ticks nothing stays the post-supervisor remediation block, which gets no new `N.M` numbers.

carried by `state`, `context`, `view` and both exports, so a caller gets an answer and knows what it
excludes. Refusing the whole read would have had one corrupt card halt every query — enforcing a stoppage

**The spec guarantees containment, not disclosure.** `record-retrieval` → *Concurrent work does not
corrupt the record* → scenario **Damage is contained**: "**WHEN** one card's record is corrupted /

is silent on *telling the caller*. **Do not go hunting for a scenario that specifies the response shape —
there isn't one.** The obligation to report comes from the task line, ruled by the Product Owner: a read
**reports** what it could not parse rather than refusing, because refusing would let one corrupt card
halt every query.

**Why this is a task and not a note.** It is the reviewer's **A3**: `CardStore.cs:2950` and
`FindBlockingOpenProductOwnerQuestion` omit unreadable cards **in the permissive direction**, and after
13.5 nothing reports it either.

**13.5 and 13.7 are different kinds of fail-open and must not be confused.** 13.5 was **fidelity** — the
tool answered confidently and was wrong, but nothing was wrongly permitted (§12 ruling 3). **A3 is
enforcement**: if a blocking Product Owner question will not parse, **it stops blocking**, and a corrupt
file silently becomes permission to proceed. That is the incumbent's failure mode — a process violation
that can only be recorded after the fact — in the tool built to refuse it. **A fidelity fail-open makes
the tool a bad witness; an enforcement fail-open makes it an accomplice.**

Two rulings fall out of it, both of which bind future blocks:

1. **When a card cannot be read, ask what its absence permits.** A reader that omits it answers a question
   *incompletely*; a **guard** that omits it answers *permissively*. The same discarded parse failure is a
   fidelity defect in one and an enforcement defect in the other, and only the second is a hazard.
2. **13.7 must be built before 13.8 verifies it.** 13.8's sentence is "the loop proceeds unenforced when
   the tool cannot run" — which is very nearly A3's subject, and verifying it against a tool that fails
   open on an unreadable guard would be verifying the wrong property and calling it green.

**[architect]** Brief — **13.6, one block, one task**: distinguish a corrupt card from a missing one when
a card is addressed by id.

**Premise re-checked before briefing (§13 ruling 4).** It holds, and it is narrower than this file said.

- `CardIdentityResolver.cs:62-67` still discards each parse failure with `onFailure: static _ => null`,
  keeping only the path. ✅ `NitResolver.cs:32-34` does the same. ✅
- Both `--id` resolvers in the dispatcher — `ResolveCardReference` (`CommandDispatcher.cs:4101`) and
  `ResolveAnyCardReferenceWithCard` (`:4143`) — refuse `card-id-unresolvable` on `Unreadable`. ✅
- **What this file did not say, and it is the whole difficulty:** a card's id lives only in its
  frontmatter, and `CardFileParseResult.Failure` carries a bare `Reason` string and nothing else. **No
  shipped code can attribute an unparseable file to an id.** So "10 of the 19 `onCardCorrupt` arms become
  reachable when the resolver stops discarding the reason" was wrong as stated: keeping the reason is
  necessary and not sufficient. Attribution has to be built.

**The Product Owner has ruled the shape** — best-effort id recovery, this session:

```
resolve(id):
  a file that parsed carries id        -> Found / Duplicate   (unchanged, and takes precedence)
  else a file that would not parse
       declares that id in frontmatter -> Corrupt(...)        [NEW CASE]
  else at least one file unreadable    -> Unreadable(UnreadableCard[])
  else                                 -> NotFound            (unchanged)
```

**The distinction being bought is wrong-remedy, not wrong-verdict.** An agent told an id does not resolve
hunts for a typo; an agent told the card is corrupt opens the file. That is the entire point of the task —
keep it in view when you word the refusals.

**Tasks in this block:** 13.6, and nothing else. **13.7 is the enforcement fail-open** (`CardStore.cs:2950`
and `FindBlockingOpenProductOwnerQuestion` omitting unreadable cards permissively) — a different task, a
different block. Do not fix it here, and do not widen a guard on the way past.

**What to build**

1. **Recovery is evidence, not record.** A parsed file's frontmatter is the record; an id scraped from a
   file that would not parse is a claim about a file the tool has already refused to trust. So: matches
   over *parsed* files decide `Found`/`Duplicate` first and unconditionally, and recovered ids are
   consulted **only** when no parsed file carries the id. Say this in a doc comment — the precedence is the
   part a later reader will get backwards.
2. **Scan the frontmatter block, not the file.** Recovery reads a declared `id:` from the leading `---`
   fenced block only. A body line that happens to read `id: blk-0007` must not produce an attribution —
   that is the §11 family of defect (a document-parsing assumption about text a caller controls) and this
   task must not add a fresh member to it. If the fence itself is what failed to parse, there is nothing
   to recover and the file stays in the `Unreadable` set; that is correct, not a gap.
3. **`Corrupt` carries a list, not a single file.** More than one unparseable file can declare the same
   id. One case with `IReadOnlyList<UnreadableCard>` is right; a fourth case for "several corrupt
   claimants" is not.
4. **Refuse `card-corrupt`, with the reason and the path.** Both dispatcher resolvers gain the arm. The
   code already exists and already means exactly this — 21 `onCardCorrupt` arms in `CommandDispatcher`
   spell `new CommandOutcome.Refusal("card-corrupt", corrupt.Reason)`. Reuse it; do not mint a synonym
   (§9.1's rule against two spellings of one fact, and `card-id-unresolvable` reporting the wrong thing is
   what put this task on the board).
5. **`card-id-unresolvable` survives, improved.** It is still the honest answer when files could not be
   read and none of them claims the id. It must now name **why** each one failed, not just where it lives,
   and its remedy must point at repairing those files rather than at checking the id — **§9.3: a refusal
   names its remedy as a command that exists.**
6. **The twins.** 13.5 held `NitResolution` and `CardIdentityResolution` as a pair on purpose, and this is
   the task that was to converge them. Converge both onto 13.5's `UnreadableCard` (path **and** reason) —
   that half is mechanical for `NitResolver` too. On the attribution half, a nit id lives one level down,
   on a `CardComment` inside the thread, so recovering it from an unparseable file is **not** the same
   operation as scraping a frontmatter key. Either do it and defend the scan, or **state plainly why nit
   attribution is not honest** and leave `NitResolution` with reasons but no `Corrupt` case. Both answers
   are acceptable; an unmentioned twin is not.
7. **Account for the arms.** Report how many of `CommandDispatcher`'s `card-corrupt` arms this block
   actually makes reachable, by verb, and which remain unreachable and why. **Verify it, do not infer
   it** — §13 ruling 5: a regression test nobody has watched fail is a guess.

**Binding decisions.** **D3** — cards are the record, the file is authoritative. **D4** — the index is
derived and never authoritative; that a file will not parse is a fact about the file and must never be
answered from the index. **D2** — NativeAOT: no reflection-based serialisation; any new response shape
needs its source-generated context. **ADR-0004** — resolution reads the record, never the index, and takes
no lock.

**Done-gates.** A corrupt card addressed by `--id` refuses `card-corrupt` naming the file and the parse
reason; a corrupt card *elsewhere* while the addressed id is genuinely absent still refuses
`card-id-unresolvable`, now carrying per-file reasons; a corrupt file whose frontmatter fence is itself
broken degrades to `card-id-unresolvable` rather than to a wrong attribution; a parsed file carrying the id
wins over a corrupt file claiming it. Tests for each, and — §11's ruling, *a test can cover a content class
and still not cover the thing that makes it content* — **assert on the parse reason and the path in the
refusal message, not merely on the refusal code**.

**Gates:** `make gates` → `GATES_EXIT:0`, and quote the exit lines; a gate passed only if you saw its
`LABEL_EXIT:0`. **Boundaries:** you do not commit, do not tick, do not edit `tasks.md`, the `Makefile`,
`CLAUDE.md` or `.claude/`. **Card bodies come from stdin; there is no `--body` flag.** And — §13's new
lesson, from a worker who followed the codebase over a brief that contradicted it and said nothing — **if
any part of this brief contradicts the codebase, say so in the DEVLOG and stop; do not silently do the
right thing.** Post to the DEVLOG as `[worker]` under `## 13.`, then `→ @reviewer`.

returns `null` — nothing recovered, not a guess. `CardIdentityResolver.Resolve` calls it only inside the

frontmatter still decides `Found`/`Duplicate` unconditionally before any recovered id is even considered —
built ruling 1, direct.

there makes the tool a *bad witness*: it is confidently wrong and nothing is wrongly permitted. 13.7 is
**enforcement** — a fail-open here makes the tool an *accomplice*: the process violation it exists to
refuse goes through because a file would not parse. **Ask of every site: what does this card's absence
permit?** If the answer is "nothing — the caller is merely told something inaccurate", it is 13.5's family
and you leave it alone.

index is derived and never authoritative; that a card cannot be read is a fact about the file and must
never be answered from the index, and these guards take no lock. **D2** — NativeAOT: any new response
shape needs its source-generated context.

refusing. A duplicate-id blocking question refuses on the write paths too. Tests for each — and §11's

**[architect]** Brief — **13.8, one block, one task**: verify the record stays readable and the loop
proceeds unenforced when the tool cannot run.

**The requirement, in full, because this task is a verification and its spec is its specification**
(§11 ruling 3 — *a verification task that reads as a check on an implementation task may be its
specification*). `record-retrieval` → **The record is legible without the tool**:

> The primary record SHALL be plain text, human-readable, and committed to the repository. A reader with
> no access to the tool SHALL be able to determine a card's status, owner and history from the record
> alone. **The tool SHALL be an optimisation and an enforcement layer, never a precondition for
> comprehension.**
>
> **Scenario: Tool unavailable** — **WHEN** the tool cannot run **THEN** the record remains readable and
> the loop can proceed unenforced rather than blocked.

**13.8 is that scenario. 13.9 is the requirement's *other* scenario** (*Card read without the tool* —
status, owner, scope and full thread determinable by a reader). They are one requirement and two tasks;
**do not do 13.9's half here**, and do not assume it is done.

**This block ends at the Product Owner and cannot be finished without her** (CLAUDE.md §4). You implement
and self-test as far as automation reaches, then produce a **recipe** she runs by hand. **You do not tick
13.8**; nobody does until she confirms.

**The brief's own premise, checked (ruling 4, and 13.6's sharpening — checked for truth).** 13.8 sits
directly downstream of 13.7: until an unreadable card stopped permitting what it should block, verifying
"the loop proceeds unenforced" would have been verifying the wrong property against a tool that failed
open, and calling it green. 13.7 landed (`c7069a5`), so the premise now holds.

**Part 1 — what automation *can* establish.** Build these as tests:

1. **The index is not a precondition.** Delete `callboard/.index` entirely; every read path still answers,
   rebuilding or reading the record as D4/ADR-0004 require. **The index is derived and never
   authoritative** — this is the test that proves it rather than asserting it in a comment.
2. **Rebuild is faithful.** Derived state built from a scratch index equals derived state built from an
   existing one, over the same record. If those can differ, the index is authoritative in practice
   whatever the ADR says.
3. **Nothing essential lives outside the committed record.** Identity counters, locks, index — establish
   that what a fresh clone contains is sufficient, and that no state the tool needs to be *correct* lives
   anywhere a `git clone` would not bring.
4. **A stale lock does not wedge the record.** A lock left by a process that died must not make the record
   unreadable. Reads take no lock (ADR-0004) — prove that holds with a lock file present.
5. **A hand-written card round-trips.** A card composed in a text editor, by hand, with no tool — parses,
   and is indistinguishable to every read path from a tool-written one. **This is the automatable half of
   "the loop proceeds unenforced":** work done without the tool is not rejected when the tool returns.

**Part 2 — the recipe, and this is the part that actually satisfies the task.**

**§12 ruling 5 binds hardest here: a verification recipe can satisfy the paperwork and not the task.** The
worked example is 13.4, whose first recipe would have rendered the Product Owner an *empty board* while
asking her to confirm lanes and shading. **Ask what the automation is structurally unable to see, and put
*that* in the recipe** — not a re-run of Part 1 by hand.

What automation here is structurally blind to: **every test runs with the tool present.** A test suite
cannot observe a world with no binary, because it *is* the binary. So the recipe must have her actually
remove it — rename or move the built `callboard` executable so no invocation can succeed — and then:

- read a card's status, owner and thread with nothing but `cat`/an editor;
- append to the record by hand as a role would;
- confirm the loop *proceeds*: the next step of work is possible, unenforced, rather than blocked;
- restore the binary and confirm the tool accepts what was written by hand while it was gone.

**Write the recipe as exact, copy-pasteable commands, with what she should see after each**, and against
a **realistic** record — the 13.4 lesson: never ask her to confirm a property of an empty board.

**One interaction you must confront rather than discover.** 13.4's hook boundary (`deny_store`) blocks
**agents** from editing card files directly and tells them to use `callboard <verb>` — verbs that, in this
scenario, cannot run. **My reading, which the recipe should state and let her judge:** the escape hatch is
already in the guard's own message — *"if no verb records what you have, that is a gap to report to the
Architect, not to route around"* — and the Architect is unconstrained by the hooks. So the loop proceeds
via the Architect, unenforced, and the spec is satisfied. **If your work shows that reading is wrong —
that an agent is genuinely blocked with no route — stop and say so in the DEVLOG. That is a spec
contradiction and the Product Owner's call, not something to design around.**

**Binding decisions.** **D3** — cards are the record; the file is authoritative. **D4 / ADR-0004** — the
index is derived, never authoritative, and reads take no lock. **D2** — NativeAOT.

**Done-gates.** Part 1's tests exist and pass. Part 2's recipe is written into the DEVLOG, is
copy-pasteable, names what she should see at each step, runs against a non-empty record, and covers the
tool-absent case that no test can reach. **13.8 stays unticked.**

**[architect]** ❓ answered by the Product Owner — **the guard interaction is not a spec contradiction;
the loop proceeds via the Architect.**

**The question.** 13.4's `deny_store` blocks agents from writing card files and routes them to
`callboard <verb>`. When the tool cannot run, those verbs cannot run either — so an agent can neither
record through the tool nor edit the card by hand. `record-retrieval`'s *Tool unavailable* scenario says
the loop **proceeds unenforced rather than blocked**. For an agent specifically, it looks blocked.

**The ruling (Product Owner).** The spec holds and **nothing is to be built**. The route already exists
and the guard's own message names it: *"if no verb records what you have, that is a gap to report to the
Architect, not to route around."* The Architect is unconstrained by the hooks. So:

- an agent **reads** the record freely — `cat`, `grep`, `ls`, `sed -n` are explicitly not blocked;
- an agent **cannot write**, and reports what it would have recorded to the Architect;
- the **Architect** hand-edits the card file, no hook binding her;
- the loop **proceeds, unenforced** — through a narrower channel, which is what *unenforced* means here.

**Enforcement narrowing to a single unconstrained role is the degraded mode, not a failure of it.** The
tool is "an optimisation and an enforcement layer, never a precondition for comprehension" — losing it
costs the enforcement and the convenience, and costs the record nothing.

**What this obliges of 13.8's recipe:** it must exercise *that* path — an agent reporting, the Architect
writing by hand — and not merely a human reading files. Confirming legibility alone would satisfy the
paperwork and not the task (§12 ruling 5).

**Evidence note, and it is the interesting part.** I quoted `deny_store`'s wording to the worker as the
basis for this reading. **The worker could not verify the quote** — guard rule 2 blocks an agent from
*reading* `.claude/` — and it said so rather than adopting my reading on my authority. The reviewer hit
the same wall independently. **Neither auditor can check the Architect's evidence about the boundary**,
which is precisely the carved-out item below: a read rule that fires on the agents auditing the file it
protects. This is now the third live instance. I verified the quote myself
(`.claude/hooks/dmons-guard.sh:54`); that I *had* to is the finding.

### Defect 1 — the parse fails on a blank line, and an ordinary editor produces one

**What she did.** Followed Step 4: appended a hand-written comment block to a card while the tool was
gone. Restored the tool. `card show` refused `card-corrupt`; `state` reported the card `unreadable`, with
the reason *"expected a comment header, a handover line, … or end of file, found: ''"*.

**Why.** `CardFileParser.Parse` (`:177-178`) strips **exactly one** trailing newline, splits on `\n`, and
the block loop (`:415`) reads `lines[cursor]` with **no blank-line skipping anywhere**. So in the appended
region a single empty line is fatal. Two ordinary edits produce one:

- a blank line between the previous `<!-- /callboard:comment -->` and the new header — the natural way to
  separate blocks, and it mirrors what the tool's own output *looks* like;
- **a trailing newline at EOF** — the file already ends `\n`, so an editor that guarantees a final newline
  yields `\n\n`; one is stripped, the other becomes an empty line.

**The trap in the file's own appearance:** the blank line visible before a closing tag is part of the
comment **body** (`AppendContent` splits the body on `\n` and the body ends with one). Blank lines inside
a block are fine; between blocks they are fatal; nothing distinguishes them by eye.

**Product Owner's ruling: fix the parser.** In the block loop, an empty line at the cursor is **skipped**,
not failed — between blocks and at EOF. **The writer is unchanged**, so no existing file's bytes move and
round-trip output stays exactly what it is today.

**Build it as:**

1. The skip lives **only** in the appended-region block loop. Body parsing is untouched — a blank line
   inside a body is content and must stay content, and a body line that looks like a header is still
   escaped by `EscapeContentLine`. **Do not "simplify" by trimming the whole file.**
2. **Say what this normalises.** A file with stray blanks parses, and the next tool write re-emits it
   without them. That is acceptable and deliberate — write it in the doc comment so a later reader does
   not mistake it for drift.
3. Tests, and the §11 ruling binds — *a test can cover a content class and still not cover the thing that
   makes it content*. Cover at minimum: a blank line **between** two comment blocks; a **trailing** blank
   at EOF (the editor case — this is the one that bit her); several consecutive blanks; a blank line
   inside a comment **body** still preserved as content; a blank line before the *first* block; and a
   non-blank junk line still failing exactly as it does now. **Watch each fail against current code first**
   — that discipline is yours alone (§13.7), and here you have a genuine prior defect to run against, so
   this is a real red-then-green cycle, not the invariant-test scoping 13.8 Part 1 used.
4. **Check the sibling parse paths.** `CardFileParser` has a second `Split` at `:145`. Establish whether
   it has the same exposure and fix it or say why not. **A site you do not mention reads as a site you did
   not see.**

### Defect 2 — the recipe names a binary that cannot exist where it puts it

**What she hit.** Step 0 copies the executable to `./callboard`, then Step 1 runs
`question create callboard/register/q-0001.md` — which needs to create the directory `callboard/`. **A
file and a directory cannot share a name.** She renamed it to `cb` to proceed.

**Why three reviews missed it.** The guard blocks a worker (and an auditor) from writing or copying to any
path ending in `callboard`, so **both agents ran under a renamed binary** — the worker as `./cbtool`, the
reviewer likewise. Neither ever created a file named `callboard` in that directory, so neither could hit
the collision. **The boundary that forced the substitution also concealed the defect the substitution was
silently working around**, and the recipe then told her to type the one name nobody had tested.

**Fix:** the recipe uses a binary name that cannot collide with the store root — `./cb` is what she used;
use that. Then **re-run the whole recipe, top to bottom, in final form, from a pristine directory, as the
last thing you do**, and paste only that run's output — the round-two standard, unchanged. Include the
Step 4 hand-edit **with** a deliberate trailing blank line, so the recipe now demonstrates the case that
used to fail and no longer does.

**And carry the lesson into the recipe's own text:** state that the binary must not be named `callboard`
inside a directory that will hold the store, and why. She should not have to rediscover it.

predicate:


Placed at the top of the `while (cursor < lines.Length)` loop, so it fires between blocks and at EOF —
nowhere else. **The writer is unchanged.** **Body parsing is untouched**: the pre-append body loop, and

the new block states what it normalises: a hand-edited file with stray blanks now parses, and the next
tool write re-emits it without them, deliberately.

unrecognised line — it only recognises the closing fence or an `id: ` line, and falls through (skip via

a later reader doesn't have to re-derive it.

   nothing else, used to corrupt it.

line's last character is `:` — `key:value` (colon, no space, non-empty tail) still falls through to
`Failure($"malformed frontmatter line: '{line}'")` unchanged, and so does a line with no colon at all.

one's findings stand and are closed; this pass is scoped to what's new. **Verdict: Approve.**

**Probe 1 — the tolerance is exactly as narrow as ruled.** Worked every shape by hand against the actual
code (`CardFileParser.cs:196-224`):
- `key:` (colon as the line's last character) → new: `key`, empty value. Ruled, intended.
- `key:value` (no space, non-empty tail) → `IndexOf(": ")` finds nothing (no colon-space substring), and
  the line's last char is `e`, not `:`, so it falls to `Failure`. Still fails, confirmed by
  `Parse_NoColonFrontmatterLine_StillFails`'s sibling shape and by hand-tracing the branch.
- `key : value` (space before the colon) → `IndexOf(": ")` matches at the *second* space (between the
  space-before-colon and the value), so `key` becomes `"key "` (trailing space, an unrecognised key) and
  `value` is `"value"`. This is **pre-existing `separatorIndex`-branch behaviour, untouched by this
  diff** — the `else if` only triggers when `IndexOf(": ")` finds nothing at all, and here it does. Not a
  new widening.
- `key:` with trailing whitespace after the colon (e.g. `"key: "` or `"key:  "`) → these already contain
  `": "` as a substring, so they take the original `separatorIndex` branch, value = whatever follows
  (`""` or `" "`). Also pre-existing, unaffected by the new branch.
- A key containing a colon, or a value containing `": "` — `IndexOf` returns the *first* match, so the
  split point is wherever the first `": "` occurs in the line; this is the original, unmodified splitting
  rule and out of this diff's reach entirely (the new branch is `else if`, gated on zero occurrences).
- A bare `":"` line (colon, nothing else) → new: empty key, empty value, filed as an unknown field with
  key `""`. Real but inert — no known key is ever the empty string, and no writer path ever emits a bare
  `:` (it only ever emits `key:` for a genuinely empty *value*, never an empty *key*). Noting it as a nit,
  not a blocker: the doc comment could say "at least one character before the colon" but doesn't need to
  for this to be safe today.
- **Whether any of these should have stayed a failure**: no — `key:value` and `key : value` retaining
  their pre-existing behaviour (fail / mis-key respectively) is correct and unchanged; the only new
  acceptance is the exact shape the ruling named. I did not find a case where a previously-refused,
  meaningfully-different-content line now silently parses.

### The finding that matters most in §13, and it is about the loop rather than the code

**The Product Owner found two defects that three reviewer rounds had passed, one of which re-ran the
recipe end to end.** Neither was a lapse. Both were **structurally invisible from inside the boundary**:

- the **binary-name collision** — Step 0 copied the executable to `./callboard`, then Step 1 had to create
  the directory `callboard/`. A file and a directory cannot share a name. **Every agent ran under a
  renamed binary** (`./cbtool`) because the guard forbids writing any path ending in `callboard`, so no
  agent could ever create the colliding file. The recipe then told her to type the one name nobody had
  tested.
- the **blank-line parse failure** — it needs a real editor's trailing newline, which no test harness
  produces by accident.

**The ruling this earns.** §13 already carries *ask what the automation cannot see*. That is not enough,
because it invites you to imagine the gap. Add the operational form:

> **Ask what the agents had to change in order to test at all — that difference is the untested surface.**
> A substitution made to satisfy a boundary does not merely leave a gap; it can *conceal the very defect it
> is working around*. The worker and both auditors renamed the binary for hook reasons and thereby
> silently fixed, and hid, the collision.

This is checkable rather than imaginative: every agent that reports a workaround is reporting a coordinate.

### Two more, smaller

1. **An architectural note's stated severity is not its real one.** The reviewer flagged the frontmatter
   loop's blank-line exposure as a note, out of brief, for my call. Following it up found a **second and
   worse** case in the same loop: the writer emits `key: value`, so an empty-valued field is `section: `
   with a trailing space, and the parser required the two-character `": "`. An editor stripping trailing
   whitespace on save — VS Code's default — corrupted an **untouched, tool-written** card. **Opening and
   saving, changing nothing, was enough.** The note was right to be raised and undersold. **Auditors
   should raise adjacent exposures they cannot size; sizing is the Architect's job, not a precondition for
   reporting.**
2. **Tolerance is where a wrong-but-parsing card is born, so it must be bought narrowly.** 13.6 exists
   because a card that will not parse is safer than one that parses wrongly. The fix therefore accepts
   **only** a bare trailing colon as an empty value; `key:value` and `key : value` keep their existing
   paths, and no previously-refused line now parses to different content. Verified by hand-tracing every
   shape, not by testing the happy case.

### Carried, not fixed — and it is the quiet-wrong-answer case

**`FrontmatterEscapeForwardTable` (`CardFileFormat.cs:191-198`) never escapes a space.** A frontmatter
value that legitimately *ends* in whitespace — a `title`, say — is silently truncated by an editor's save.
**The card still parses; it just holds different content.** That is the failure mode this whole
remediation was written to avoid, surviving one field over. It is **pre-existing**, reachable today,
neither introduced nor widened here (the `key:` branch fires only on an empty value), and the reviewer
flagged it explicitly rather than folding it into "no exposure". **Put to the Product Owner once §13
closes; it is arguably 13.9's, since 13.9 is about what a reader can determine from the file and this is
about what a writer can safely author.**

**[architect]** Brief — **remediation block, §13: frontmatter values must survive a whitespace-stripping
save.** No new `N.M` numbers, nothing ticked. Product Owner's ruling: fix this separately from 13.9, which
stays a read-half verification task.

**The defect.** `CardFileFormat.FrontmatterEscapeForwardTable` (`:191`) escapes `\`, `\n` and `\r` — **not
space**. So a frontmatter free-text value that ends in a space (`id`, `title`, `status`, `section` — in
practice `title`) reaches disk as trailing whitespace **indistinguishable from layout**, and an editor
that strips trailing whitespace on save silently changes it. **The card still parses. It just holds
different content.** That is the quiet-wrong-answer case, one field over from the two loud failures the
last remediation fixed, and the reason 13.6 exists is the principle that refusing to parse beats parsing
wrongly.

**The mechanism already exists.** `CommentHeaderEscapeForwardTable` (`:194`) escapes space as `\s`, and
`FrontmatterEscapeTable` (`:180`) already carries the reverse mapping `['s'] = ' '` — **the unescape side
is built and waiting**. Verify that before you build anything: if the reverse table already round-trips
`\s`, this is a forward-side fix and possibly nothing else.

### The constraint that decides the whole design — read it before writing code

**Do not copy the comment-header table.** It escapes **every** space because that format is
space-delimited. Frontmatter is not: it is `key: value` to end of line, and interior spaces are
unambiguous. Escaping them all would render a real card as:

```
title: Which\sretry\spolicy?
```

**That would destroy the property 13.9 exists to verify** — "a reader with no access to the tool SHALL be
able to determine a card's status, owner and history from the record alone", and "the tool SHALL be an
optimisation … never a precondition for comprehension". A fix that makes every card harder for a human to
read, in order to protect a rare trailing space, is a net loss against the requirement.

**So: escape only where the ambiguity actually is — a leading or trailing space on the value.** Interior
spaces stay literal. A value with no edge whitespace must serialise **byte-for-byte as it does today**, so
that no existing card changes when it is next written.

### What to build

1. **Forward side only, and narrowly.** `EscapeFrontmatterValue` escapes a leading and/or trailing space
   (and consider whether a leading/trailing tab needs the same treatment — decide and say which).
   `EscapeUsing` maps char→string over the whole value, so this is **not** a table entry; it is a
   positional rule and needs its own small function. **Do not force it into the table** — say so in the
   doc comment, because the next reader will wonder why this one escaper is not table-driven.
2. **Confirm the reverse already works.** `UnescapeFrontmatterValue` reads `FrontmatterEscapeTable`, which
   maps `s` → space. If `\s` already unescapes correctly, state that and add the round-trip test rather
   than touching it. **If it does not, say so before changing it** — an unescape change affects every
   existing card on disk and is a different risk class from an escape change.
3. **Round-trip is the property, and it is two-sided.** `Escape` then `Unescape` returns the original for:
   a value with a trailing space; a leading space; both; interior spaces only (**unchanged bytes** — assert
   the serialised form, not just the round trip); a value that is entirely spaces; an empty value; and a
   value containing a literal `\s` sequence already (the invertibility case — a backslash is escaped first
   and must stay so).
4. **The keystone test, mirroring the last remediation's.** A full tool-written card whose `title` ends in
   a space, serialised, put through a **trailing-whitespace strip on every line**, then parsed — and the
   title comes back **with its space**. That is the Product Owner's failure mode; reproduce it, do not
   approximate it. **Watch it fail against current code first** — there is a genuine prior defect here, so
   this is a real red-then-green cycle.
5. **Check the neighbours.** `FrontmatterListItemEscapeForwardTable` (`:197`) escapes `\`, `\n`, `\r`, `,`
   — **is a list item with edge whitespace exposed the same way?** Decide, fix it or justify leaving it,
   and **say which**. A site you do not mention reads as a site you did not see.

### Corrected scope: both sides, and a behaviour change on existing data

1. **Forward** — `EscapeFrontmatterValue` escapes a **leading and/or trailing** space as `\s`. The
   original constraint stands and is the most important line in this brief: **interior spaces stay
   literal.** `CommentHeaderEscapeForwardTable` escapes every space because that format is
   space-delimited; frontmatter is `key: value` to end of line and is not. `title: Which\sretry\spolicy?`
   would destroy the plain-text legibility the record-retrieval requirement demands. A value with **no
   edge whitespace must serialise byte-for-byte as it does today** — assert that on the serialised form,
   not merely on a round trip.
2. **Reverse** — `FrontmatterEscapeTable` gains `['s'] = ' '`. **This changes how cards already on disk
   are read**, and you must handle that consciously rather than incidentally:
   - A **tool-written** card is unaffected: the forward escaper escapes `\` → `\\` first, so a title
     `match \s+` is stored `match \\s+` and unescapes correctly before and after this change.
     **Verify that claim with a test rather than trusting my reasoning — I have already been wrong once
     in this brief.**
   - A **hand-written** card containing a bare `\s` changes meaning: literal `\s` today, a space
     afterwards. **Architect's call, made deliberately and recorded:** trailing-space truncation happens
     *passively*, when an editor saves a file nobody meant to change; a bare `\s` in a card title requires
     someone to type it on purpose. The passive, near-universal failure outweighs the deliberate, rare
     one. Put this in the doc comment so the trade is legible to whoever finds it next.
3. **`UnescapeUsing` already handles `\\` generically** (`:438-446`) and falls through on unknown escape
   letters, so no change is needed there. Confirm rather than assume.
4. **`FrontmatterListItemEscapeForwardTable` (`:197`)** — now actually evaluate it, since it was skipped
   as downstream of the false premise. Does a list item with edge whitespace have the same exposure? Fix

---

### The finding of this block, and it is not about whitespace

**Five stated enumerations in this remediation were wrong, and each survived because someone read it
instead of re-deriving it.**

1. **My brief** claimed `FrontmatterEscapeTable` already mapped `s` → space. It does not — that is
   `CommentHeaderEscapeTable`, two lines below, backing a different function on a different format. **The
   worker verified and stopped without building.** Had it complied, an escaped `\s` would have had no
   reverse mapping and leaked into parsed values literally: **a new quiet-wrong-output defect, in the
   block whose subject is quiet wrong output** — and it would have passed a round-trip test written to my
   stated scope.
2. **The worker's list-escaper justification** — "every list-valued field holds generated identifier
   tokens" — omitted `extent_value`, which is free text from `--extent-explicit`. The reviewer disproved
   it by tracing the CLI path, not by arguing with it.
3. **The corrected enumeration** still mislabelled `gate_results` as generated.
4. **A test named as a regression guard could not detect the defect.** The reviewer rebuilt the pre-fix
   escaper in a scratch harness and ran it: green under the old code. §13 ruling 5 in miniature — *a
   regression test nobody has watched fail is a guess* — with the guess wearing the guard's name.
5. **The generated-vs-hand-typed distinction itself was false.** Re-deriving all seven fields dissolved
   it: **all seven** trace to a hand-typed CLI argument. What actually separates them is whether a field's
   convention admits legitimate edge whitespace.

**The ruling.** §13 already says *verify the premise, then brief*, and *a brief is not evidence*. This
block sharpens both into something checkable:

> **An enumeration or a regression claim is worth exactly what the independent re-derivation behind it is
> worth. Reviewing one by inspection launders it.** Every one of these five was caught by re-deriving from
> the code, or by rebuilding the old implementation and running the test against it — never by a closer
> read. **The corollary for auditors: re-derive from the source, not from the finding that prompted the
> correction**, or you confirm your own earlier work.

**A method worth keeping, from the reviewer:** to test whether a regression test was genuine, it
**reconstructed the pre-fix implementation in an isolated harness** and ran the suite against it. The
auditor boundary forbids editing source (§13.7's noted limit), and this routes around the limit without
breaking the rule.

**And one from the worker, on refusing to manufacture evidence:** told to make the misnamed test fail
pre-fix or rename it, it traced why no strip step *could* have made it fail — a leading space from the
CLI's untrimmed split sits after a comma, never at a physical line's trailing edge — and renamed it
instead, calling the alternative theatre. **A test made to fail by a step invented to make it fail proves
nothing.**
