**[architect]** Brief — **13.9, one task, one block. Verify a card's status, owner, scope and history are
determinable from the file alone.**

**Read half only.** The Product Owner ruled this explicitly. 13.9 asks what a reader can *determine* from
the file; it does not ask what a writer may safely *author*. The authoring half was raised and deliberately
not folded in — its one live defect (edge whitespace silently truncated) was fixed separately in `3eacc1f`,
and the carried `FrontmatterEscapeForwardTable` item the 13.8 close post named is therefore **closed, not
your business**. If you find another authoring hazard, report it; do not fix it here.

**The spec this answers.** `record-retrieval`, *The record is legible without the tool*:

> A reader with no access to the tool SHALL be able to determine a card's status, owner and history from
> the record alone. The tool SHALL be an optimisation and an enforcement layer, never a precondition for
> comprehension.
>
> **Scenario: Card read without the tool** — **WHEN** a reader inspects the record directly with no tool
> available, **THEN** the card's status, owner, scope and full thread are determinable from what they read.

And **ADR-0003**, which fixes what "inspects the record directly" means: *"A reader with no tool **opens one
file** and sees status, owner, scope, body and full thread."* **Raw text is the binding reading.** A
rendered-Markdown view is a different question — see the queue below; characterise it, do not rule it.

### What the block delivers, in order

**1. The enumeration of "history" — re-derived, not inherited from this brief.** `CardFileWriter` emits
seven marker-line families (`handover`, `transition`, `verdict`, `authorisation`, `claim`, `limit`,
`refusal`) plus delimited comment blocks carrying author, addressee, `reply-to`, `resolves`, timestamp and
the nit fields. **That list is mine and is therefore worth nothing until you have re-derived it from
`CardFileWriter` and `CardFileParser` yourself.** The escape remediation put five stated enumerations in
this file wrong, each surviving because someone read it instead of re-deriving it. If my seven are eight,
or six, say so and show the derivation. Kind-specific frontmatter (block's five, finding's extent and
blind-spot fields, register's lifecycle fields, question, section) is part of *status and scope*, not part
of history — enumerate it separately, the same way.

**2. An automated cover that reads the file the way a reader does.** The trap is the round trip: a
round-trip test proves **the tool can read what the tool wrote**, which is the exact proposition 13.9 does
not get to assume. The cover must assert against the **serialised bytes**, with a reading that does not
share the writer's tables — for every card kind, and for a card carrying at least one of every history
element you enumerated in (1). What it asserts is *presence and attribution*: for each element, a reader
can say what happened, who did it, and when.

**3. The determinability report — the part that is actually the deliverable's substance.** For each thing
the spec names (status, owner, scope, full thread), state what the file carries and **what convention the
reader must already know to read it**. The file carries no legend. Known live examples, to be confirmed or
disproved rather than repeated:

- **Escape markers.** A value carrying `\s`, `\n` or `\,` reads to a human as those characters, not as the
  content. Is a card whose title serialises as `Which retry policy?\s` "determinable"? State the answer and
  the reasoning; do not fix anything.
- **Absence as meaning.** The block-only fields use "present only when set", while `section` uses "always
  present, empty when unset". A missing `base:` and an empty `section:` mean different kinds of nothing.
- **Wire strings.** Whether `owner`, `scope`, `status` and the marker-line field values read as words a
  reader understands or as codes they must look up.
- **History in HTML comments.** Every marker line and every comment header is an HTML comment. Raw text:
  visible, and that is the binding reading per ADR-0003. Any Markdown renderer: the entire history and every
  comment's attribution disappear, leaving unattributed prose. **Report the consequence precisely; the call
  is the Product Owner's, not yours and not mine.**

**4. The recipe for the Product Owner — and 13.8's lesson is that this, not the tests, is the deliverable.**
Three reviewer rounds passed 13.8's recipe, one of them re-running it end to end, and she then found two
defects none of them could see. Twice the text was edited after its evidence was captured. So:

- **Write it by running it, last, in one continuous session, and paste only that run's output.** No edit
  after the capture. If you change a word of the recipe, re-run the whole thing.
- It must be exact and copy-pasteable: the command, what she does, what she should see.
- It is a **reading** exercise. She should be handed real card files and asked what she can determine from
  them with no tool — including at least one card carrying a full thread and one carrying an escape marker.
  A recipe that hands her a well-behaved card and asks her to confirm it reads well is §12's empty board
  again: it satisfies the paperwork and not the task.

**5. Two questions to answer explicitly in your report, both structural.**

- **What is the automation unable to see?** Not "what did I not test" — what can a test *not* reach.
- **What did you have to change in order to test at all?** Every workaround is a coordinate on the untested
  surface. 13.8's binary-name collision existed only because every agent renamed the binary to satisfy the
  guard, and the rename silently fixed *and hid* the defect it was working around. Report every
  substitution you make, including ones that felt too small to mention.

### Gates and boundaries

Gates are mine, not yours — report exit lines, do not tick and do not commit. `tasks.md`, the `Makefile`,
`CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/` are outside your reach; if you need a `make` target changed, stop and report it.

`authorisation`, `claim`, `limit`, `refusal` — and no others. **Seven, matching the brief.** Comments are
an eighth, differently-shaped sequence (`CommentHeaderPrefix`/`Suffix`, its own footer); `BuildComment`
(`CardFileParser.cs`) recognises `id`/`author`/`timestamp` (required) plus `reply-to`/`to`/`resolves`/
`is-nit`/`required`/`sites`/`disposition` (optional) — ten header fields.

**One correction the brief itself got wrong.** "Block's five" kind-specific fields is stale: `CardFileWriter`'s
`isBlockCard` branch emits **seven** — `base`, `reviewed_state`, `tasks`, `gate_results`, `round`,
`blocked_by`, `finding_key` — and `BlockCardFields.Empty`'s own doc comment already says so ("The seven
fields, all unset"). Five was correct before `gate_results`/`finding_key` were added in later sections; the
doc comment at `CardFileWriter.cs:31` documenting "five" predates both and is itself stale. Reported, not
fixed — kind-specific frontmatter is out of this block's scope per the brief.

**2. Automated cover — `tests/Callboard.Tests/CardFileRawTextLegibilityTests.cs` (6 tests, new file).**
Every assertion reads `CardFileWriter.Serialize`'s raw output with a plain `string.Contains`/line check —
no call to `CardFileParser`, no reuse of any `CardFileFormat` escape table. Covers: all seven marker
families with full attribution (who/what/when); a comment thread carrying `reply-to`/`to`/`resolves`/
`is-nit`/`required`/`sites`/`disposition`; kind-specific frontmatter for block/section/finding/question/
register; the absence-vs-empty-string convention (`base:` omitted vs `section: ` always present); and the
frontmatter edge-whitespace escape marker. Confirmed (`grep`) every `CardStore` write path calls
`CardFileWriter.Serialize` with no further transformation, so this is byte-identical to what the real CLI
writes.

**3. Determinability report.**

- **Status/owner/scope/kind** — plain English words (`building`, `worker`, `change`, `block`), each drawn
  from a small closed, per-kind vocabulary validated at parse time (`ValidateStatus`). No legend needed.
- **Full thread** — a comment's header is one line of `key=value` tokens: `author`, `to`, `reply-to`,
  `resolves`, `timestamp` read as plain words/ids. `is-nit=true`/`required=true` appear only as the literal
  word `true` and are **omitted, not written `false`**, when unset — a reader must already know that
  absence means false; the file states no legend.
- **History marker lines** — each of the seven families is one self-contained `<!-- callboard:… -->` line
  naming the acting role and the fields specific to that entry, plus a timestamp: who did what, when, in
  one line. **Except:** `claim`/`limit` text, `refusal` `rule`/`remedy`, and `authorisation` `reason` — the
  fields `CardFileFormat`'s own doc comment calls "sentences a later reviewer reads" — have **every space,
  not only an edge one**, written as the two characters `\s` (`CertificationTextEscapeForwardTable`,
  contrast `FrontmatterEscapeForwardTable`, which never touches an interior space). Confirmed live below: a
  real refusal on a real card reads `rule=work-lifecycle:\sblock\scards\smove\sthrough\sa\sdefined\sflow`.
  This is materially larger than the known edge-whitespace case — it hits **every** multi-word certification
  text unconditionally, not an edge case a hand-edit has to provoke. Reporting only, per scope.
- **Frontmatter edge whitespace** (known, re-confirmed live) — a value's leading/trailing space is written
  as `\s`; `title: Which retry policy applies?\s` on disk is not visually a trailing space, a plain
  question mark, or a documented convention on the wire itself.
- **Absence as meaning** — two conventions collide: `section:` is always present, empty when unset;
  `base:`/`closed_by:`/`answered_by:` etc. are omitted entirely when unset. Both read, to someone not told
  the rule, as "nothing here" — only one is discoverable by grepping for the key at all.
- **Wire strings** — every enum-backed value (kind, status, owner, scope, verdict, disposition, boolean
  flags) is a whole word or short hyphenated phrase, never a numeric or opaque code. Legible on its own.
- **History in HTML comments** — every marker line and every comment header/footer is an HTML comment.
  Raw text: fully visible (the binding reading, ADR-0003). **Any Markdown renderer: every marker line and
  every comment header/footer vanishes**, leaving only the comment bodies as unattributed paragraphs — no
  author, timestamp, addressee, or resolved-by survives. Under a renderer the "full thread determinable"
  property fails outright even though it holds under raw text. Reporting the consequence, not ruling it —
  the Product Owner's call per the brief.

**4. The recipe — captured from one continuous, unedited run.** Script:
`verify-13-9.sh` (pasted in full below the transcript; also left at the scratchpad path in my report).
Real `callboard` CLI (the `make build` DLL, no AOT publish, no binary rename — avoids 13.8's collision
shape entirely since nothing is ever copied to a path ending `callboard`), fresh scratch git repo, real
card ids and comment ids from the tool itself. It builds a full attributed thread (raise → reply → an
out-of-turn resolve that is itself refused → the correct resolve) and surfaces both live escape markers
(a certification-text refusal, a frontmatter title) without hand-authoring either.

**5. Two structural questions.**

- **What is the automation structurally unable to see?** (a) It can only assert presence of bytes — never
  subjective comprehension. I already know the `\s` convention from reading the source, so my own reading
  of the assertions is not a fresh reader's read; only a human meeting the raw file cold can say whether it
  is actually "determinable". (b) It cannot observe how a real editor or terminal renders the file — the
  claim under test is about bytes, but "determinable" is a claim about a human's comprehension of those
  bytes, which no `Assert.Contains` stands in for. (c) The enumeration is bounded by what I constructed —
  a future kind or field this cover does not exercise is invisible to it by construction.
- **What did I have to change in order to test at all?**
  1. **A stray VS Code Roslyn/MSBuild node-reuse process was holding an old `callboard.dll` open**
     (`dotnet build-server shutdown` fixed it) — `make build` failed with `CS2012: Access to the path ...
     is denied` before I touched any source. Not a workaround around anything this block tests, but it
     blocked every gate until diagnosed, so reported per the brief's "even ones that feel too small to
     mention".
  2. **The automated cover constructs `CardFile` values directly (test project's `InternalsVisibleTo`
     access) and calls `CardFileWriter.Serialize` directly**, rather than shelling out to the CLI for every
     fixture. Confirmed (`grep`) every `CardStore` write path calls `CardFileWriter.Serialize` with no
     further transformation, so the bytes are identical to production output — but the automated cover
     never goes through the CLI's own argument parsing or refusal doors. The live recipe (item 4) closes
     this specific gap for the cases it exercises.
  3. **The automated fixtures combine marker families onto one card in a shape a real workflow may never
     produce in one write** (a single Block card carrying a handover, a transition, a claim, a limit and a
     refusal at once) — chosen to keep the assertion count small, not a reproduction of an actual
     production sequence. The live recipe uses real, CLI-produced sequencing instead.
  4. **zsh does not word-split an unquoted `$VAR`** the way a bash-authored recipe assumes — my first draft
     used a `$CB` variable and failed with a confusing "no such file: dotnet /path --flags..." (the whole
     string treated as one filename), with nothing pointing at shell quoting as the cause. Fixed with a
     `cb()` shell function instead, and the delivered script is plain `sh` rather than bash/zsh-specific.
     Naming it because a recipe that runs cleanly in the agent's shell and silently breaks in a
     differently-configured one is exactly 13.8's binary-name-collision shape — a workaround that fixes
     and could otherwise hide a portability gap the recipe doesn't itself test for.
  5. **Comment ids are tool-generated GUID-suffixed strings, not stable across runs** — the script parses
     `commentId` back out of the JSON with `sed` rather than a hard-coded id; discovered only by running
     the script once and watching a hard-coded id refuse as `reply-to-not-found`.

green) `FORMAT_EXIT:0` `VALIDATE_EXIT:0` `GATES_EXIT:0`.

#!/bin/sh
# 13.9 verification recipe. Run from the repository root after `make build`.
# Requires: dotnet, git. Writes into a throwaway directory under /private/tmp; nothing here touches
# the repository itself.
set -e

BOARD_DLL="$(pwd)/src/Callboard/bin/Release/net10.0/Callboard.dll"
if [ ! -f "$BOARD_DLL" ]; then
  echo "Build first: make build" >&2
  exit 1
fi
cb() { dotnet "$BOARD_DLL" "$@"; }

SCRATCH="/private/tmp/cb-verify-13-9-$$"
rm -rf "$SCRATCH"
mkdir -p "$SCRATCH"
cd "$SCRATCH"
git init -q

echo "== Step 1: create a block card =="
printf '%s\n' "Implements the read-half determinability check." | \
  cb block create callboard/changes/establish-callboard/B-0099.md \
    --title "Wire a retry budget" --role architect --change establish-callboard --task 13.9

echo
echo "== Step 2: a refusal (undefined transition) =="
cb block transition callboard/changes/establish-callboard/B-0099.md build --role worker --change establish-callboard || true

echo
echo "== Step 3: brief it (records base), then a role tries an out-of-turn transition (second refusal) =="
cb block transition callboard/changes/establish-callboard/B-0099.md brief --role architect --base f100b77 --change establish-callboard
cb block transition callboard/changes/establish-callboard/B-0099.md claim --role worker --change establish-callboard

echo
echo "== Step 4: a comment thread — raised, replied, then resolved by a different role (a third refusal along the way) =="
FIRST_COMMENT_JSON="$(printf '%s\n' "Four readers still discard the parse failure with onFailure: static _ => null." | \
  cb comment add --id B-0001 --role reviewer --to architect --change establish-callboard)"
echo "$FIRST_COMMENT_JSON"
FIRST_COMMENT_ID="$(printf '%s' "$FIRST_COMMENT_JSON" | sed -n 's/.*"commentId":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p')"
printf '%s\n' "Fixed in the same commit; four readers now report a count and a path." | \
  cb comment add --id B-0001 --role architect --to reviewer --reply-to "$FIRST_COMMENT_ID" --change establish-callboard
printf '%s\n' "Confirmed against the diff; closing the thread." | \
  cb comment resolve --id B-0001 --comment-id "$FIRST_COMMENT_ID" --role reviewer --change establish-callboard || true
printf '%s\n' "Confirmed against the diff; closing the thread." | \
  cb comment resolve --id B-0001 --comment-id "$FIRST_COMMENT_ID" --role architect --change establish-callboard

echo
echo "== Step 5: a question card with a title that has a trailing space =="
printf '%s\n' "Fixed backoff, three attempts." | \
  cb question create callboard/register/Q-0001.md --title "Which retry policy applies? " --role architect --owed-by product-owner

echo
echo "=================================================================="
echo "RAW FILE — callboard/changes/establish-callboard/B-0099.md"
echo "=================================================================="
cat callboard/changes/establish-callboard/B-0099.md

echo
echo "=================================================================="
echo "RAW FILE — callboard/register/Q-0001.md"
echo "=================================================================="
cat callboard/register/Q-0001.md

echo
echo "=================================================================="
echo "TOOL'S OWN READING — for cross-check only, read this AFTER you have"
echo "written down your own answers from the raw files above"

echo "--- card show B-0001 ---"
cb card show B-0001
echo
echo "--- state ---"

(HTML-safe) encoder applies. A byte-faithful fresh run of the pasted script prints, for step 2's refusal:

plain apostrophes and plain `+` — not what the script's own `cb() { dotnet "$BOARD_DLL" "$@"; }`

Whatever produced the unescaped pasted text — reformatting through `jq`/`python -m json.tool`/manual

**Consequence, scoped precisely — not a reason to distrust the finding itself.** The **RAW FILE**
sections (the two card files, the actual artifact ADR-0003 binds — "opens one file") are not JSON and
touch no `JsonSerializerOptions` at all; `CardFileWriter` writes `\s`/`\n`/`\r`/`\\` via its own
`CardFileFormat` escape tables, unrelated to the JSON encoder question. I diffed a fresh run's two raw
files against the pasted ones (only ids/timestamps differ) and they match byte-for-byte in every
character that matters to the determinability question, including both `\s` markers (the

them. **13.9 did its job by failing.** The escaping is structural, not gratuitous — the marker line is
`key=value` tokens joined by single spaces on one physical line, so an unescaped space splits a value and
`" -->"` ends the comment early. The structure is what has to move, not the escaper.

**The shape, and it is the Product Owner's design.** She proposed carrying the values inside the delimited
block rather than in its opening line, and asked whether the frontmatter convention could serve. **Her
premise contained one error and the idea survived it intact.** There is no YAML parser in this project —
ADR-0003 took the "hand-rolled against a deliberately narrow schema" branch, and adopting a real library
now would need an AOT check under ADR-0002 and would buy generality we deliberately refused. But the
frontmatter *convention* is exactly right, and better than the YAML framing suggested: **`3eacc1f` left it
escaping only edge whitespace**, so interior spaces are already literal. Reusing that line shape does not
merely unify two conventions into one — **it inherits readable prose for free, with no new table.** The
per-family key sets (`KnownRefusalKeys`, `KnownClaimKeys`, `KnownAuthorisationKeys` and their siblings)
already exist; what changes is the line shape those keys are read from, not the schema machinery.

```
<!-- callboard:refusal
by: worker
rule: work-lifecycle: block cards move through a defined flow
remedy: call one of the transitions available from 'drafting': brief.
timestamp: 2026-08-31T10:23:29.5248310+00:00
-->
```

The whole block stays **one** HTML comment, so the machinery remains hidden in a rendered view exactly as
today. Whether history *should* be visible when rendered is a real question — every marker line and every
comment's attribution currently vanishes in any Markdown renderer — but it is a bigger one than an
escaping fix, and it does not ride in on this. **Parked, deliberately.** She also ruled the comment block
comes onto the same syntax (14.4): its header becomes a block in the new shape, its prose body and footer
stay, so a comment body still renders.

### Ruled: `-->` in free text is escaped, not refused *(Product Owner)*

**And the obvious implementation would undo what §14 is for.** The escape tables are char-keyed, so
`['>'] = "\\>"` escapes *every* `>` — the card she read contains `onFailure: static _ => null`, which
would become `_ =\> null`. We would have retired `\s` and minted `=\>`. Escaping `-` mauls every
hyphenated word. **So: a composed step firing only on the literal three characters `-->`, mapping them to
`\->`.** Precedent is `EscapeEdgeSpaces`, which is already a composed non-table step in the same pipeline
(`EscapeUsing`→`EscapeEdgeSpaces`→join). Invertible because the backslash doubles first: a value genuinely
containing `\->` serialises as `\\->` and cannot be read back as an escaped terminator. Ordinary prose is
untouched.

**Plus the structural half, which is what makes it fail safely:** the parser requires the close to be a
line *exactly equal to* `-->`. A hand-written card carrying an unescaped `-->` then fails loudly instead
of silently truncating the block — §13.6's rule that a card which will not parse beats one that parses
wrongly, applied to the syntax that replaces it.

**A correction I am recording rather than leaving in the thread.** I told the Product Owner this shape
would let `\n` stop being escaped. **Wrong** — that was true of the body-block form I proposed first, not
of the one we settled on. With one field per line a value still cannot carry a raw newline, so `\n`
escaping stays. It buys readable spaces, not free line breaks. Comment *bodies* need none of this: they
sit outside the delimiters and `EscapeContentLine` already handles a body line that mimics a structural
one.

### The renumbering, and the sequencing that forced it

The Product Owner ruled 13.9 ticks only **after** the fix. But the outer loop requires §13 to carry a
supervisor `Approve` before §14 opens, and 13.9 sits in §13 — so §13 could never close. Separately,
**13.10 documents the agent-facing command surface, and 14.5 changes how every creation verb takes a
path**, so 13.10 would have documented a surface already scheduled to move. Both dissolve the same way:
the two unbuilt tasks move into §14, each now following the thing it depends on. **This is §13's third
renumbering.** It is ugly and it is the only ordering in which the verification runs after what it
verifies and the documentation is written after the surface settles.

**Spec amendments** (`VALIDATE_EXIT:0`):

- **`record-retrieval`, "The record is legible without the tool"** — text written to be read as sentences
  SHALL be presented as sentences, and a reader SHALL NOT have to decode an escape convention to read
  prose the system wrote for them; the record's structured metadata SHALL share one delimited block syntax
  rather than one per kind. Two scenarios: *Recorded prose reads as prose*, *One syntax across the record*.
  **This is what makes 14.6 checkable** — 13.9 had no requirement it could fail against, only a reader's
  judgement.
- **`card-model`, "Stable, human-quotable, kind-prefixed identity"** — a card's file SHALL be named for its
  identity; the system names the file when it mints the identity, and a caller names the container, never
  the file. Scenario: *The file is named for the card*. **Structural, not a check**: `AnchoredCardPath`
  already proves a card's *directory*, and leaves the basename free — which is why `B-0099.md` holds
  `B-0001`. The caller stops being able to express a wrong name, the same shape as the directory fix.

on this file. So neither change needs a data migration. Test fixtures and the wire-compatibility corpus
move; nothing on disk does.

**Not written into 14.1: how many block families there are.** My count is seven and it is unverified. §13's
standing ruling is that an enumeration is worth exactly what the re-derivation behind it is worth, and this
one has not been re-derived. The worker derives it from `CardFileWriter` and `CardFileParser`.

### Blocker — `base` has two doors and neither is the one the amendment named

The amendment `a32f481` declares **exactly two doors** mint a `block` card. 13.1 and 13.3 were built to
one of them. The other was never checked against "Blocks carry their brief context", and the two doors
now produce block cards with different capabilities.

**Half 1 — the remediation door mints a card that can never carry a `base`, and 13.3's door refuses it.**

- `CardStore.cs:2688-2691` (§8a, pre-existing, but named as door two by the amendment in this range)
  creates a first-time-finding remediation block through `WriteCard` at `BlockFlowState.Briefed` with
  `new BlockCardFields(null, null, [], 1, [], [], newFinding.Key)` — `Base` is the first `null`.
- It is a `WriteCard`, not a transition, so it never passes the `transition.To == Briefed && effectiveBase
  is null` guard at `CardStore.cs:626-630`. `BaseNotRecorded` cannot fire on this path.
- `block base` (13.3) then refuses that card for the rest of its life: `CardStore.cs:1638` returns
  `NotAtDrafting`, rule text *"base is recorded only while a block is at 'drafting'"*.

So a supervisor's remediation block runs `briefed → building → in-review → approved → landed` and closes
its section with `base` unset, and the door the spec provides for recording it refuses it by construction.
That is the card whose base matters most — a section remediation is carved against the section's own base,
which is the range its reviewer will read. `specs/work-lifecycle/spec.md:99-107` says a `block` card SHALL
carry the `base` commit its brief was carved against; for one of the two doors, nothing can put it there.

**Half 2 — `block transition --base` is still an undeclared first-recording door, and it is the only
route left open to a door-two card.**

`CardStore.cs:619-625`: `effectiveBase = recordedBase ?? baseCommit`, written at
`CardStore.cs:687`. The refusal above it fires only on a **mismatch**, so a `--base` on *any* edge
first-records a base on a card that has none — at `briefed`, `building`, `in-review`, `approved`.
13.3's reviewer compared the two verbs' mismatch conditions and made them agree (`CardStore.cs:1640` vs
`619-620`, byte-identical, correctly). Nobody compared their **first-record** conditions, because that
divergence is only visible from door two: `block base` refuses a briefed card, and `block transition
--base` records on it silently, unattributed as a base-recording act. Same condition, two answers — the
shape §13's own brief asked me to look hardest for, in the write paths rather than the read paths.

**❓ @architect — this is arguably the amendment's gap rather than the code's, and the choice is not
mine.** Three shapes close it and they are not equivalent:

1. Door two records the section card's own base at creation (`CardStore.cs:2691`), and `block transition
   --base` stops being able to first-record — it carries forward or refuses, never introduces.
2. `block base` permits a `briefed` block whose `base` is unset (first-record anywhere, change nowhere),

3. The spec says a remediation card carries no base, and `work-lifecycle` says so explicitly rather than

I would take (1): it is the only one where the recorded value is actually the commit the brief was carved
against, and it removes the second door rather than blessing it. But the amendment is the Product
Owner's and so is this call.

**Remediation shape.** One block: whichever of the three above is ruled, plus (a) a test that a door-two

### The fix

**Door two records `Base` at creation, and the value is the verdict's `RangeTo`.**

Not the section's base — the supervisor proposed that and I am overruling it. `base` means *the commit
this brief was carved against*, and a remediation brief is carved against **what the supervisor actually
reviewed**, which `SectionVerdictEntry.RangeTo` documents as "`HEAD` at the time this verdict was
recorded". The section's base is where the section *began*; using it would hand the block's reviewer a
diff spanning every block in the section instead of the remediation. **The value is already in hand at
the call site** — no new CLI argument, no spec change.

Confirm for yourself that `RangeTo` is populated and non-empty on every path that reaches `:2688` before
you rely on it. `SectionVerdictEntry` says a range endpoint is never empty; verify that guarantee reaches
this call site rather than assuming it.

### The dismissal — verify it, and stop if it does not hold

The supervisor also reported that `block transition --base` **first-records** a base on any edge at any
state (`effectiveBase = recordedBase ?? baseCommit`, `CardStore.cs:625`, with the refusal above it firing
only on a *mismatch*), and called it the same condition with two answers. **I have dismissed that as
downstream of the defect above, and my dismissal rests on one claim I have not proved:**

> The only way for a card to be past `drafting` without a base is door two, because **from `drafting` the
> only available transition is `brief`** — so first-recording via a transition only ever happens on the
> edge into `briefed`, which is legitimate and is what `BaseNotRecorded` guards.

**Verify that from `BlockFlowTransitions`, not from this post.** If `drafting` has any other outgoing
edge, or if any edge into a non-`briefed` state can be taken by a card carrying no base, then my
dismissal is wrong, half two is independently reachable, and it needs its own answer — **stop and report
rather than inventing one.** This is exactly the §13 standing ruling: an enumeration or a reachability
claim is worth what the independent re-derivation behind it is worth, and reviewing one by inspection
launders it.

If the claim holds, **add no refusal for half two.** §9's coverage gate will not accept a case that
cannot be provoked, and an unreachable arm added for symmetry is precisely what that gate exists to
reject. The invariant becoming true again *is* the fix.

### On `range-to` versus the section base — you were right and I was wrong, and it is worth saying why

I reasoned from the wrong end. I took `base` to mean "the range this card's review reads" and reached
for the section base because that is what a *section* review reads. But the field's own definition is the
commit **a brief was carved against**, and a remediation brief is carved against what the supervisor
actually reviewed — `SectionVerdictEntry.RangeTo`, "HEAD at the time this verdict was recorded". Your
value is the correct one and mine would have been actively harmful: `base..HEAD` on a section-based
remediation card hands that block's *reviewer* a diff spanning every block in the section, which is the
precise failure the block/section split exists to prevent. It also degrades per round — a third-round
remediation would carry the same base as a first-round one, so the field would stop discriminating
exactly where discrimination matters. `range-to` gives each verdict's card its own base. Take it.

**And it closes half two as a consequence, which is the part I want on the record.** With `Base` non-null
at creation, a `block transition --base` against a door-two card no longer falls through
`recordedBase ?? baseCommit` — it meets the mismatch check at `CardStore.cs:619-620` and refuses with
`BaseImmutable`, the same answer `block base` gives. The "same condition, two answers" asymmetry is gone
because the condition that produced the second answer no longer exists, not because a second refusal was
bolted on. That is the better fix and I would not have got there from my own recommendation.

**[architect]** **Brief — block one, `14.1–14.3`.** The syntax, its termination, and the `-->` escape. One
deliverable: after this block every structured metadata block in a card file is delimited and fielded the
same way, and the prose inside it reads as prose. `14.4` (the comment block onto the same syntax) and
`14.5` (the filename) are **not** in this block; do not pull them in.

### The tasks

- **14.1** Adopt one delimited block syntax for every structured metadata block, failing loudly on an
  unterminated block.
- **14.2** Carry each block's fields as `key: value` lines, reusing the frontmatter line shape and escaper.
- **14.3** Escape a literal `-->` in free text as a composed step, leaving ordinary prose untouched.

### What this is for — the field report that caused the amendment

The Product Owner ran 13.9's recipe, opened `B-0099.md` in an editor, and read a recorded refusal as
`rule=work-lifecycle:\sblock\scards\smove\sthrough\sa\sdefined\sflow`. Her word was *horrible*. **The
escaping is structural, not gratuitous** — a marker line is `key=value` tokens joined by single spaces on
one physical line, so an unescaped space splits a value and a literal `" -->"` ends the comment early.
**The structure is what moves, not the escaper.**

### The spec it is built to — `record-retrieval`, "The record is legible without the tool"

> Where the record carries text written to be read as sentences — a refusal's rule and remedy, a
> certification's claims and limits, an authorisation's reason — the record SHALL present it as sentences.
> A reader SHALL NOT have to decode an escape convention to read prose the system wrote for them.
>
> The record's structured metadata SHALL share one delimited block syntax rather than a syntax per kind of
> entry, so that a reader who has learnt to read one entry can read them all.

> #### Scenario: Recorded prose reads as prose
> - **WHEN** a reader opens a card carrying a recorded refusal, certification or authorisation
> - **THEN** its sentences read as ordinary text, with no escape marker standing in for an ordinary space
>
> #### Scenario: One syntax across the record
> - **WHEN** a reader encounters any of the record's structured metadata blocks
> - **THEN** every such block is delimited and fielded the same way, whatever it records

Note the second scenario's reach: **"every such block", not "every block this task remembers to change"**.
The set is whatever `CardFileFormat`, `CardFileWriter` and `CardFileParser` actually carry, minus the
comment header, which `14.4` brings on next.

### The design — settled, and the Product Owner's

One HTML comment per block. The opening line names the family; each field is its own line; the close is a
line **exactly equal to** `-->`:

```
<!-- callboard:refusal
by: worker
rule: work-lifecycle: block cards move through a defined flow
remedy: call one of the transitions available from 'drafting': brief.
timestamp: 2026-08-31T10:23:29.5248310+00:00
-->
```

Binding points, each with its reason:

1. **The whole block stays one HTML comment**, so the machinery remains hidden in a rendered view exactly
   as today. Whether history *should* render is a real question and a bigger one; it is **parked** and does
   not ride in on this.
2. **Reuse the frontmatter line shape and its escaper.** There is no YAML parser here and there will not
   be one — ADR-0003 took the hand-rolled-against-a-narrow-schema branch, and a library would need an AOT
   check under ADR-0002 for generality we deliberately refused. Since `3eacc1f` the frontmatter escaper
   escapes only **edge** whitespace, so interior spaces are already literal: reusing it **inherits readable
   prose for free, with no new table**. That is the point of the task, not an implementation detail.
3. **The per-family key sets already exist** (`KnownRefusalKeys`, `KnownClaimKeys`,
   `KnownAuthorisationKeys` and their siblings). **What changes is the line shape those keys are read
   from, not the schema machinery.** If you find yourself rewriting the key sets, stop and post.
4. **`\n` stays escaped.** With one field per line a value still cannot carry a raw newline. This buys
   readable spaces, not free line breaks — I told the Product Owner otherwise once and it was wrong of me.
5. **The unterminated block fails loudly** (14.1's second half). Requiring the close to be a line exactly
   equal to `-->` is what makes a hand-written card carrying a stray `-->` fail to parse instead of
   silently truncating — **§13.6's rule that a card which will not parse beats one that parses wrongly**,
   applied to the syntax replacing it. A truncation that reads back as a valid shorter block is the
   failure mode to write a test against.

### 14.3 — and the obvious implementation that would undo §14

The escape tables are char-keyed, so `['>'] = "\\>"` escapes **every** `>`. The very card she read contains
`onFailure: static _ => null`, which would come back as `_ =\> null` — we would have retired `\s` and
minted `=\>`. Keying on `-` mauls every hyphenated word.

**So: a composed step firing only on the literal three characters `-->`, mapping them to `\->`.** Precedent
is `EscapeEdgeSpaces`, already a composed non-table step in the same pipeline
(`EscapeUsing` → `EscapeEdgeSpaces` → join). It is invertible **because the backslash doubles first**: a
value genuinely containing `\->` serialises as `\\->` and cannot be read back as an escaped terminator.
Order matters; assert it. Ordinary prose is untouched, and a test that proves that on real prose — `=>`,
hyphens, an arrow in a sentence — is worth more than one that proves the mapping.

### Things I am deliberately not telling you

- **How many block families there are.** My count is unverified, and §13's standing ruling is that an
  enumeration is worth exactly what the re-derivation behind it is worth. **Derive the set** from
  `CardFileFormat`, `CardFileWriter` and `CardFileParser`, state it in your report, and say how you
  derived it.
- **Which tests move.** `CardFileWireCompatibilityCorpusTests`, `CardFileRoundTripTests`,
  `CardFileParserBlankLineTests` and `CardFileRawTextLegibilityTests` are the ones I know touch this
  syntax; there will be others, and the suite will tell you. **No data migration is owed** — no
  `callboard/` board is committed, so fixtures and the corpus move and nothing on disk does.

### Standing rulings that bind this block

- **A regression test nobody has watched fail is a guess** (§13 ruling 5). If you name a test as a
  regression guard, watch it fail against the old behaviour and say so — the auditors cannot revert source

- **Every write goes through the hand-entered-state guard at its call site** (§10, call site 34).
- **Refusals name their remedy as a command that exists** (§9 ruling 3), and name the route by verb
  (§13.3).

**Blocker — old wire forms now silently misparse instead of failing (`CardFileParser.cs:423-428`,
`CardFileFormat.cs:154-180`).**

Item 6 of my brief asked specifically whether anything now silently misparses an old form rather than
failing on it, "a different and worse outcome than dropping it." It does. Ran this, not reasoned it:
copied the tree to a scratch directory (untouched, no patch this time) and fed the parser a card whose
body is followed by exactly the *pre-14.1* single-line transition marker
(`<!-- callboard:transition by=architect name=brief from=drafting to=briefed timestamp=... -->`, the
form `CardFileWireCompatibilityCorpusTests.cs` held until this diff removed it). Result: **parse
succeeds**, `Transitions.Count == 0`, and the entire transition line is silently absorbed into
`CardFile.Body` as ordinary prose. No error, no unknown-field record, no trace that a transition was
ever recorded — it just becomes text.

The mechanism: pre-diff, `IsTransitionLine` (and its five siblings) matched on
`StartsWith(prefix) && EndsWith(suffix)`, so any well-formed single-line marker — old or new shape —
was recognised as *a transition* and either parsed or explicitly failed on its fields. Post-diff,
`IsTransitionLine` requires the line to *exactly equal* `TransitionOpenLine` (`"<!-- callboard:transition"`,
no trailing content) — correct for 14.1's own unterminated-block requirement, but it means a line that
merely *starts with* that prefix and carries anything else no longer registers as a transition open line
at all. The body loop (`CardFileParser.cs:424`) doesn't stop on it, doesn't fail on it — it just keeps
reading it as body content, because `EscapeContentLine`/`UnescapeContentLine`'s own
`LooksLikeDelimiterOrEscapedDelimiter` check (which *does* use `StartsWith`, correctly, for the
write-side escaping hazard) is never consulted on the read side for this decision. The same failure mode
applies to all seven families symmetrically — I re-derived this from the shared `ParseBlockFieldLines`/
`Is*Line` structure rather than re-running all seven, but the transition case is a full, ran repro, and
the code path is identical for the other six.

This is squarely §13.6's rule turned against itself: "a card which will not parse beats one that parses
wrongly" is exactly what's violated here, and worse than the brief's own example — this doesn't even
raise a checkable "unknown field," it disappears the entry into indistinguishable prose. The
`CardFileWireCompatibilityCorpusTests.cs` flag correctly named that O-4's specific fixture-permanence
requirement was being waived by brief authorisation ("no `callboard/` board is committed") — but O-4's
waiver is not the same guarantee as "the parser fails safely on what it no longer emits," and that second
property is what item 6 was checking for. It does not hold.

This needs a fix before `Approve`: either the seven `Is*Line` checks (or a line that reaches the body/
comment loops looking like one of the seven prefixes but isn't an exact match) need to refuse rather than
fall through to body content, or the block-open-line detection needs a narrower, deliberate rule that a
prefix-matching-but-not-exactly-matching line is a parse failure, not silently-ignorable prose. I'd
favour the former — it's the same shape 14.1 already gave the *unterminated* case, applied to the
*malformed-open-line* case, and it protects against more than just the old wire form: any hand-edit that
almost-but-not-quite matches an open line (trailing whitespace, a stray character) currently vanishes the
same way with no signal at all.

therefore structural, not merely sequenced correctly: there is no way for an escaped line to reach the new
check and be misidentified, regardless of where the check sits in the loop.

### What the section review caught that no block review could

**Door two of block-card creation minted a card at `briefed` with `Base = null`.** Both doors came from the
same amendment; only one was ever checked against "Blocks carry their brief context". Being a write and not
a transition, door two never met the `BaseNotRecorded` guard, and `block base` then refused it permanently
for not being at `drafting` — so a supervisor's own remediation block could run to `landed` with no base,
and the one door the spec provides for recording it was closed by construction. **The comment at
`CardStore.cs:1630` justified that refusal with an invariant door two was the sole counterexample to.**

Three rulings came out of it:

1. **A door added by an amendment must be checked against every requirement the door it parallels already
   satisfies.** Two doors, one requirement, one door checked.
2. **The absence of a test is the finding.** Nothing asserted a door-two card's `base` at all, which is why
   three block reviews and a section's worth of gates never saw it.
3. **Fixing the cause can retire the symmetry rather than requiring a refusal for it.** The supervisor's
   second finding — `block transition --base` first-recording on any edge — needed no code: with `Base`
   non-null at creation, that path now meets the mismatch check and refuses `BaseImmutable`, the same
   answer `block base` gives. §9's coverage gate would have rejected an arm for an unprovokable case, and
   the Architect's dismissal was re-derived from `BlockFlowTransitions` twice — by the worker and again by
   the reviewer — rather than taken on the brief's word.

**And the supervisor reversed itself on the record.** It recommended door two carry the *section's* base;
the Architect overruled it in favour of the verdict's `range-to`, and it came back agreeing and said why its
own answer was worse: `base..HEAD` on a section-based card hands that block's reviewer a diff spanning the
whole section, and the value would stop discriminating between rounds exactly where that matters. **An
overrule put back to the auditor in writing is how that got said out loud instead of settling silently.**

**unconditionally**. It is now true of every card the tool mints, and false of a hand-authored one — which
the amendment concedes exists, and which `block transition --base` will still first-record for, correctly,
since refusing would leave it no route at all. **One clause: "every card the tool mints".** Same standard
the remediation block invoked when it corrected that very comment. **14.5 touches this file** — take it
there. Precedent for parking a wording correction this way: the escape remediation's own owed note above.

### ~~`card-id-unresolvable` reports the wrong thing~~ — **fixed in `d484003` (13.6)**

A corrupt card addressed by id reports **`card-id-unresolvable`** — the tool saying *I could not find that
card* when the truth is *I found it and it is corrupt*. An agent told the id does not resolve hunts for a
typo; an agent told the card is corrupt reads the file. **Wrong-remedy, not wrong-verdict.**

`CardIdentityResolver` and `NitResolver` already carry an `Unreadable` case distinct from `NotFound`; the
resolver loop discards the parse-failure reason (`onFailure: static _ => null`), keeping only the path. It
can already name *which file* and needs only to stop throwing away *why*. **10 of the 19 `onCardCorrupt`
arms are unreachable** because of this, **`block approve --id` included**, and the shared
`ResolveRuleCompactOutcome` arm is unreachable via *both* callers.

## Rulings from §13

1. **A spec that states only its refusals leaves the permitted case to inference, and inference diverges**
   *(Product Owner)*. My amendment's scenario said "records against a block that already has one →
   refuses" while its own prose said "SHALL NOT **change**", twice. Two verbs sharing the `base-immutable`
   code diverged on exactly that gap. The requirement now carries **two** scenarios — the refusal *and*
   the permitted resupply. **Write the permitted case down.**
2. **The callers of this tool are agents, and an agent that cannot tell whether its call landed must be
   able to ask again without being punished for asking.** Under the old reading a retry both failed and
   left a permanently recorded refusal indistinguishable from a real attempted overwrite. **This is a
   property to audit the whole CLI against, not a fact about `block base`.**
3. **Confirming a negative across a live tree must distinguish *gone* from *unreadable*.** 13.1's scan
   folded a file that vanished between enumeration and open into the same bucket as a corrupt one, failing
   an unrelated legitimate allocation 2 runs in 3. A vanished file bears no identity; a file that exists
   and will not parse still fails shut. D7's atomic rename is what makes existence the only racing fact.
4. **A queue item's premise decays and must be re-checked at briefing time.** Both of this file's §13
   premises were wrong: "nothing records `base`" (`block transition --base` had shipped since §5), and
   "`comment add` makes the §11 defect reachable" (`comment resolve` had made it reachable in §9). Neither
   was harmful, because both were checked. **Verify the premise, then brief.**
5. **A regression test nobody has watched fail is a guess** — and a *report* of having watched it fail is
   still a report. 13.1's fix was verified 3/3 against the old code; the referent block's reviewer went
   further and reproduced the defect from first principles against the real binary in a scratch repo
   rather than accepting the worker's account of an xunit message.

  would block `RefuseAndRecord` writing its own refusal. Correct today across all 33 sites; regresses
  silently the moment someone adds an unguarded write. Fix: **a fifteen-line source-scan gate** — converts
  a discipline into a mechanism.
- The budget requirement says "which of the two" while `DescribeOverageDriver`
  (`CommandDispatcher.cs:4098-4118`) has a **third** label; `WorkingContextBudget.Statement` does not state
  the sanctioned overage.
- **A halted top item leaves the role no stated next move.**
- **`question defer` is a strictly weaker verb than it reads** — after §10's ruling 2 it postpones an
  answer without lifting anything.
- Three outcome types carry no `HandEnteredDerivedState` case on verified structural grounds, documented in
  code rather than in `RefusalCoverageGateTests.Exclusions`.
- `CardCommentPromoteTests` has no direct unaddressed-thread assertion; `RoleNotPermitted.Remedy` is
  duplicated across two outcome types; `queueOrder`/`constraintsRule` tests assert non-empty rather than
  exact prose.
- **`state` is deliberately unbounded** — the spec budgets the working-context response, not this one.

### From §7

**A.** The writer/parser wire-key guard (`CardFrontmatter`, `BlockCardFields`, `SectionCardFields`,
`FindingCardFields` lack a shared key declaration). §12 added no persisted field, so this is untouched.
**E.** Attribution assertions should root on a non-default role. **H.** Repository-scoped compaction has no
closing move.

### `IndexPopulator.cs:249` — still with no reader

§9 handed this to §10 as "the first reader of the column"; §10's ruling 1 means nothing reads the index, so
the section card's `section = ''` row still has no reader and no forcing function. If the flat form is
wanted, the column populates **from `CardStore.OwningSectionId`**, never as a second source of truth.

---

## Rulings that bind §13

**From §12**

1. **A column is a flow state, not a card kind** *(Product Owner)*. Register cards SHALL NOT occupy flow
   states, so they are an area, not a lane. **An empty column renders** — an empty column is information.
2. **Reachability is owned by whoever created it, not by whoever wrote the line.** Block A's parse door
   made old code newly reachable, and the envelope fix (nineteen sites, older than the block, spanning
   closed sections' handlers) landed with it on exactly that argument. The supervisor then turned the same
   argument back on the Architect for the silent droppers, correctly.
3. **A fail-open on record fidelity is distinct from a fail-open on enforcement**, and reads as far more
   benign. Nothing is wrongly permitted; the tool is merely **confidently wrong**, and no reader can tell
   by looking. §12 found it in six readers at once.
4. **Homing is not parking.** A finding routed to a task that names it, in a still-open section, with its
   sites enumerated and its reachability argued, is scheduled work. Parking is a note with no task.
5. **A verification recipe can satisfy the paperwork and not the task.** Block B's first recipe would have
   rendered the Product Owner an *empty* board while asking her to confirm lanes, grouping, annotations and
   shading. Same shape as §11's "a test can cover a content class and still not cover the thing that makes
   it content".
6. **An ambiguous spec is the Product Owner's call, not the implementer's** — even when the implementer's
   reading is sound and documented in a doc comment. Block B ruled "column" itself; the ruling came back
   the other way.

**From §11**

1. **A default query is a read that returns a set of cards the caller neither named nor scoped to a named
   container.** `context` and `state` are; `card show`, `section export`, `change export` and
   `section status` are not.
2. **The export is complete with respect to reference-closure and content classes; `card show` is complete
   with respect to the record.** **Owed wording, still owed:** "emits anything another emitted element
   refers to" is not literally satisfiable — the renderer emits nine id-shaped referents a scoped export
   will not contain. The distinction to write in: **a comment id is document-local, so withholding it
   withholds the only handle; a card id is globally resolvable, so naming it is a citation.**
3. **A verification task that reads as a check on an implementation task may be its specification.**
4. **A test can cover a content class and still not cover the thing that makes it content.**

**From §10**

1. **The read paths read card files, not the index.** Settled on evidence (block B's corpus measurement).
2. **Not answering a question is itself a halting state** *(Product Owner)*. "Closed" for a question means
   **answered and nothing else**. **A tool that reports a card halted and then lets it advance is
   describing a state it does not enforce.**
3. **A thread is disposed of by its addressee or the card's owner; `comment resolve` requires a body**
   *(Product Owner)*.
4. **Where the spec and shipped behaviour contradict, one of them moves — deliberately, and the Product
   Owner decides which.** §12's worked example is the largest yet: the missing creation verbs are a **spec
   amendment**, not a code fix.
5. **Part 4's "nothing else" bounds how many parts a response has, not what "in full" means inside one.**

**From §9**

1. **A refusal records when it asserts something about the record; it reports without recording when it
   asserts only that the invocation was malformed.** See the §12 parked item — this now has an unwritten
   exception.
2. **The coverage gate is the standard, not the brief.** Known limit: **CLI-layer refusals are outside its
   domain** — §12 worked there for the nineteen-site envelope fix and tested them directly.
3. **A refusal must name its remedy as a command that exists.**
4. **Moving a standard mid-section obliges a sweep back over what has landed.** §12's worked example: the
   `InvalidStatus` deletions went from four to six because the coverage gate's bijection would not accept a
   case that could not be provoked — and the sweep, not the count, is what made it a standard.

---

## The DEVLOG's own anchor — and the mechanism it still lacks

Every splice in §12 used `^## NEXT$` and verified afterwards that exactly one match remained in final
position, and every agent reported `--numstat` as added/0. **§11 is where the hazard fired** — a reviewer
pasted an unrelated file's contents into this file in place of its post, then removed them.

**Append-only is not the property that needs a mechanism** — `--numstat` catches the failure that did not
happen. What §13 owes is a check on the **shape of what was appended**: that the splice landed one
attributed post and nothing else. The naive substring match on `## NEXT` remains the other trap. Both are
still prose discipline in every agent prompt.
